The fixes:

  • Mud: a left-hand note that makes a close interval below its limit with the pedal or another left-hand note moves up an octave. The limits are an arranger’s rule of thumb; the roughness model only ranks the intervals.
  • The tune on top: verse 4’s chords stay strictly under the unison tune. That restores the second edition’s rule (749.8), which the third edition had relaxed for fuller voicings, and both checks now agree.

Roughness (Sethares, six harmonics) is unchanged across the editions: a mean of 0.57 a slice. Semitone clashes are 20 eighths, against 18 in the third edition and 28 in the second.

Each sung line lasted about 8.2 seconds at ♩ = 88 (median of 19 lines), just over the 8-second limit of short-term memory for a phrase. At the writer’s choice, the tempo is now ♩ = 92 (“gently rocking” still), and a line lasts 7.8 seconds.

Consistency: 62 of 62 checks pass, with new ones for the low intervals, the tune on top and no choir crossings.

Brought to Luthier’s own limits (Module 9.14). Luthier v7 already holds these voice-leading rules (Huron 2001), with stricter low-interval limits than the first sketch here: no third below F3 and no second below C4. Measured by them, the organ broke the limits at 117 places, mostly the pedal doubling the choir’s basses at pitch, with the left hand a third above it. The fixes:

  • The pedal in its own octave: the pedal is now written there (C2 to D3), sounding an octave lower again on the 16′ stops.
  • The link’s left hand: now open fifths.
  • Voicings: verse 4’s voicings are chosen clear of the limits.
  • The rest: any remaining close pair is settled by moving the left-hand note an octave, or by thinning an inner chord. The pedal never moves.

Violations: 0. The tune is on top at 99.2% of sung onsets. 99% of the sopranos’ and altos’ notes still sound in the organ, and every bass note sounds in the pedal at the octave. Clashes are 20 eighths, with no outer parallels. All 62 checks pass.

Findings

749.11 A hymn needs a hymn mode and hymn tables

Problem. The engine has no strophic mode: one tune for every stanza, the rhythm’s frame set by the stanza’s meter (here Common Meter, iambic), stressed syllables on downbeats. And the Essen folk tables do not describe hymn tunes: in a hymn frame every bar is one of three rhythms.

Evidence. Song 53’s sketch built the frame by hand and drew inside it. Every survivor’s distinct rhythms over bars sat under the kept 3/4 range (the pick 16%, kept 35% to 67%); onsets on the beat 100% (kept 57% to 82%); notes a bar 1.9 (kept 2.8 to 4.0): all set by the form, so printed, not charged.

Fix (proposed). A hymn mode: the stanza’s meter (CM, LM, SM, 87.87 and so on) gives each line’s pickup, stressed downbeats and held ending; the tune is drawn once and checked against every stanza’s stresses. Kept tables from a hymnal corpus (tunes with their meters) for the readings the frame leaves free.

Check. A Common Meter tune whose rhythm readings sit inside kept hymn-tune quartiles, sung to every stanza with every stressed syllable on a downbeat.

749.12 A descant module

Problem. The engine has no descant. Song 53’s descant was written with song 52’s harmony-as-lines search (above the sopranos, their rhythm and words, chord tones, the summit pinned).

Evidence. The descant’s readings: moves with the tune 26%, against it 35%, holds 39%; no parallels; its top, A5, once on “world”. A first pass pinned the summit after the search and left a parallel fifth beside it (G4 to F4 under D5 to C5, in the refrain’s first line); the pin moved inside the search, and the floor was lowered to let the line step down; the parallel went.

Fix (proposed). A descant module: a line above the tune for the last stanza or refrain, its own rhythm allowed (longer notes), the summit placed late and pinned inside the search, kept tables from published descants.

Check. No parallels with the tune or the bass, the summit in the last quarter, the line above the tune throughout.

749.13 Choral documents from one timeline

Problem. A choir and an organist need their pages to agree bar for bar. Engraving each document separately leaves bar numbers, breaks and notes free to drift.

Evidence. Song 53’s two documents come from one record and share one line (time, keys, bar lines, marks, a break every fourth bar); bars 1-80 fall on the same systems in both; every voice read back from MIDI; the choir notes compared between the two sources.

Fix (proposed). The engine’s standard for choral output: one timeline record, one shared global line with forced breaks, every document written from it, and the readback per voice.

Check. On any choral song: the same bars at the start of every system in every document, and every voice matching the record.

749.14 The engine has no accompaniment

Problem. Nothing in the engine writes an accompaniment. Song 53’s first organ part doubled the choir’s four parts for most of the carol, and its introduction and verse 4 were in the same texture: correct, and too plain for an organist’s score.

Evidence. First version: outside the introduction and link, the organ’s notes were the choir’s (right hand two notes, left hand one, pedal the bass); no eighth notes; a 4-bar introduction; no coda. Rewritten: the introduction 8 bars; three notes in the right hand on 41 of 57 chords in verses 1-3; the left hand rocking in eighths (263 notes); verse 4’s right hand below the tune throughout, with a suspension; the final refrain over a tonic and a dominant pedal; a 4-bar coda; every note read back from MIDI.

Fix (proposed). An accompaniment module for keyboard-led songs: a texture plan by section that builds through the song (doubling and support early, independence late), figures by metre (the rocking eighths in 3/4), pedal points at phrase openings and before cadences, suspensions at chord changes, an introduction from the refrain’s tune and a coda from its last phrase.

Check. On any keyboard-led song: the accompaniment’s texture grows by section, the late sections do not double the tune, and every note fits its chord or resolves by step.

749.16 An accompaniment plan by section role

Problem. The engine gives every section of an accompaniment the same treatment, so a song with repeated verses sounds static and an organ part looks thin even when each bar is correct (song 53, first and second editions: the organ’s right hand 0.52 onsets a beat, 19% of bars held chords).

Evidence. Organ practice gives each verse a role: hymnal harmony with changes of colour for the inner verses, free harmony for the introduction, the interludes and the last verse (the research report “Accompaniment corpora and music theory”). Human arrangements repeat an accompaniment within a section type and change it between types; same-type sections are about 1.68 times more alike (POP909 studies). Song 53’s third edition, written to such a plan, raised the organ’s right hand to 0.89 onsets a beat and the refrain’s complementarity from 0.13 to 0.67, with fewer clashes and no outer parallels.

Fix. Before arranging, assign each section a role (introduction, support, lift, interlude, climax, close) and a texture for each hand from the accompaniment tables (by metre: textures, onsets a beat, complementarity). Write the bass first in free sections. Repeat a section’s texture when the section repeats and change it when the role changes. Where repeats share printed bars, vary by registration or orchestration. Patterns are stored apart from chords and fitted to each chord, as the published systems do.

Check. Per section, each hand’s onsets a beat and complementarity sit inside the table’s middle half for its role, or the plan says why not. Sustained bars are no more than the table’s share. There are no parallel fifths or octaves between the outer voices, and no more clashes than the plain hymnal version.

Part 14. Chromatic harmony: views, covers, our songs, hymns and art song

Chromatic harmony: views, covers and our songs

The question

The maintainer’s review of 28 of our songs found that the engine places one borrowed chord or one modulation well, but never lives in chromatic harmony: secondary dominants and borrowed chords as part of the ordinary language, modal mixture across a whole section. It suggested pushing in that direction, and noted that it had not analysed every song chord by chord. This study checks both: how chromatic our songs actually are, and whether chromatic harmony goes with what audiences watch or what musicians re-record.

Why the engine behaves this way

Luthier v7 does it on purpose. The Departure Cost Framework (Window 19.9) charges 1 departure unit for any borrowed chord or secondary dominant and 2 for a secondary dominant resolving, a parallel-minor lift or a deceptive cadence, against a ceiling per song. The engine spends one unit where it counts and returns home. Only the synthetic modal homes (Dorian for mixed songs) and the lament schema (♭VI and ♭VII at no cost) let chromatic chords become ordinary.

Data and method

  • Corpus: the Hooktheory clips (CC BY-NC-SA via Sheet Sage), 25,705 clips with a key and chords, averaged per song: 10,749 songs with YouTube views; 2,355 with Discogs-VI cover counts and a first release year; 781 with SHS100K version counts. Clips with a key change were left out.
  • Home key: each chord’s notes against plain major, or natural minor plus the leading tone (so V in minor is at home and a Mixolydian ♭VII counts as borrowed).
  • Measures per song:
    • chromatic share: the share of chord time outside the home key;
    • the kinds, as shares of chord changes: mixture (from the parallel mode), applied dominants (a major triad or dominant seventh outside the key that moves to the chord a fifth below), and other chromatic chords;
    • lives: the share of a song’s sections with two or more chromatic chord changes.
  • Models: the controls of the earlier studies (subscribers, video age, duration, music category, clips, chord events, major or minor; for covers also log views and song age or first performer). Each measure set was tested alone, then again with the earlier note measures (melody and chord surprise, uncertainty, repetition) held fixed. Standardised betas, errors clustered by artist; views also within artist.

How chromatic popular songs are

Measure (per song) Median 75th percentile 90th percentile
Chromatic share of chord time 4.4% 24.7% 40.1%
Mixture, share of chord changes 0% 8.0% 25.0%
Applied dominants, share of chord changes 0% 0% 6.2%
Sections with two or more chromatic chords 0% 100% 100%

Half of popular songs have almost no chromatic harmony; a quarter live in it.

Results

Outcome Chromatic share (1 SD) Mixture Applied dominants Sections that live in it
Views, across songs (10,749) −0.14 (p < .001) −0.06 (p < .001) −0.02 (p .06) −0.10 (p < .001)
Views, same note measures held −0.07 (p < .001) −0.03 (p < .001) +0.00 (p .78) −0.04 (p < .001)
Views, within artist (7,597) −0.13 (p < .001) −0.06 (p < .001) −0.02 (p .07) −0.08 (p < .001)
Covers, Discogs-VI (2,355) +0.01 (p .61) −0.02 (p .19) +0.03 (p .13) +0.02 (p .29)
Covers, SHS100K (781) +0.08 (p .10) −0.02 (p .65) +0.08 (p .06) +0.07 (p .06); +0.10 (p .01) with note measures

Standardised betas over the controls. The chromatic-share model also has a square term: for views it is positive (+0.07), so the loss is steepest from none to some and then levels off.

  1. Audiences watch chromatic songs less. The effect is small (0.1% to 1% of the variance) but holds within one artist’s songs and with the note measures held fixed. Mixture carries most of it.
  2. Musicians do not re-record chromatic songs more. There is no effect in the larger source (Discogs-VI). The smaller source (SHS100K) leans positive for sections that live in chromatic harmony and for applied dominants, but the larger one does not confirm it. The covers finding of 749.22 is about chords that change within a section, not chords outside the key.
  3. Applied dominants are the safest kind. With the note measures held they carry no views penalty, and they lean positive for covers in both sources (not significant in either).

Our songs

Chord symbols from the scripts of 31 songs (p21 to p63), read against each song’s key. This is an inventory of the chords written, not a count of bars, so it can miss a chord written another way.

  • 15 songs have no chromatic chord, 9 have one, 4 have two, and 3 have three or four.
  • The median song has 2.5% of its chord mentions outside the key, a little under the popular median of 4.4%.
  • The commonest chromatic chord is ♭VII (9 songs). Applied-dominant shapes appear in 6 songs. Only The World Is Asking (song 49: V/ii, V/vi, V/V) and A Wire Pulled Tight (song 51) use several.

The maintainer’s reading is right: the engine uses chromatic chords as single colours, mostly ♭VII.

What it means for the engine (749.23)

  • Keep the departure budget as the default. The audience data support rationing chromatic chords in a song meant to reach many listeners, and the musician data give no reason to spend more.
  • Add a chromatic home as a style option, not a default. For songs whose style lives there (gospel, jazz, prog, art song, some worship), chosen at intake. A section declares its chromatic vocabulary: each chord costs 1 unit when it first enters, then nothing for the rest of that section, as the synthetic modal homes already work.
  • Within it, prefer applied dominants that resolve, and use mixture outside the lament and groove homes sparingly.
  • Keep the sung line plain over it: melody surprise at or below the corpus median (749.18).

Evidence grade: B for the views penalty (large sample, holds within artist); C for applied dominants and covers (one source leaning, not replicated).

Hymns and art song

The popular corpus says nothing about the styles where chromatic harmony is ordinary, so the same chord measures were taken from Roman-numeral analyses: When in Rome (Gotham and others, CC BY-SA 4.0; human analyses of Goudimel’s psalms, Bach’s chorales and OpenScore Lieder) and the OpenScore Lieder corpus’s automatic analyses (AugmentedNet, CC0 scores). Each chord is read in its local key, so a modulation is not counted; the second column counts it, against the piece’s first key. Popular songs are read in a single key (sections with a key change were left out). Medians throughout; applied dominants, mixture and other are shares of chord changes; chromatic passages are the share of 8-bar spans (for popular songs, of sections) with two or more chromatic chords.

Corpus Pieces Chromatic share (median; 90th) With modulations Applied dominants Mixture Other Chromatic passages
Popular (Hooktheory) 10,749 4.4%; 40.1% n/a 0% 0% 0% 0%
Psalms (Goudimel) 41 4.2%; 9.1% 7.1% 2.4% 0% 0% 20%
Chorales (Bach) 371 6.2%; 14.8% 15.6% 2.1% 1.8% 2.4% 50%
Art song (human) 179 13.3%; 27.8% 25.0% 2.7% 1.8% 7.5% 46%
Art song (automatic) 1,083 15.4%; 29.8% 27.2% 3.8% 2.5% 9.1% 50%

English hymns (Open Hymnal, 295 four-part hymns) have no analyses, so they were measured from the notes: the share of beats whose sounding notes leave the key. The median hymn has 4.7% such beats (90th percentile 19.8%); the same measure gives 12.5% for Bach’s chorales, close to their analysed figure with modulations counted (15.6%). The most chromatic hymns by this measure are mostly modal Lutheran tunes, whose modal notes count as chromatic, plus Victorian tunes such as St. Louis (“O Little Town of Bethlehem”).

  1. The kind differs more than the amount. Popular songs that use chromatic chords use mostly mixture (mean 6.3% of chord changes, against 1.6% for applied dominants). Hymns and art songs use applied dominants as much as or more than mixture, and art songs add diminished sevenths, augmented sixths and the Neapolitan (“other”).
  2. Plain hymns are barely more chromatic than popular songs, but steadily so: one or two applied dominants a verse, rarely more (90th percentile 9%).
  3. Bach and art song live in chromatic harmony: about half of their 8-bar spans hold two or more chromatic chords. Art songs have about three times the chromatic share of popular songs.
  4. Our songs (median 2.5% of chord mentions, mostly ♭VII) sit below plain hymns, and use the popular kind (mixture) even in the hymn-like songs. Song 53 has one applied dominant (F♯7 to B minor, in the last verse’s reharmonisation) and one ♭VII; song 52 uses ♭VII and ♭VI.

For the engine: the chromatic home should carry style norms, not one number:

  • Hymn mode (749.11): applied dominants are ordinary vocabulary, about 2% to 4% of chord changes (one or two a verse, often at a cadence: V/V, V/vi, V/ii), costing nothing in hymn mode. Mixture stays rare (under 2%).
  • Chorale or art-song style: chromatic chords in about half of 8-bar spans; local chromatic share of 6% (chorale) to 13% to 15% (art song); add diminished sevenths, augmented sixths and the Neapolitan; tonicise and modulate freely.
  • Popular styles: keep the v7 budget; mixture is the native kind there, and the kind audiences penalise most.

Cautions: Roman-numeral analyses label every chord, including passing ones, while Hooktheory transcribers simplify, so the popular figures may be a little low by comparison. The automatic Lieder analyses broadly agree with the human ones (a little more chromatic). Modal tunes inflate the English-hymn note measure.

Cautions

The views and covers results come from popular song only; hymns and art song were measured for how chromatic they are, not for outcomes. Users transcribe sections, not whole songs. Genre is only partly controlled (within artist helps). Views measure exposure as much as music.

Files

studies/chromatic: chromatic_features.py, study_chromatic.py, chromatic_our_songs.py, chromatic_styles.py, chromatic_hymn_beats.py, and their results (chromatic_results.json, chromatic_our_songs.json, chromatic_styles.json, chromatic_hymn_beats.json).

Intake

Sixteen questions, one a turn, every answer logged verbatim in intake.py.

Findings

749.24 The engine assumes a bridge

Problem. Song 54 has no bridge. Six readers in the v7 file read BAR0["Bridge"] or LINES["Bridge"] and stopped the run: the bridge plan draw, the era reading’s three windows, 278’s aims, 208/279’s bridge-opening gate, the lift’s bridge median and the reading’s bridge axes.

Evidence. The first smoke test failed on each in turn; songs 48–51 all had bridges.

Fix. Make the bridge optional: draw its plan only if it is sung; read the era over the windows present (two here); leave the bridge’s aims and gate unread when there is none.

Check. A song with no bridge runs with no song-specific guard; songs 48–51 reproduce their orders.

749.25 Placement deaths at nine- and ten-syllable lines with borrowed rhythms

Problem. Two-thirds of builds died for want of a placement (667 main, 662 control), the most of any song since v7 (songs 49–51: 741, 747, 749.3).

Evidence. A trace wrapped the rhythm draw and logged every call over 80 control builds. Failed and kept calls had the same room (earliest start and latest last onset alike), so the window is not the cause. The failures fall on lines of 9 and 10 syllables in two-bar slots whose rhythm is borrowed: verse lines sung again on verse 1’s onsets (712), and verse 1 and chorus 1 lines drawn on a partner’s or a returning unit’s bars (310, 361). Of the 58 sung lines, 18 have 9 syllables or more.

Fix. When a borrowed rhythm cannot take a line’s syllables, split its longest note (as 682 does for the template) or draw the bar fresh, rather than end the build.

Check. Song 54’s main run keeps its pick; placement deaths fall under a third; songs 48–51 reproduce.

749.26 Two syllables on one onset, in most of the clean survivors

Problem. 749.1 again, and larger: 87 of 143 clean survivors (61%) sing two syllables on one onset, and the judge’s pick was one of them (“coffee” / “can”, verse 4).

Evidence. Main run; re-pick by 730’s rule over the other 56 (42 eligible), d12c2728e6f1.

Fix. A note of no length is a death (or 715 makes the build ineligible); find where the second onset is lost (a melisma split on the line’s last note, by the look of the case).

Check. No survivor with two syllables on one onset; the pick unchanged where it had none.

749.27 The band-over-the-tune limit does not carry over to a low lead

Problem. 749.21’s limit (the accompaniment above the sung tune at most 2% of the time) was set on organ and choir, where the tune is the top line. With a baritone under guitars, fiddle and steel, 81% of his notes have something above them, as on most country records.

Evidence. Song 54: him 81%, her 15% (her accompaniment was kept below her); within a second of the tune, 13%; the voices sit 5.2 dB over the band.

Fix. Keep the 2% limit where the tune is the top line (choir, organ, a high lead). For a lead below the band, read salience by level and by what lies within a second of the tune.

Check. Songs 52, 53 and 54 each pass under the rule that fits them.

749.28 A story’s turn falls later than the shape targets

Problem. 749.17 puts the high point at 0.65–0.85 of the song and 749.19 the breath at 0.55–0.60. In a story song whose twist is in the last verse, both fall late: the breath at 0.853, the top at chorus 4 (0.857–0.952).

Evidence. Song 54’s form (A), the writer’s; her entry is the payoff and cannot move earlier without changing the story.

Fix. Read the targets against the song’s turn when the type is Narrative: the breath before the turn and the high point at it, wherever the story puts them, with the release after.

Check. A Narrative song’s breath and top fall at its turn; other types keep 0.55–0.60 and 0.65–0.85.

749.29 The lexicon check: dialect forms and “a.m.”

Problem. Five of the six unknown words were g-dropped forms of known words (sleepin’, mornin’, fixin’ and so on), and “Git ‘n’ Split” read its “n” as the letter N, stressed. “a.m.” splits into “a” and “m”. Protocol 0b v67 asks one word at a time; the writer’s rule is one question a turn, so the six went as one question.

Evidence. Song 54’s intake; readings in gen_l7_p64.py (LEX64); “‘n’” added to the function words.

Fix. Derive -in’ forms from the -ing entry; read “‘n’” as unstressed AH0 N; read “a.m.” as one word, EY2 EH1 M; ask only words with no derivable reading, all in one question.

Check. Song 54’s lyric needs only “mildewed” asked.

Blind pick

The three 10.20 slots (q1020.py): remembered, “For a boy who’s been gone too long”; middle, “The man Mama prayed I’d be”; annotated, “And sir I’m finally fixin’ to be”. Offered shuffled as A (annotated), B (remembered), C (middle); the writer chose C, “The man Mama prayed I’d be”: Middle.

Part 17. Luthier audit: harmony and arrangement

16 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Luthier audit: harmony and arrangement.

Summary

The engine writes one thing: the sung melody. On harmony and arrangement, the record (Luthier v7, 15,350 lines, plus its tables) holds a great deal of research but almost no code that writes anything.

  • Harmony. 24 items, among them six measured tables. In code: the chord chart’s redraw (438), the bass’s inversions (440), and the melody’s fit to the chords (375, 386, 431, 432, 441, 442). Missing: anything that writes a section’s chord progression. Every song’s chord plan has been typed by an AI, including song 36’s “chords by the section jobs (177)”, which were a hand-written list.

  • Arrangement. Module 9 (9.1 to 9.14), the rock and metal modules (9-R, 9-M), Windows 118, 119, 143 and 144, and the offline findings 749.14, 749.16 and 749.21. In code: the bass routine (Windows 143 and 144) and the readers (9.12 energy arc, 9.13, 9.14). Missing: drums, the chordal part, instrumental figures, the texture plan and parts playing. Every band part but the bass has been written by an AI, per song, in that song’s build script.

So a v8 that writes everything needs two new generators, harmony and arrangement, built the way the melody is: drawn from tables measured on real songs, and tested. Much of the measuring is done already; the main gaps are sequence data (what follows what) and data by genre and section role.

How to read the status

Status Meaning
Writes The engine’s own code makes these notes or chords, the same way every run, with no AI choosing.
** Reads** The engine’s code measures or checks it (a reading, a gate, a consistency check) but writes nothing.
** Table** The numbers were measured from real music and saved; no code writes from them yet.
** Rule** Written in the spec as what a song should do; applied only by an AI writing each song by hand, if at all.
** Missing** Not in the record.

Evidence is the fix or Window number in the spec, and the file where the code lives (the engine of record is songs/p66/melody_l7_p66.py ; the bass routine bass_v134.py).

The gaps, and the research that would fill them

The record already describes what real harmony and bands do on average; what it lacks is what follows what, and how it differs by genre and by section. Those are the two things a generator needs.

ballad at 72 does not run sixteenths

Two cautions from the record itself: harmony and arrangement features have never separated hits from other songs (Windows 28, 38, 56), so these tables should describe what real songs typically do, not promise success; and every new table needs a kept-song test, as the melody’s do.

Proposed order of work for v8, and the test

Harmony first, then the band, then a test that makes “the engine writes everything” checkable.

  1. ** Research H1 to H3**, then build the harmony writer. The engine’s order becomes form, harmony, melody, arrangement; the chart redraw (438) and the bass’s inversions (440) stay as they are.

  2. A5 : make the bass routine read the tempo. A small job, and it removes the one place the routine failed.

  3. Research A1 to A4, then build the drum, texture, chordal-part and fill writers, each with its own kept-song test.

  4. H4 : the harmony-voice writer.

  5. The no-hand-input test. A run may take only the writer’s intake answers (from a fixed questionnaire written from the spec’s Q0 to Q8) and his locked lyric. The song’s generator may set only those. The test report lists every input that did not come from the engine, and a song fails if any chord or band note came from a hand-typed list.

  6. Rerun songs 54 to 56 under the test, and compare them by ear with the versions already delivered.

Until then, a delivered song should say plainly what wrote it: the engine’s melody, an AI’s chords and band.

Part 18. Harmony research for Luthier v8: what follows what

16 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Harmony research for Luthier v8: what follows what.

A chord writer for the engine is feasible from measured sequences: on verses and choruses in major keys, a simple model drawn from 592 training songs already passes as kept on every measure tried. Minor keys, bridges and pre-choruses need more data, genres need data this session cannot reach, and real progressions loop in a way the simple model does not.

The data

Two collections were read in full; the two largest genre-labelled collections could not be reached from this session.

Collection What it is Used for Licence
McGill Billboard 890 chart slots, 739 unique songs charting 1958 to 1991; chords bar by bar with section labels and the tonic; raw files from ChoCo v1.0.0 (Zenodo 7706751) Every measure here, and the prototype CC0
Rolling Stone 200 de Clercq and Temperley’s Roman-numeral analyses of 200 songs, written as section rules The replication Research corpus
Chordonomicon Over 666,000 user-made chord charts with section, genre and date labels Not reached: its download host is refused by this session’s network, and its dataset card says CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial), against the paper’s CC BY 4.0 CC BY-NC 4.0 (card)
de Clercq’s country corpus 200 famed country songs in Nashville numbers Not reached (its site is refused) Unknown

The Billboard songs carry no genre labels, so nothing below is by genre. Mode was read per song: minor when the tonic chord is minor more often than major (128 minor, 611 major).

What the published research says

Pop harmony has its own grammar, not common practice’s: IV and ♭VII matter as much as V, progressions loop, and genre labels are a weak guide.

  • Rock harmony (de Clercq and Temperley 2011). A hand analysis of 100 songs from Rolling Stone’s 500 Greatest Songs, 20 a decade from the 1950s to the 1990s, with over 90% agreement between the two analysts. IV is the most common chord after I and most often precedes it; the five commonest chords are I, IV, V, ♭VII and VI; II, VI and III form one group of chords that go together, and ♭VII, ♭III and ♭VI another, which the authors read as a modal organisation. paper; slides

  • Root motion. The asymmetries of common-practice music (fourths up preferred to fourths down) are mostly absent in rock, so a chord’s place before or after the tonic is the useful distinction. summary

  • The McGill Billboard set (Burgoyne, Wild and Fujinaga 2011). 890 slots sampled at random from the Billboard charts, annotated by experts with sections and chords; released under CC0. paper; licence

  • Loops since 2000. A corpus of 2002 to 2021 songs is more repetitive than McGill’s; most chord loops appear in only one song, and the most schematic loops were shared more widely in the McGill era (Chander and Quinn 2023). preprint Loops of IV, V and vi hovering above the tonic (the “plateau loop”) became widespread in recent pop (Duinker 2019). article In post-2000 EDM-pop the loop is mostly one diatonic collection, with the melody moving independently above it (Park 2025). dissertation

  • Genre. User tags put as much as 60% of recent songs under “pop/rock”, and song-by-song uniqueness makes corpus averages a weak stand-in for any one song. article Country was studied by corpus only recently: de Clercq built a 200-song country corpus to test the “three chords” caricature, which Jocelyn Neal calls a misconception. talk

  • Writing chords by model. MySong (Simon, Morris and Basu 2008) chose chords for a sung melody with a hidden Markov model trained on a song database, and listeners rated the results positively. paper A semi-Markov version adds each chord’s duration, so it finds where the harmony changes as well as what it changes to (Groves 2013). paper Comparative studies judge generated chords by listening tests on fit and interest against the human progression. study

  • Chords first or melody first. Songwriters do both; some start from a progression and let its mood draw out melody and lyric, others hand a melody to a co-writer to harmonise. No study found settles which works better, so the engine should choose by its own test. example

What the Billboard songs show

Each section kind has its own job, and the jobs are sharp enough to write by: verses open on I three times in four, bridges end on V nearly half the time, and pre-choruses hardly touch the tonic.

What else the songs show:

  • Chords from outside the key. In major, ♭VII is in 18% of verses and choruses and 22% of bridges; II (V of V) in 12% to 22%. In minor, a major IV, Dorian’s raised sixth, is in 23% of verses and 24% of choruses, the commonest chord from outside the key.

  • The joins. A pre-chorus or bridge hands to the chorus on V→I most often (24% and 36% of joins); a chorus hands to a bridge on I→IV (18%).

  • Returns. A later verse keeps the first verse’s chords bar for bar 60% of the time, a chorus 55%, a pre-chorus 81%.

  • Loops. Under a strict reading (90% of bars repeat at the period), 29% of major choruses and 31% of verses loop in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars, more in minor (47% of choruses); most sections vary their cell.

  • Over time. Harmony moved faster: the median verse changed chord every two bars in the 1950s and once a bar by the 1980s and 1990s.

A prototype chord writer, tested

Where the data is plentiful, chords drawn from kept sequences pass as kept; where it is thin, the model does no better than drawing chords at random by frequency.

The prototype is a variable-order Markov model (up to three chords of context) over each section kind’s chord changes, by mode, trained on 592 songs and read against the heldout 147. Each change’s length is drawn from the kind’s kept lengths. The baseline draws chords by their frequency alone. A first-chord or last-chord distance of 0 means the same distribution as the held-out songs, 1 means none in common.

Section Held out First chord: model / baseline Last chord: model / baseline Distinct chords: kept / model Tonic’s share: kept / model Bits a change: model / baseline
Verse, major 339 0.10/ 0.47 ** 0.14**/ 0.32 4 / 4 34% / 33% ** 3.81**/ 4.52
Chorus, major 329 ** 0.11**/ 0.32 ** 0.14**/ 0.31 4 / 4 29% / 29% ** 3.45**/ 4.44
Bridge, major 68 0.30 / 0.23 0.38 / 0.42 4 / 4 17% / 13% 3.98 / 4.79
Pre-chorus, major 38 0.28 / 0.35 0.46 / 0.74 4 / 4 0% / 10% 4.26 / 4.77
Verse, minor 68 0.15 / 0.50 0.26 / 0.33 3 / 4 49% / 32% 4.62 / 4.33
Chorus, minor 80 0.24 / 0.36 0.29 / 0.33 3 / 4 30% / 25% 4.40 / 4.38

Three things it shows:

  1. ** Verses and choruses in major pass.** First and last chords, distinct chords, the tonic’s share and changes a bar all sit with the held-out songs, and the model predicts the next chord about one bit better than frequency alone.

  2. Minor keys, bridges and pre-choruses do not. With 51 to 293 training sections, the model learns little beyond frequency (minor verses and choruses: no better in bits) and minor verses hold the tonic too little (32% against 49%). These need more songs, or rules from Table CP as gates.

  3. It rambles where real songs loop. Drawn sections run on (“I ii iii V vi iii IV I iii ii IV I”) where kept ones repeat a two-or four-bar cell. The writer needs a structural step: draw a cell, then repeat or vary it at the kept rates.

The same measures on a second collection

The section jobs hold on the Rolling Stone 200, a different collection analysed by different people: endings agree almost exactly, openings closely.

Section RS200 sections Last chord: RS200 / Billboard First chord: RS200 / Billboard Top moves, RS200

Chorus 162 I 33%, V 27% / I 35%, V 28% I 43%, IV 15% / I 57%, IV 15% I→IV 13%, IV→I 11%, V→I 8%
Bridge 69 V 59% / V 46% I 29%, IV 23% / IV 34%, I 15% IV→I 10%, I→IV 8%
Intro 127 I 38%, V 22% / I 38%, V 22% I 64% / I 63% I→IV 11%, IV→I 11%

The RS200 figures mix major and minor songs (minor openings, i, take 12% to 15% of them), which accounts for most of the gap in first chords. Both collections change chord about once a bar and use three or four distinct chords a section.

What this means for v8’s harmony writer

Build it in three layers, chords first, and test it the way the melody is tested.

  1. The cell. For each section, draw a loop cell of one, two or four bars from the kept cells of its kind and mode, or decide not to loop, at the kept rates (about seven sections in ten in major do not repeat strictly).

  2. The sequence. Fill the cell, or the whole section when it does not loop, from the variable-order model of what follows what, by section kind and mode. Draw each chord’s length from the kind’s kept lengths, at the decade’s harmonic rhythm.

  3. The jobs as gates. Keep a section only if its first and last chords, distinct chords, tonic share and out-of-key share fall inside the kept quartiles (Tables CN and CP and these new tables). A verse opens on I; a pre-chorus or bridge ends off the tonic, usually on V; joins follow the kept moves.

Then the existing chart redraw (438) and the bass’s inversions (440) run unchanged, and the melody is drawn over the written chords, as it is now. Chords first suits the engine, whose melody search already aims at chord tones; the published systems that go melody first (MySong and its successors) remain a fallback if the fit test fails.

Mode and colour. Minor sections draw ♭VI, ♭VII, ♭III and Dorian’s IV at their kept rates; in major, ♭VII and II are the common outside chords. This replaces the hand-picked chord vocabularies by song type, which become a light preference on top.

What still needs data. Genre (country, soul, gospel, worship): the Billboard songs carry no labels, and the two labelled collections are unreachable here. Two routes: allow this session’s network to reach the Chordonomicon host (and settle its non-commercial licence for an engine that writes songs for release), or obtain de Clercq’s country corpus. Minor keys, bridges and pre-choruses: more songs, or the section-job gates carrying them until then.

The tests. (a) Every drawn section passes the gates; (b) on held-out songs the model beats frequency alone in bits a change for every kind it writes; (c) a listening check, drawn against kept progressions in the same section, as the published studies do; (d) the no-hand-input test from the audit: no chord in a song may come from a hand-typed list.

Files and sources

The scripts and tables are in the repo under studies/harmony (commit d8055b9): parse_billboard.py, measure_billboard.py (writes billboard_tables.json), prototype_writer.py (writes prototype_results.json) and rs200.py (writes rs200_tables.json). The raw data is ChoCo v1.0.0 from Zenodo record 7706751, not kept in the repo. This study follows the harmony and arrangement audit.

Sources:

  • de Clercq and Temperley, A corpus analysis of rock harmony (Popular Music, 2011), and conference slides

  • Harmony and Syntax in Contemporary Pop Music (Vassar thesis)

  • Burgoyne, Wild and Fujinaga, An expert ground-truth set for audio chord recognition and music analysis (ISMIR 2011); the CC0 licence, via mirdata

Part 19. Arrangement research for Luthier v8: what the band does

16 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Arrangement research for Luthier v8: what the band does.

A band writer for the engine can be drawn from measured parts the same way the melody is: real songs thin the intro to about 70% of their fullest band, thicken the chorus by about a quarter, play bass about once a beat at any tempo, and keep one drum bar for about half the song. Genre changes the details more than the plan.

The data

Two collections were measured; three more that would answer the open questions could not be reached from this session.

Collection What it is Used for Licence
POP909 with phrase labels 909 Chinese pop songs, each a lead melody, a secondary melody and a professional piano accompaniment; human phrase labels (intro, sung phrases A, B and others, instrumental phrases, outro) from Dai, Zhang and Dannenberg Texture by section role CC BY 4.0
Lakh Pianoroll Dataset (LPD-5 cleansed) 21,425 songs in five parts (drums, piano, guitar, bass, strings), 4/4; 9,329 read, up to 1,500 per genre The band by genre CC BY 4.0
Million Song Dataset artist terms (via Gold-Caps) Genre words per artist The genre of each Lakh song: the family of the artist’s top term CC BY 4.0
Groove MIDI Dataset Human drumming with fills labelled, many styles Not reached (its host is refused) CC BY 4.0
Timbre in Popular Song (TiPS) Texture and timbre by section in 400 songs, 100 each of country, pop, metal and hip hop Not reached; only the pop part is published so far Open, in progress
Lakh MIDI (raw) The original files with every instrument Not reached (its host is refused); the piano-roll version above stands in CC BY 4.0

Two limits run through the Lakh readings: piano rolls merge repeated strikes of one held pitch, so chordal onsets are undercounted; and genre comes from the artist, not the song.

The academic record

Scholars describe a pop band as a few functional layers whose entrances and exits mark the form; the most successful accompaniment systems retrieve real phrases and fit them to new chords rather than inventing parts note by note.

  • Functional layers (Moore 2012; Lavengood 2020). Allan Moore’s four layers: the explicit beat, the functional bass, the harmonic filler and the melody. Open Music Theory The harmonic filler fills the registral space between the bass and the melody. Lavengood, MTO Lavengood adds a fifth, the novelty layer: intermittent, cutting in and out, often in call and response with the melody, the least common of the layers. slides

  • The bass as its own line (de Clercq 2019). Bass and harmony often move independently, a “harmonic-bass divorce” like the melody’s. article

  • Form by texture. Most work on pop form has centred on melody and harmony, with drums studied less (Geary 2024). MTO Texture change cues listeners that a section is changing; the verse-to-chorus step intensifies by layering new instruments and changing register, and a late surge of new events often comes about two-thirds of the way through (Schwitzgebel 2025, after White 2020). MTO A 665-song McGill subset annotated for texture and timbre found these changes are formal markers, though only general trends were identified. McGill

  • Accumulation (Spicer 2004). “Accumulative” and “cumulative” forms build by layering, tied to multitrack recording. chapter

  • Genre norms are still being measured. TiPS encodes texture by section in 400 songs from the 1990s across country, pop, metal and hip hop on Moore’s and Lavengood’s layers. project Its genre norms have not been published yet.

  • Accompaniment systems. POP909 offers several professional piano arrangements of 909 popular songs for arrangement research. paper AccoMontage arranges whole pieces by retrieving phrase montages from a database, recombining them by dynamic programming, then fitting their chords to the lead sheet, and beat learning-only baselines. paper PopMAG generates multi-track accompaniment for pop. summary

Texture by section role (POP909)

The accompaniment lifts the chorus by playing more notes, not by moving register or holding longer: in 88% of songs the B phrases (usually the chorus) are busier than the A phrases (usually the verse).

Medians over 11,431 labelled phrases in 909 songs (piano accompaniment).

Phrase Phrases Piano notes a beat Notes struck together Share of time sounding Secondary melody, notes a beat
Intro 872 2.31 1.42 86% 1.24
A (usually the verse) 2,936 2.93 1.51 92% 0.50
B (usually the chorus) 3,074 3.78 1.65 92% 0.63
Other sung phrases 2,199 3.56 1.67 91% 0.69
Instrumental phrases 1,799 3.25 1.65 92% 1.36
Outro 551 2.82 1.41 91% 1.06

Paired within each song (865 songs with both): B over A by a median 0.73 notes a beat; B strikes more notes together in 61% of songs; register and sustain barely move (each about half up, half down). The secondary melody plays hardest where the voice rests: in intros and instrumental phrases at about twice its rate under sung phrases. The last chorus is no busier than the first (a median change of 0; busier in 49% of songs), unlike the build Window 38 reads in Western records; POP909’s piano-only Chinese pop may simply not build by the piano.

The band by genre (Lakh)

The plan is shared across genres and the details are not: every genre’s commonest snare bar is 2 and 4 and in every genre shown the intro starts at about 70% of the fullest band, while kick patterns, bass syncopation and piano voicing tell country from soul.

Medians unless noted; kick bars on sixteenths, x an onset, the bar starting left.

Genre Songs Snare on 2 and 4 (commonest bar) Commonest kick bars Hats in eighths / sixteenths Bass notes a beat Bass off the eighths Piano notes struck together Intro’s band, share of the fullest
Country 805 69% x.......x....... 28%, x.....x.x....... 23% 63% / 11% 0.91 1% 1.90 72%
Soul and R&B 598 67% x...x...x...x... 15%, x.......x....... 13% 61% / 17% 1.12 11% 2.16 70%
Gospel 274 62% x.......x....... 18%, x.....x.x....... 18% 59% / 12% 0.92 3% 1.83 69%
Pop 1,495 62% x...x...x...x... 20%, x.....x.x....... 16% 54% / 16% 1.05 5% 1.89 68%
Rock 1,498 64% x.....x.x....... 14%, x.......x....... 13% 57% / 13% 1.10 2% 1.92 67%
Folk 620 59% x.......x....... 14%, x.....x.x....... 14% 56% / 12% 0.98 3% 1.84 70%

What else the songs show:

One drum bar for half the song. The commonest kick-and-snare bar fills about half a song’s bars (country 61%, the steadiest; rock 48%), around ten other bars filling the rest.

  • The bass plays about once a beat at any tempo. Across all genres, a median 1.0 bass notes a beat below 85 beats a minute and 1.15 above 130. Slow songs syncopate more: 16% of bass notes fall off the eighths below 85, against 0.3% above 130. The engine’s routine, run at song 56’s doubled tempo, would have played about three a beat.

  • Chordal parts. Guitar’s commonest bar is straight eighths (15% to 23% of songs by genre). Country piano most often holds one chord a bar (20%), soul’s plays eighths (15%) with thicker chords. Strings hold whole notes. About half of chordal strikes land with a bass note (country guitar 44%, soul piano 57%). Registers, 10th to 90th percentile medians: piano about D3 to B4, guitar D3 to G4, strings A3 to F5.

  • Parts playing. The first tenth of a song carries about 70% of its fullest band, the second to the ninth tenths at the fullest, the last tenth about 93%. Drums enter by bar 1 or 2 in most songs.

  • What could not be read. Where fills fall: Lakh songs do not start on a phrase boundary, so fills by place in an 8-bar group come out flat. That needs phrase-aligned drums (the Groove MIDI Dataset labels its fills) or section labels.

What this means for v8’s arrangement writer

Build it the way AccoMontage and the melody search both work: draw real parts from kept tables, fit them to the engine’s chords, and gate them by the section plan.

  1. The section plan first. For each section, draw the number of parts and each part’s density from kept rates: the intro about 70% of the fullest band and its accompaniment about 0.6 times the chorus’s notes a beat; the chorus about a quarter busier than its verse; the middle of the song at the fullest; the last tenth about 93%. This writes Module 9.12’s arc and fix 238’s parts playing instead of hand-arranging to pass them.

  2. The four layers, one writer each (Moore’s layers, as in the spec’s Window 118 and 119 rules):

    • Explicit beat: the genre’s kick-and-snare bar drawn from the kept bars, held for about half the song with about ten variants; hats or ride in eighths unless the genre’s sixteenth rate is drawn; a fill and crash at section ends (fix 236).

    • Functional bass: the routine, made tempo-aware: about one note a beat at any tempo, syncopating off the eighths at the slow-song rate (16% below 85 beats a minute) and the genre’s rate (soul 11%, country 1%).

    • Harmonic filler: one bar rhythm per section from the instrument’s and genre’s kept rhythms (fix 237), voiced on the engine’s chords inside Module 9.14’s limits and the kept registers, about half of its strikes with the bass.

    • Novelty: short answers only in the voice’s gaps (the kept fill table, fix 235), intermittent, call and response, never under a sung word (fix 379).

  3. Tests. Every drawn arrangement passes 9.12, 9.13, 9.14, 236 to 238 and 379; its readings fall inside the genre’s kept quartiles above; and the no-hand-input test: no band note from a hand-typed list.

What still needs data. Fill placement and fill shapes by style (the Groove MIDI Dataset, refused here); texture by section in Western multitrack records (POP909 is Chinese pop and piano only; TiPS’s country, metal and hip-hop parts are unpublished); song-level genre labels (Lakh’s are the artist’s). Allowing this session’s network to reach those hosts, or attaching the files, would close most of it.

Files and sources

The scripts and tables are in the repo under studies/arrangement (commit 36a16ef): pop909_texture.py, lpd_genres.py, lpd_band.py and lpd_band_tables.py, with their JSON outputs. The raw data is not kept in the repo. This study follows the audit and the harmony study.

Sources:

  • Moore’s layers and Lavengood’s novelty layer: Open Music Theory, Texture in Pop Music; Lavengood, The Cultural Significance of Timbre Analysis (MTO 2020); Instrumental Timbre slides

  • de Clercq, The Harmonic-Bass Divorce in Rock (2019)

  • Geary, drums and form (MTO 2024)

  • Schwitzgebel, texture, cues and expectation in post-millennial pop (MTO 2025)

  • Interactions of timbre and form, McGill

  • Spicer, (Ac)cumulative form in pop-rock music (2004)

  • The Timbre in Popular Song (TiPS) corpus (2023)

  • Wang et al., POP909 (ISMIR 2020); Dai, Zhang and Dannenberg, phrase labels and paper (2020)

  • Zhao and Xia, AccoMontage (ISMIR 2021); Ren et al., PopMAG (2020)

  • Lakh Pianoroll Dataset (Zenodo); Gold-Caps LMD-Matched (Zenodo); Groove MIDI Dataset

Part 20. Tension research for Luthier v8: building and releasing tension

16 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Tension research for Luthier v8: building and releasing tension.

Summary

v8 should plan tension and energy as two separate curves before writing any notes. Harmonic tension should build in the pre-chorus and bridge and resolve on the chorus’s first bar; energy should peak in the chorus. Both should come late in the song, and the chord, melody and band writers should be gated by measured targets. v7 has no such plan, and its one harmony measure (a 1-to-3 number per chord) predicts nothing.

  • The research record. Every tension model that fits listeners reads trends, not levels. It gives harmony a long memory (about 20 seconds) and pitch, loudness and density short ones (2 to 4 seconds). Listeners track tension mostly from cadence to cadence, not across the whole song’s tonal plan.

  • Structure. Full structural analysis by computer is still unreliable, and listeners hear only a level or two. The engine needs phrase goals and section goals, which it already knows because it writes its own chords.

  • Pop theory. Each verse, pre-chorus and chorus cycle builds to an arrival. Melody and harmony build a “syntactic” climax; texture, register and loudness build a “statistical” one. The late breakdown and rebuild that soul and gospel gave pop sits at about 0.62 and 0.80 of the song.

  • Measured here, on 214 charting songs (100 rated by listeners):

    • Harmonic tension is highest in the pre-chorus (+0.54 standard deviations) and bridge (+0.37), with the dominant just before each chorus (+0.51) and the tonic on its first bar (+0.43). Arousal peaks in the chorus.

    • Harmonic tension peaks at about 0.68 of the song, energy at about 0.74.

    • Per bar, harmony says almost nothing about arousal; given a long memory, it adds a little. Melodic height is the score’s best signal, and loudness does better still.

  • The engine’s songs 54 and 55. Both put the dominant before every chorus. Song 54 never lands a chorus on the tonic and puts its harmonic tension in the choruses, the reverse of kept songs.

What Luthier v7 does with tension now

v7 uses the word tension on almost every page, but it measures tension in four crude ways and never plans it before the notes exist. Read from the spec (15,350 lines) and the engine of record ( songs/p66/melody_l7_p66.py ).

Item Where in v7 What it does Its limit
Tension timeline Module 8 Scores rendered audio with the TenseMusic weights (Barchet et al. 2024): loudness 0.25, pitch height 0.20, tonal tension 0.20, roughness 0.15, tempo change 0.10, onsets 0.10; flags a peak outside the bridge Runs only after the song is written and rendered; nothing writes toward it
A chord’s tension Table CO, 27.29 A hand number per chord: V and vii° 3, IV and ii 2, vi and iii 1; Lerdahl’s distance from the tonic printed beside it One number per chord, blind to what came before, to the melody, to the key’s deeper plan
The hook at maximum tension Windows 17, 42, 45; 27.4 The hook was to land where the chord is most tense Window 42: the title’s word sits at the chorus’s most tense chord in only 27% of hits, and listeners’ arousal rises at peak notes (p 0.0021) but not at the most tense bars (p 0.77). Window 45: harmonic tension is the weakest leg (nothing in choruses)
Structural tones Module 7 Rewards structural tones reached by step, and a stepwise fall across the sections’ high points (the Urlinie flag) The only notion of deeper structure; which notes are structural is decided by simple rules
Surprise Window 46; 749.18 Melody and chord surprise from a variable- order model Window 46 found no arousal signal from it (coefficient 0.092, p 0.46)
Intensity curve 749.17 (proposed) A per-bar curve from melodic height, singing, texture and dynamics, peaking at 0.65 to 0.85 of the song Leaves out harmony and expectation, the two things tonal tension is made of
Departure budgets Parts VII to IX; Module 2 Hand-set costs for each departure, by song type A budget, not a curve: it says how much, not where tension rises and falls

The gap, in one line: nothing models how tension builds and resolves through a phrase from the chords and the melody together, nothing tests such a curve against listeners, and nothing writes toward one. The weak listener result in Windows 42 and 45 tested the engine’s 1-to-3 chord number, not tension as the research models it, so it may say more about the measure than about tension.

The academic record: models of tension tested against listeners

Four decades of listening experiments agree on three things v7 does not do. Tension is heard as a trend, not a level. Harmony works on a long clock (about 20 seconds) while loudness, pitch and note density work on short ones (2 to 4 seconds). And listeners track tension locally, cadence to cadence, more than through the whole song’s tonal plan.

Model What it reads Tested on Fit to listeners
Lerdahl’s tonal tension model (Lerdahl 1996, 2001; Lerdahl and Krumhansl 2007) Four parts: a tree of which events are structural, distance in tonal pitch space, surface dissonance (the top note’s degree, inversion), and melodic attraction Classical passages; continuous and stop- tension ratings Average adjusted R² about .72 against listeners, as summarised by Ruiz- Marcos, Willis and Laney (2020); the hierarchical part matters, the attraction part has not been supported ( Farbood and Upham 2013)
Farbood’s parametric, temporal model (2012) Slopes of pitch height and loudness (weight 3), tempo and onset rate (2), harmony from Lerdahl’s model and the bass’s and inner lines’ height (1), over 3-second windows; a trend that continues is amplified 2,661 web listeners; 33 in the lab with a slider; 10 excerpts r .67 to .99; models of feature levels predicted poorly and overfit; melodic expectation was dropped for lack of a clear direction
Farbood and Upham (2013) The same model, with each feature’s window fitted A Schubert song and its harmonic reduction, 25 listeners Harmony’s best window 21.5 s against 2 to 4 s for the rest; harmony correlated best with mean tension (ρ.58), loudness .52;ρ.79 on held-out verses
Spiral-array tension (Herremans and Chew 2016) Spread of the notes in tonal space, movement of their centre, and distance from the key Compared by eye with Farbood’s web data Agreement 30% to 60%; no melody, register or inversion; it drives MorpheuS, which rewrites a piece to a given tension profile
Tonal Interval Space model (Navarro- Cáceres et al. 2020) Dissonance, a tree from Rohrmeier’s harmonic grammar, distance from the key, voice leading 15 trained listeners, 12 progressions r .75 (R² .56), against .64 to .68 for Lerdahl’s refitted; weights dissonance .40, hierarchy .25, distance .20, voice leading .19
TenseMusic (Barchet et al. 2024; v7’s Module 8) Six audio features, a weighted sum of slopes, fitted by Lasso 38 classical pieces Held-out r about .60
IDyOM melodic expectation (Gingras et al. 2016) Note-by-note surprise and uncertainty A Couperin prelude, 12 performances, 50 listeners Modest: model r .54 to .65 by group, and it added nothing once performance timing was included

What the experiments add beyond the models:

  • Trends, not levels. In Farbood’s web study, a feature mattered when it moved in a clear direction; in her words, a clear trend “generated the expectancy that the trend would continue”.

  • Local before global. Bigand and Parncutt (1999) found tension in long chord sequences mainly set locally by cadences, heard through a short window sliding from cadence to cadence; the hierarchical model fit best only because it caught those local cadences. Farbood (2016) found listeners’ memory of a home key fades within tens of seconds in a new key.

  • Which layers carry it. In Lehne et al. (2013), the outer voices alone kept most of the tension curve (ρ .71 and .73 with the original), and removing dynamics kept its shape (.83, .71). Melody or harmony led depending on the piece: melody where the harmony changed slowly.

  • Parameters interact. Granot and Eitan (2011), 132 listeners: loudness change, pitch direction and register each raised tension and tempo did not, with strong interactions between them, so fixed weights are an approximation.

  • Tension is not arousal. Lehne and Koelsch (2015) define tension as conflict, instability, dissonance or uncertainty that sets up a prediction of something significant; high tension always brings high arousal, but not the reverse. Huron’s tension response is likewise uncertainty felt as stress before an event (Sweet Anticipation).

  • Expectation and pleasure. Cheung et al. (2019) found, on Billboard chords, pleasure where a surprise follows low uncertainty, or where an uncertain moment resolves as expected. v7 already carries this as 749.18.

  • Builds in dance-pop. In Turrell et al. (2025), felt tension rose almost linearly through EDM build-ups (ρ .998), peaked at the drop and fell 2 to 3 seconds after; tension tracked arousal (ρ .92) and ran against valence (−.69).

This explains Windows 42 and 45. They read one fixed number per chord as a level, bar by bar, against arousal. Every model that fits listeners reads slopes, gives harmony a long memory, and treats arousal as related to tension but not the same.

Structure: which notes are structural

Full structural analysis by computer is still unreliable, and listeners mostly hear structure one or two levels deep. So v8 should model a shallow hierarchy (phrase goals and section goals), not a full Schenkerian or GTTM tree.

Approach What it builds How well it works
GTTM (Lerdahl and Grouping, metre, a time-span The latest, deepGTTM-IV,
Jackendoff 1983) and its tree and a prolongation tree: got the right time-span tree
programs: ATTA, FATTA, which note each note for 29 of 30 test pieces;
σGTTM and deepGTTM elaborates Ruiz-Marcos et al.’s
(Hamanaka, Hirata and Tojo, automatic tension program
2005 onward) reached only .33 tree accuracy ( 2020)
Learned Schenkerian analysis ( Kirlin and Jensen 2015) The most probable tree of prolongations for a melody, learned from 41 textbook analyses 64% of links right with no hints, 90% when told the background notes, 22% by chance; experts graded textbook analyses half a grade to a grade higher
What decides a structural note ( Kirlin and Yust 2015) Removes features one at a time from that model Melodic features matter most (interval pattern, then scale degree); harmony is the best single feature and lifts accuracy from about 52% to 60%; metric strength next; chord tone or not is nearly useless alone
Proto-voices ( Finkensiep and Rohrmeier 2021) Neighbour and passing notes and arpeggiations built up recursively, with no fixed voices A grammar and a chart parser for free textures, a base for schemata and harmonies
Harmonic grammars (Rohrmeier 2011; Harasim, Rohrmeier and O’Donnell 2018; 2019) Trees of chord dependencies (prolongation and preparation); a version with rhythm Parses jazz; adding harmonic rhythm improves the grammar; used for the hierarchical term in the Tonal Interval Space model above

What pop theory adds:

  • Melody and harmony can run on separate frameworks. Temperley (2007) found rock’s unresolved non-chord tones come mostly in pentatonic melodies and in verses, with choruses tightening melody to harmony (“loose verse, tight chorus”). Nobile (2015) names three kinds of divorce (hierarchy, loop and syntax), and de Clercq (2019) finds the same independence between harmony and bass. So in pop the structural line may live in the melody alone, over a loop.

  • The chorus closes. Nobile’s Form as Harmony in Rock Music (2020, already in v7’s citations) treats the chorus as the section that brings harmonic closure; Biamonte notes that pop phrases often end without a cadence, their momentum pointing to the next unit.

For the engine, three consequences. Module 7’s rule (structural tones on strong beats, reached by step) is the right instinct but weighs the wrong things: melodic interval pattern and harmony matter more than metric weight, and chord-tone status alone says almost nothing. The deeper level the engine needs is two goals: each phrase’s arrival note and chord, and each section’s. And a tight chorus over a loose verse is itself a tension move the engine can make.

Tension in popular song

Pop theory describes tension as two kinds working together: a syntactic build in the chords and melody toward a goal, and a statistical build in texture, register, loudness and rhythm. Each verse, pre-chorus and chorus repeats the cycle, and the song’s largest build comes late.

  • Two kinds of climax. Carter (2025), after Meyer, separates them: melody, rhythm and harmony build toward a syntactic climax, while timbre, texture, register and dynamics build toward a statistical one. In v8 terms the first belongs to the chord and melody writers, the second to the band writer.

  • The cycle has a goal. Nobile (2022) calls it the telos principle: the verse initiates (holding tonic), the pre-chorus builds (moving to IV, ii or vi and ending on V, its phrases shrinking to one or two bars, its texture thickening), and the chorus arrives, its first downbeat the structural cadence. After 1991 texture, timbre and vocal delivery could carry the build over a single loop; after 2010 songs stretch the build, make the chorus the quietest point (the anti-telos chorus), or move the release to a drop. Summach (2011) traces the pre-chorus to the ‘d’ phrase of srdc, whose job is momentum.

  • Rhythm and drums build too. Biamonte: verses are looser, choruses tighter and thicker; a pre-chorus can drop the drums to half time so the chorus backbeat lands harder; denser fills at section ends act as pickups; a shortened bar at a phrase end drives forward. Fink (2011) shows the same goal-directed rhythm in late-1960s Motown soul (JAMS).

  • Builds at the start. Attas (2015) on the buildup introduction, which adds layers to an arrival; Spicer (2004) on accumulative form (both via Biamonte’s references).

  • The late rebuild. Carter’s 118 songs (1959 to 2024) break down to almost nothing at a median 62.6% of the song and arrive back at full strength at 79.9%, a median 33 seconds later, usually in three stages of four bars, usually into the chorus. Texture and density build in steps, dynamics and timbre smoothly. He traces it to gospel and soul

(“What’d I Say”, “Shout”, both 1959) and estimates up to one pop or rock song in eight uses it. These are the places v7’s own findings 749.19 (a breath at 0.55 to 0.60) and 749.17 (a high point at 0.65 to 0.85) already name, now with a mechanism.

  • The ending as climax. Osborn (2013): in terminally climactic forms, common in rock after 1990, the real high point is new material heard once at the end, beyond the chorus.

  • Builds and drops measured. In EDM, felt tension rises almost linearly through the build and peaks at the drop (Turrell et al. 2025); drops brought higher skin conductance than the rest of the break routine (Solberg and Dibben 2019).

  • Tension as its own dimension. Temperley’s The Musical Language of Rock (2018) models expression in three dimensions, valence, energy and tension, and traces shifts in them within songs (publisher’s summary). Energy (v7’s intensity) and tension are not the same axis.

For Jason’s songs this matters directly. Soul and gospel are where the breakdown and rebuild come from, and Fink’s case is Motown. Song 56’s soul ballad is exactly the kind of song whose tension plan v8 must write, not leave to a hand arrangement.

Measured here: tension readings on real songs and the engine’s

Harmonic tension and the listeners’ felt energy are two different curves in real hits: harmonic tension peaks in the pre-chorus and the bridge and resolves on the chorus’s first bar, while arousal peaks in the chorus itself. Neither the engine’s 1-to-3 chord value nor any per-bar harmony reading predicts arousal, which is why Windows 42 and 45 found nothing.

CoCoPops Billboard (Condit-Schultz, Arthur et al.; CC BY-NC 4.0): studies/tension/section_results.json

The data. CoCoPops Billboard (GitHub): 214 charting songs from 1959 to 1991 with expert melody and chord transcriptions, 100 of them with four listeners’ continuous arousal and valence and the recording’s loudness. Each bar got Lerdahl’s chord distance from the tonic and from the previous chord (it reproduces Table CO’s values: V and IV 5, vi and iii 7, ii and vii° 8), the engine’s old chord value, chord dissonance, melodic height and highest note, onsets per second, how much of the bar is sung, and the share of sung time on nonchord tones.

Models against listeners (100 songs, 10,289 rated bars; R² on held-out songs, arousal taken within song, each feature given a memory of its own length):

Reading Best memory R², held-out songs
Engine’s old chord value 32 s 0.009
Lerdahl distance from the tonic 32 s (0.000 with none) 0.017
Melody and texture 8 s 0.060
Everything in the score harmony 32 s, the rest 8 s 0.066
The recording’s loudness 8 s 0.084
Score and loudness harmony 32 s, the rest 8 s 0.126

What the numbers say:

  • The ceiling is low. Two halves of the listeners agree at a median of .49 (corrected; quartiles .10 and .77), so no model can reach far.

  • Melody height is the score’s best signal. It correlates .14 with arousal within songs (positive in 68% of songs); the highest note .13. Loudness does more (median song r .20).

  • Harmony works only on a long clock. Per bar it correlates about .03 with arousal. Given a memory, its value keeps rising out to 48 seconds, the same long harmonic window Farbood and Upham found in a Schubert song.

  • Harmony carries the syntactic build. At the last bar before a chorus the dominant is 0.51 standard deviations above its song’s mean; on the chorus’s first bar the tonic is 0.43 above, harmonic distance falls (−0.22) and the melody jumps (+0.38). The arousal ratings lag behind this by a bar or two.

  • Both builds come late. Smoothed harmonic tension peaks at a median 0.68 of the song (quartiles 0.48 and 0.86), a little before melodic height (0.75), loudness (0.73) and arousal (0.74), as a bridge or rebuild comes before the last chorus.

The engine’s songs 54 and 55 (country, no pre-chorus or bridge; chords typed by an AI, melody by the engine). Both put the dominant in the last bar before every chorus. Song 54 starts none of its four choruses on the tonic and carries its highest harmonic tension in the choruses (+0.54), where kept songs keep the chorus near the song’s mean (+0.05) and build in the pre-chorus. Song 55’s tension peaks at 0.93 of the song. The engine’s melodies already lift strongly at the chorus (+1.25 and +1.41 at bar 1, against +0.38 in kept songs). Two songs show only what a tension reader would flag, not a rate.

Cautions: arousal is not tension, the ratings are of 1959 to 1991 hits, and Lerdahl’s distance here has no tree above the phrase. The result is clear enough to build on: plan harmonic tension and energy as two curves, and give harmony a long memory.

What this means for v8: a tension plan the writers follow

v8 should plan two curves before any notes are written, harmonic tension and energy, and have the chord, melody and band writers draw toward them, with the measured targets below as gates. Because the engine writes its own chords, it already knows where its cadences fall; it does not need to parse a tree.

  1. The tension reader (score only).

    • Harmonic tension: Lerdahl’s distance from the tonic and from the last chord, plus chord dissonance, with a long memory (about 30 seconds), and two levels of goal: each phrase’s arrival chord and each section’s.

    • Energy: melodic height and onset rate with an 8-second memory, plus the band’s parts playing and dynamics from the band writer (749.17’s curve). Expectation: 749.18’s surprise and uncertainty, unchanged.

  2. The plan, per song type, drawn from kept songs.

    • Pre-chorus: harmonic tension about half a standard deviation above the song’s mean, moving off the tonic and ending on V (in kept songs the dominant is +0.51 at the last bar before a chorus).

    • Chorus: lands on the tonic at bar 1 (+0.43) with a melodic jump (+0.38); its harmonic tension near the song’s mean; the energy high. The chorus resolves; it is not the tense part.

    • Bridge: the second harmonic build (+0.37), its smoothed peak at about 0.68 of the song (quartiles 0.48 to 0.86), just before the energy peak at about 0.74.

    • Optional rebuild (soul, gospel, rock ballads): thin to almost nothing at about 0.62, rebuild in about three four-bar stages, arrive at about 0.80 on the chorus (Carter 2025). This is the mechanism behind 749.19 and 749.17.

    • Verse looser than chorus: more melody off the chord tones in the verse, tighter in the chorus (Temperley 2007).

  3. How each writer uses it. The chord writer (from the harmony study) draws section progressions and keeps those whose harmonic-tension profile fits the plan. The melody search keeps aiming at chord tones and adds the chorus-bar-1 lift. The band writer (from the arrangement study) builds the energy curve: half-time pre-chorus drums, fills as pickups into sections, the rebuild’s terraced entries.

  4. The hook lands on the release. In kept hits the title’s word sits over the tonic (37%) more often than over the chorus’s most tense chord (27%), and listeners’ arousal rises at peak notes, not at the most tense bars (Window 42). The convergence rule’s “maximum harmonic tension” leg should be restated as “the resolution after the build”.

  5. What to retire or restate. The 1-to-3 chord value (Table CO) is retired; it predicts nothing. Module 8’s audio scorer stays as an after-the-fact check, not the plan. Module 7’s structural-tone rule is reweighted toward melodic interval pattern and harmony, and chord-tone status alone is dropped (Kirlin and Yust 2015).

Tests. (a) On held-out kept songs the reader reproduces the section profile (pre-chorus above verse, V before the chorus, I and a lift at chorus bar 1, peak at 0.5 to 0.9); (b) every v8 song passes its type’s tension plan or says why not; (c) the no-hand-input test: the plan comes from the intake answers, not from typing; (d) a listening check of plan against no plan on the same lyric.

Still open. No open dataset of continuous tension ratings on pop songs turned up; the closest are CoCoPops’ arousal ratings and EDM build clips. A small listening study rating tension on 20 to 30 of the engine’s songs and kept songs would settle the weights. MorpheuS (Herremans and Chew), which rewrites music to a given tension profile, is a working precedent if the draw-and-gate approach falls short.

Files and sources

The scripts and results are in the repo under studies/tension (commit 29ab2a7): parse_cocopops.py , tension_features.py , ratings_test.py , section_test.py , profile_test.py and engine_songs.py , with their result files. The CoCoPops data is not kept in the repo; the README says how to fetch it. This study follows the audit, the harmony study and the arrangement study.

Sources (opened for this study; others named above were found in these papers’ reference lists):

Farbood, A parametric, temporal model of musical tension (Music Perception, 2012); Farbood and Upham, Interpreting expressive performance through listener judgments of musical tension (Frontiers in Psychology, 2013); Farbood, Memory of a tonal center after modulation (Music Perception, 2016)

  • Ruiz-Marcos, Willis and Laney, Automatically calculating tonal tension (2020), on Lerdahl’s model and its implementations

  • Herremans and Chew, Tension ribbons (2016) and MorpheuS (IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing, 2017)

  • Navarro-Cáceres et al., A computational model of tonal tension profile of chord progressions in the Tonal Interval Space (Entropy, 2020)

  • Barchet et al., TenseMusic (PLOS ONE, 2024)

  • Gingras et al., Linking melodic expectation to expressive performance timing and perceived musical tension (JEP: HPP, 2016)

  • Bigand and Parncutt, Perceiving musical tension in long chord sequences (Psychological Research, 1999)

  • Lehne, Rohrmeier, Gollmann and Koelsch, The influence of different structural features on felt musical tension (Music Perception, 2013); Lehne and Koelsch, Toward a general psychological model of tension and suspense (Frontiers in Psychology, 2015)

  • Granot and Eitan, Musical tension and the interaction of dynamic auditory parameters (Music Perception, 2011)

  • Cheung et al., Uncertainty and surprise jointly predict musical pleasure (Current Biology, 2019); Huron, Sweet Anticipation (2006)

  • Turrell, Halpern, Bannister, Chai-Wi-Ting and Javadi, Building the anticipation (Music Perception, 2025); Solberg and Dibben, Peak experiences with electronic dance music (Music Perception, 2019)

  • Kirlin and Jensen, Using supervised learning to uncover deep musical structure (AAAI, 2015); Kirlin and Yust, Analysis of analysis (Journal of Mathematics and Music, 2015)

  • Hamanaka, Hirata and Tojo, deepGTTM-IV (CMMR, 2023); Finkensiep and Rohrmeier, Proto-voice structure in free polyphony (ISMIR, 2021); Harasim, Rohrmeier and O’Donnell, A generalized parsing framework for generative models of harmonic syntax (ISMIR, 2018) and Harmonic syntax in time (ISMIR, 2019)
