Part 21. Metre research for Luthier v8: bars, phrases and hypermeter

16 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Metre research for Luthier v8: bars, phrases and hypermeter.

Summary

v8 should time sung lines in seconds rather than bars, give each section a four-bar plan, and let phrases stretch, shrink or overlap at the rates real songs use. Placement should choose the best setting by weighted rules instead of dying when no setting is perfect. All four placement failures of songs 54 to 56 come from v7 fixing a line’s length in bars before the words are known.

  • The research record. Theory treats bars as beats of a larger metre, which listeners infer from repetition and harmony. Rothstein’s expansions and overlaps let phrases bend over it. Hayes’s text-setting model treats placing words as weighing competing rules, learned from singers.

  • Pop. The average bar is about two seconds at any time signature (de Clercq 2016). Four-bar groups are the norm, and real songs expand, elide and insert bars freely. Metric irregularities cluster at section joins, and country is the most regular genre.

  • Measured here, on 9,313 lines in 198 charting songs:

    • Slow songs give a line fewer bars. Lines of 6 to 8 syllables take one bar 36% of the time in slow songs against 6% in fast ones, while slots in seconds change much less.

    • One-bar lines have spans that grow with their syllables.

    • Rests inside a line stay under a beat and a half.

    • Sung lines overlap the harmony’s four-bar groups with long pickups.

  • For v8: slots in seconds; the felt tempo chosen at intake; phrase operators drawn at kept rates; placement by weighted rules. These would close 749.25, 749.30 and 749.31, and let song 56 run at ♩ = 72.

What Luthier v7 does above the bar now

v7 measures beats inside a bar well, and phrase lengths as counts. But it has no model of strong and weak bars, of how a phrase can stretch, shrink or overlap, or of a tempo felt in half time. Lines are placed into fixed slots of one, two or four bars, and when the words do

not fit, the build dies.

Item Where in v7 What it does Its limit
Beat weight inside the bar Window 47; the Longuet-Higgins and Lee weights Sixteenth-note weights for syncopation Stops at the bar line; the word “hypermeter” appears nowhere in the spec
A line’s slot 27.41, fix 230 (Window 117) From syllables: one or two bars up to 5, two bars for 6 to 8, four bars from 9; a three-bar slot (8% of kept lines) only by design; a section’s slots must sum to a multiple of four Slots are set in the song’s file, not drawn; nothing says which bar of a four-bar group is strong
Where a line starts and lands 27.41, fix 231 55% of pop lines start with a pickup, 20% on the downbeat; the last stress lands on beat 1 in 23%, beat 3 in 20%, off the beat in 38% Shares within the bar only
Odd lengths Window 37 31% of chart sections are not a multiple of four bars; 21% of phrases are odd; offered as departures (a 9-bar chorus, a 6-bar bridge, a 2/4 bar before the chorus) A menu the writer picks from, priced in departure units; nothing writes them
Section lengths Windows 29, 41 Sections of eight bars; the first chorus near bar 20 Counts, not a phrase grammar
Felt tempo Window 131 Admits a song felt in half time would move its tempo bands Not modelled; song 56 at♩= 72 had to be written at 144 with a half-time feel

Where songs 54 to 56 broke.

  • Song 54 (749.25). Two-thirds of builds died for want of a placement, on 9- and 10syllable lines in two-bar slots with borrowed rhythms.

  • Song 55 (749.30). 678 of 1,000 builds died, 591 of them at the chorus’s one-bar lines of 4 to 6 syllables.

  • Song 55 (749.31). The survivors included short lines spread over two bars with a rest of three and a half beats in the middle.

  • Song 56. At ♩ = 72 with a line a bar, every one of 40 test builds died; it ran only at double tempo.

All four are the same gap: a line’s length in bars is fixed before the words are known, and nothing above the bar lets it stretch, shrink or overlap the next phrase.

The academic record: hypermeter, phrase rhythm, text-setting

Theory treats the bars of a phrase as beats of a larger metre. Phrases can stretch, overlap or shrink against that larger metre without breaking it. And setting words to a rhythm is a trade-off between rules, not a fit-or-fail test.

  • The metric hierarchy has limits in time. London’s Hearing in Time sets metric entrainment between about 100 milliseconds and 5 to 6 seconds. A four-bar group at pop tempos (6 to 9 seconds) is above that. So hypermeter is learned and inferred from repetition and harmony, not felt as a beat.

  • Phrase rhythm. Rothstein’s Phrase Rhythm in Tonal Music (1989) separates the regular hypermeter from the phrases laid over it. Phrases can be expanded internally or at their ends, or overlap so a bar ends one phrase and begins the next. An overlap can delete a bar from the pattern and shift strong and weak bars (study notes on Rothstein). Temperley (2008) adds the hypermetrical transition, a gradual shift from odd-strong to even-strong bars (as summarised by Bakulina).

  • Hypermeter is a learned expectation. Love (2015) models hypermeter as a momentto-moment expectation of two- and four-bar units, felt as accent, surprise, confusion, tension and relief, and recognised only after the cues have passed (MTO).

  • Metric dissonance. Krebs’s two kinds, carried into rock by Biamonte: displacement (a unit starts a slot early or late) and grouping (units bundled differently, as in a hemiola) (Biamonte 2014).

Text-setting as weighing rules. Halle and Lerdahl (1993) posed the problem: singers given a new verse for a known tune agree where its syllables go. Hayes (2009) models it as weighted constraints on a 16-position grid for a four-beat line:

  • stress on strong positions;

  • phrase-final stresses on strong beats;

  • strong positions filled, weak ones left empty, pauses at line edges;

  • no run of three empty positions;

  • long syllables on strong positions.

  • Weights learned from 425 folk-song lines chanted by English speakers predict their choices at r .88, and each singer’s own weights pick that singer’s favourite setting.

  • Pop text-setting is sensitive to syllable length. Ryan (2022), on 2,371 English pop songs, finds the grid placement follows syllables’ natural duration, beyond the lengthening at phrase ends.

For the engine, the text-setting work is the most directly useful. It describes placing a line as a choice among settings that each break some rules, scored by weights learned from songs. v7’s placement instead fails when no setting satisfies every rule at once.

Metre in popular song

Pop works in four-bar groups and an average bar of about two seconds. It stretches, cuts and overlaps phrases freely, and much of its metric irregularity sits at section boundaries.

  • The two-second bar. de Clercq (2016), across three rock and chart corpora:

  • Songs in four average about 120 beats a minute and songs in 6/8 about 60, so the average bar is about 2 seconds either way.

  • A bar should be read where the harmony and melody move, near 2 seconds, not where the drum pattern says.

  • Half-time is common in R&B and southern rap, double-time in metal and punk.

  • The same song can be drummed at very different speeds while its bars stay similar in length: one song’s two versions differ about sixfold in drum speed but only threefold in bar length.

In his country examples, a ballad near 72 beats a minute changes chord every two bars.

Four-bar groups, by repetition. Pop organises into quadruple hypermetre more often than not, and Temperley found half the chords on odd-numbered downbeats are the tonic (Fink 2023, citing Stephenson 2002 and Temperley 2018). Open Music Theory’s example: a four-bar chord loop sets the hypermeter (Open Music Theory).

  • Expansion, elision and insertion in real songs. Fink’s cases include:

  • an eight-bar chorus whose last bar doubles as the next unit’s first;

  • a harmony held on IV as a written-out pause;

  • a slowed harmonic rhythm making a verse 17 bars;

  • a chorus rerouted by V of vi and stretched to 11 bars;

  • a 23-bar verse built on a 16-bar phrase with an inserted passage;

  • a final chorus that drops four bars and adds a coda.

Metric dissonance, mostly at boundaries. Biamonte (2014) finds small-scale dissonances at openings, cadences and transitions, the commonest being a partial bar at a section join. Larger ones mark contrast, as in loose verses against tight choruses. About two-thirds of Beatles songs are in plain 4/4; country and songs with tambourine are the most regular; and dissonance rises over each band’s career and across the decades (MTO). Biamonte’s chapter adds pre-choruses that drop to half time and shortened bars that drive into the next section (Routledge Companion).

  • Odd lengths are ordinary. v7’s Window 37 already counts them: 31% of chart sections are not a multiple of four bars, and 71% of songs have at least one.

Measured here: how real songs place their lines

Real songs time a line in seconds, not bars. A slow song gives a line of the same length fewer bars, so its bars carry more syllables. v7’s slot table is in bars at every tempo. Song 56’s lines of 9 to 11 syllables in a 3.3-second bar ask about 3 syllables a second, inside what real slow songs sing (median 2.8, upper quartile 3.5), yet the bar-based table ruled the one-bar slot out.

CoCoPops Billboard (CC BY-NC 4.0): studies/metre/metre_results.json

The data. CoCoPops Billboard: 198 charting songs in 4/4 (1959 to 1991) with melody, syllables, sections and chord timestamps; 9,313 sung lines. A line starts at a capitalised syllable or after two beats of silence; its slot runs to the next line’s first syllable (Window 117’s rules).

Fast songs (bar under 1.8 s) Middle Slow songs (bar 2.6 s or more)
Songs / lines 75 / 3,419 98 / 4,277 25 / 1,244
6 to 8 syllables in one bar or less 6% 22% 36%
9 or more syllables in one bar or less 0% 1% 9%
9 or more syllables in four bars or more 51% 36% 18%
Median slot in seconds, 6 to 8 / 9 or more syllables 3.2 / 4.6 3.6 / 5.1 4.1 / 5.8
Syllables a second while singing (median) 3.45 3.14 2.81

What else the lines show:

  • The bar. A median 1.91 seconds (quartiles 1.67 and 2.32), close to de Clercq’s twosecond bar; 13% of songs have bars of 2.6 seconds or more. Song 56’s bar at ♩ = 72 is 3.33 seconds.

  • Pickups. 85% of verse lines and 80% of chorus lines start off the downbeat, more than Window 117’s 55% because a start anywhere after beat 1 counts here.

  • One-bar lines. 36% of lines take a bar or less; they hold a median 3 syllables (90th percentile 6), and 7% hold 7 or more. Their sung span grows with syllables: 1.5 beats for 3, 2.5 for 5, 3.25 for 7, 3.5 for 8 (medians). These are the spans a one-bar draw needs (749.30).

  • Rests inside a line. The longest rest inside a line has a 90th percentile of half a beat to a beat and a half, by syllables and slot. A silence of two beats or more is where transcribers start a new line, so song 55’s rests of three and a half beats read as two lines, not one (749.31).

  • Lines against the four-bar group. In 8- and 16-bar sections, chords put the tonic on bar 1 of the four-bar group 55% of the time (bar 3, 43%). Sung lines begin mostly in bars 3 and 4 (58%) as long pickups into the next group, and bar 3 holds the fewest sung notes (20%). The voice’s phrases overlap the harmonic groups rather than sitting inside them.

  • Odd sections. 33% of verse, chorus, pre-chorus and bridge sections are not a multiple of four bars, matching Window 37.

Cautions: these are 1959 to 1991 hits transcribed by experts; tempo is read from chord timestamps; and the line rule cannot see a long rest inside a line, so the inner-rest figures are a floor.

What this means for v8: a layer above the bar

v8 should time lines in seconds, give each section a four-bar plan, and let phrases stretch, shrink or overlap by measured rates. Placement should weigh competing rules and choose the best setting, not die when no setting is perfect.

  1. Slots in seconds, not bars. A line’s slot comes from its syllables and the song’s bar length, using the kept table above: in a slow song, 6 to 8 syllables take one bar 36% of the time, and 9 or more take two bars at the median. The singing rate stays inside kept quartiles for the tempo band (about 2.3 to 4.2 syllables a second). This replaces fix 230’s bar-based defaults and would have let song 56 run at ♩ = 72.

  2. The felt tempo is chosen, not patched. At intake the engine picks the bar level nearest two seconds where the harmony moves (de Clercq 2016) and records halftime or double-time as a feel. The double-tempo workaround of songs 51 and 56 becomes a setting.

  3. A four-bar plan per section.

    • Harmony marks bars 1 and 3 of each group (the tonic on bar 1 in 55% of kept groups).

    • Sung lines lie across the groups with long pickups (80% to 85% start off the downbeat), many entering in bars 3 and 4.

A breath falls near bar 3.

  1. Phrase operators, at kept rates. Before a build fails, the placer may: add a bar at a phrase’s end, making a 5-bar phrase or a 9- or 10-bar chorus; overlap a phrase’s last bar with the next phrase’s first;

    • hold a chord a bar longer inside the phrase;

    • split a long line into two;

drop a half bar at a section join.

Window 37’s rates set how often each may occur (31% of sections and 21% of phrases are odd), and Fink’s and Rothstein’s cases give the shapes. These are drawn by the engine, not picked from a menu.

  1. Placement by weighted rules. Score every candidate setting of a line by Hayes’s rules: stress on strong positions, phrase-final stress on strong beats, strong positions filled, no lapse of three empty positions, long syllables on strong positions. Learn the weights from kept lines and keep the best setting, as the melody judge already chooses among survivors.

  2. The three open findings, closed with these numbers.

    • 749.30: a one-bar line’s span comes from its syllables (median 1.5 beats for 3 syllables to 3.5 for 8).

    • 749.31: a rest inside a line is capped at the kept 90th percentile (half a beat to a beat and a half); a gap of two beats makes two lines.

    • 749.25: a borrowed rhythm that cannot take a line’s syllables splits notes or redraws, as operator 4 allows.

  3. Metric dissonance as a chosen tool. The shortened bar at a section join, the half-time pre-chorus and the cadential hemiola are offered by genre and section role. Country is the most regular genre (Biamonte), so its songs get few.

Tests.

    1. Songs 54, 55 and 56 run with placement deaths under one build in ten, song 56 at ♩ = 72 without the double-tempo trick.
    1. Every v8 song’s slots, by tempo band, fall inside the kept quartiles in seconds.
    1. Odd phrases and sections appear at kept rates across a run.
    1. Weighted placement predicts held-out kept settings better than the current rules.
    1. The no-hand-input test: slots come from the lyric and tempo, not typed per song.

Still open. No perception study of hypermeter in pop turned up. The kept data on line placement is 1959 to 1991 chart songs; Hooktheory’s lead sheets would add recent songs if they can be fetched again.

Files and sources

The scripts and results are in the repo under studies/metre (commit c3f7fdc): lines_cocopops.py and metre_test.py , with metre_results.json . The CoCoPops data is not kept in the repo; the README says how to fetch it. This study follows the tension study.

Sources (opened for this study; others named above were found in their reference lists):

  • de Clercq, Measuring a Measure: absolute time as a factor for determining bar lengths and meter in pop/rock music (MTO, 2016)

  • Biamonte, Formal functions of metric dissonance in rock music (MTO, 2014) and Rhythmic functions in pop-rock music (Routledge Companion chapter)

  • Fink, The ‘Anchoring vi Schema’ and its relation to phrase rhythm in popular music (Popular Music, 2023)

  • London, Hearing in Time (Oxford, chapter summary)

  • Rothstein, Phrase Rhythm in Tonal Music (1989), via study notes; Temperley, “Hypermetrical transitions” (Music Theory Spectrum, 2008), via Bakulina 2017

  • Love, Historical hypermetrical hearing (MTO, 2015)

  • Hayes, The textsetting problem (2009 talk) and Textsetting as constraint conflict (2009); Ryan, Syllable weight and natural duration in textsetting popular music in English (English Language and Linguistics, 2022)

  • Open Music Theory: hypermeter

  • CoCoPops (Condit-Schultz, Arthur and colleagues)

Part 22. Melody by genre for Luthier v8: scales, blue notes and the divorce

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Melody by genre for Luthier v8: scales, blue notes and the divorce.

Summary. v7 writes every melody from the 7-note major or minor scale and forbids the two notes that mark the blues, soul and much of rock: the flat third against a major chord (fix 200) and the flat fifth (tri()). The literature and the Billboard corpus agree that popular melody is largely pentatonic, that the flat seventh is ordinary, and that the flat third is a falling note near the tonic. In 165 major-key songs, notes fix 200 forbids appear in 63% of songs (69% in soul), and tri() mostly blocks plain diatonic notes. The engine’s two country songs have no flat 3 or flat 7, and song 54 sings the leading tone at three and a half times the country rate. v8 should take its pitch table from the style, allow flat 3, flat 7 and flat 5 where soul and blues put them, narrow tri(), and cap the leading tone.

What Luthier v7 does with scale and genre now

v7’s melody search draws from a seven-note scale and allows notes outside it only at a small kept rate, and only where they clash with nothing. In practice its code rules out the blue third over a major chord and the flat fifth. Blues tonality exists only as written rules in the blues template.

Item Where in v7 What it does Effect on country, soul, gospel and blues
The scale M.SCALE, the song’s seven-note key Every drawn note starts inside it A pentatonic line is possible, but only by chance; nothing favours the five-note scale
Notes outside the scale Fix 344 / 349 ( place_outside) A drawn share of notes, at the kept rate (half of builds draw none), moved a semitone Few, and only where the next rules allow
No chord tone a semitone away Fix 200 An outside note may not sit a semitone from a chord tone Rules out the flat third over a major tonic (a semitone below its third): the blue third of soul and blues
No tritone from the root tri() An outside note may not be a tritone from the chord’s root Rules out the flat fifth, the blues scale’s added note
Chord tones outside the scale Fix 375 A borrowed chord’s own outside tones are chord tones, and a note a semitone from one clashes Sensible for a borrowed chord; tightens the net further
Chromatic passing notes Fix 358 Off the beat, by step on both sides, over any chord The only way a blue note gets in: as a passing note
Pitch habits Window 99, the surprise band by class Melodic priors for pop, hymn, folk, standards and art song By class, not genre: country, soul and gospel are not separate
Blues tonality Window 15; Module 21 (Table: blue notes as flat 3, flat 5 and flat 7, pitch zones) Written rules for a blues song Rules, not code; the melody search above still applies

The gap: Temperley’s 2007 paper on the melodic-harmonic divorce is in v7’s citations, read only in part, and nothing in the engine lets a melody follow a five-note or blues framework over the band’s major chords. Every song Jason has written in country, soul and gospel has been drawn through these rules.

The academic record: rock and pop melody

Rock and pop melody draws on a wider collection than the major scale, leans on the flat seventh and the five-note scales, and often follows a different framework from the chords under it, most of all in verses and in songs from the blues and soul line.

  • The supermode. Temperley’s corpus work finds rock’s pitch collection spans all modal degrees except 2 and 4 flattened, ten neighbours on the line of fifths (Heetderks’s review of Temperley 2018). Most songs use only part of it.

  • Rock melody, counted (Temperley and de Clercq 2013, 200 Rolling Stone songs):

    • Melodic degrees follow the major scale’s pattern, with one exception: the flat seventh is more common than the major seventh, the reverse of classical music.

    • The “pentatonic union” (1, 2, flat 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, flat 7), the major and minor pentatonic scales together, is the second commonest set of degrees, the eight most frequent in 37 of 194 melodies; the major scale leads in 46.

    • Melodies cluster into major and minor, but 41 songs are minor in the melody and major in the harmony, a group tied to 1950s songs, blues-influenced rock and soul.

  • The melodic-harmonic divorce. In Temperley’s 2007 paper, non-chord tones that do not resolve by step mark the divorce, which comes mostly in pentatonic melodies and in verses. In rock, he writes, there are different frameworks for the melody and accompaniment (as quoted by Reed 2022). Nobile names three kinds, hierarchy, loop and syntax divorce (dissertation abstract).

  • The flat third and the major third together. Temperley, Ren and Duan (2017) measured sung pitch in “ABC” and other songs:

    • The flat third tends to come near the tonic and the major third near the fifth.

    • Descending lines to the tonic favour the flat third; choruses and cadences lean to the major third.

    • Pitches truly between the two (blue notes) are uncommon but occur, where these tendencies conflict.

    • Standard chromatic notes describe most of it.

  • Scalar shift. Temperley (2011) shows songs moving between pitch collections within a song, a borrowed flat-VII chord bringing the flat seventh with it (MTO).

  • Pentatonic harmony. Open Music Theory notes the pentatonic collection is one of the most pervasive in pop and rock, rooted in the blues, and often used as the roots of major chords (Open Music Theory).

For the engine this means three things. The flat seventh and the five-note scales are the norm, not departures. A minor-pentatonic melody over major chords is a recognised style with a known home (soul, blues, 1950s rock). And the flat third belongs near the tonic in falling lines, with the major third near the fifth and at cadences.

Blues, gospel, soul and country

The American vernacular styles share one melodic system: a mode built on the major tonic triad, with flexible thirds hanging above and below the tonic and the fifth, and dissonances against the chord that wait for the tonic to resolve. Blue notes are real but mostly fall near the chromatic notes a score can write.

  • One shared stock. Early blues and country musicians drew on the same schemes, harmonic grounds and tunes that generate many songs, and the two traditions are deeply intertwined (Stoia, OUP blog on his 2013 Spectrum article).

  • The mode and its thirds (Stoia 2010, recordings from the 1920s to the 1940s, after van der Merwe):

    • The tonic triad’s notes are the stable ones; the others are step neighbours or minor or neutral thirds above or below them.

    • A dropping third sits above a stable note and falls to it; a hanging third sits below and rises to it. They cluster around the tonic and the fifth.

    • The flat seventh is more common than in classical music.

    • Over IV the mode may move with the chord or stay put. Over V the major third keeps its flat neighbours because it is still the goal, and they resolve only when the tonic returns.

    • The minor third over the dominant is the characteristic blues sound, and tends to fall to the major third.

  • Blue notes, measured. Cutting (2019), on 15 classic blues recordings, found three blue-note clusters at about 319, 583 and 1,038 cents above the tonic (flat 3, flat 5 and flat 7 regions), with clusters particular to individual singers. In rock, Temperley, Ren and Duan found true in-between pitches uncommon (above).

  • Gospel and soul singers. Analysts describe Aretha Franklin singing mostly on the major pentatonic plus the flat third, touching both thirds and a blue note in between in a single melisma, and avoiding the leading tone (Hein on “Bridge Over Troubled Water”; on “Amazing Grace”). These are close readings of single performances, not counts.

  • v7’s own blues template already states the blue notes as flat 3, flat 5 and flat 7 in pitch zones (Module 21), from Kubik (2008); nothing in the melody code applies it.

For song 56 (a soul ballad) and the country songs, the melody needs:

  • the five-note scale as its base;

  • flat thirds that fall to the tonic or rise to the major third;

  • the flat seventh as an ordinary note;

  • dissonances over IV and V that resolve when the tonic returns.

v7’s fix 200 forbids the central one of these, the flat third against a major chord’s third.

What the songs do: measured

In 165 major-key Billboard songs, notes that v7’s fix 200 forbids appear in 63% of songs, and in 69% of soul songs; the engine’s two country songs have none, and no flat 3 or flat 7 at all.

Source: studies/genre/genre_test.py on CoCoPops Billboard (214 songs with melody, 165 in major keys) and the lead sheets of songs 54 and 55 · families tagged by artist

The method: studies/genre/genre_test.py reads every sung onset in CoCoPops Billboard with the key and the chord sounding at that moment. Families are my tagging by artist (26 soul and R&B, 20 country, 119 others), not a field in the corpus, so the family figures are rough.

  • Five-note scales. The median song puts 85% of its notes on one five-note scale (major or minor pentatonic on the tonic); 28% of songs put 90% or more there, 42% in soul. 60% of songs stay within the pentatonic union (Temperley’s eight degrees) for 95% of notes; only 58% stay within the major scale that well, and 46% in soul. Country is the most diatonic family: 85% of its songs are 95% major scale.

  • The flat third. 45% of major-key songs use it for more than 1% of their notes; 15% use it more than the major third, the minor-over-major songs (23% in soul, 5% in country). Of 1,684 flat thirds:

    • 38% sound over the tonic chord, 29% with the chord’s major third sounding, the exact clash fix 200 forbids; 25% over IV; 8% over V.

    • What comes next: 37% fall to 1 or 2, 30% repeat, 20% rise to 4 or 5, and only 8% rise by a semitone to the major third. The flat third is a falling note, as Temperley, Ren and Duan found, more than a lean into the major third.

  • The fix-200 case. A note outside the key’s scale a semitone from a chord tone comes about 29 times in 1,000 notes (59 in soul, 12 in country), and 77% of them move on by step. By degree: flat 3 (59%), flat 7 (18%), flat 5 (16%).

  • The tri() case. A note a tritone from the chord’s root comes 12 times in 1,000 notes, in 56% of songs. The commonest case is not a blue note but the plain leading tone over IV (36%), then 3 over a flat-VII chord (23%) and flat 5 over I (22%). tri() blocks diatonic, ordinary notes.

  • Verses and choruses. Choruses carry less flat 3 (2.6% against 3.6%) and flat 7 (2.5% against 3.5%) and more tonic, matching the finding that the major third belongs to choruses. Unresolved non-chord tones differ little (8.8% in choruses, 8.1% in verses, 130 songs); this measure does not reproduce the verse-heavy divorce.

  • Decades. The flat seventh is rare in the 1950s songs (1.0%) and about 3% from the 1960s on.

  • Songs 54 and 55. Both are 100% major scale, with no fix-200 notes, as the rules require. Song 55 is 90% pentatonic, close to the soul median. Song 54 puts 17.6% of its notes on the leading tone, three and a half times the country mean of 4.9%: its pitch prior treats the leading tone as an ordinary scale note.

What the further reading adds

The eight sources from the reference lists agree that blue notes are flexible zones heard against the harmony, not fixed extra pitches, and they add three rules a score can carry: where 6 goes, when a blue note becomes a chord tone, and how a phrase ends. Three were tested on the corpus ( studies/genre/genre_more.py ).

  • Blue notes are zones, not pitches.

    • Weisethaunet, from interviews and analyses of guitarists, argues the fixed out-of-tune third or seventh is a simplification; any chromatic note can be bent, and what matters is how it sits in the harmonic texture, with timbre and timing part of the effect (Popular Music 2001).

    • Curry models blues pitch as a ladder from the harmonic series (approximating C-E-G-B flat) and finds Robert Johnson sings the falling third to the tonic as a flat or neutral third over 70 times against about 14 major (Music Analysis 2017).

    • Kubik traces the blue third and seventh to African tonal systems built on the harmonic series (via Cutting); van der Merwe ranks the degrees most often treated as blue: the third, seventh, fifth and sixth (as quoted).

  • The ladder of thirds. Van der Merwe describes the blues mode as a flexible ladder of thirds piled above and below the tonic (as quoted); Stoia’s dropping and hanging thirds come from it.

  • Register (tested, not confirmed). Titon’s early blues transcriptions put the major third in the lower third zone (201 of 346 pitches) and the minor third in the upper zone (108 of 204), as reported by van der Bliek (2007). In Billboard melodies the flat third’s share of all thirds is about the same below and above each song’s median pitch (20% and 18%), so v8 needs no register rule.

  • Domesticated blue notes (tested). Wagner shows blue notes made consonant by chords of their own: flat 3 as the root of flat III, flat 7 as the root of flat VII, one flat 3 shared across I7, IV7 and V7 (Music Theory Spectrum 2003). In Billboard, 35% of flat thirds and 51% of flat sevenths are tones of the chord under them; the rest clash.

  • Where 6 goes (tested). Day-O’Connell separates the classical 6, falling to 5, from the pentatonic 6, rising to the tonic over the missing 7 (McFarland’s review). In Billboard, 6 falls to 5 32% of the time and rises to 1 20%; in soul the two are level (27% each), in country 6 rises to 1 only 14%.

  • The leading tone moves. It rises to 1 28% of the time (36% in country) and falls to 6 24%; it is a moving note, which song 54’s held leading tones are not.

  • Phrase endings. Blues vocal phrases tend to fall and end on a minor third resolving to the tonic (van der Bliek), matching the corpus finding that flat 3 falls to 1 or 2.

  • Shared forms. Stoia’s Sweet Thing (2021) traces one stanza scheme across blues, country, gospel and rock (Duke); it concerns form and is noted for the lyric writers, not the pitch table.

  • Moore (1995) maps the diatonic flat seventh in rock through examples (Cambridge); only the abstract was reachable.

What v8 should do

Make the melody’s pitch collection a style setting, as Window 99 already does for classes of song, and let the blues and soul notes in with rules for where they go rather than forbidding them.

  1. A pitch table per style. Replace the single 7-note M.SCALE draw with a degree table per style, measured from the families above and kept with the engine ( studies/genre/genre_results.json , degree_share ). Start with three: soul and R&B, country, pop and rock. Keep the major scale as the default for hymn mode and the carol styles.

  2. The five-note scale as a frame. Give each style a pentatonic share target (soul median 88%, country 82%, pop and rock 84%) and let the other two degrees in as passing and neighbour notes, so a melody is pentatonic in its long notes and diatonic in its short ones.

  3. Flat 3 and flat 7 as notes with a place (Stoia’s dropping thirds; Temperley, Ren and Duan):

    • flat 3 near the tonic, mostly falling to 1 or 2 or repeated, rarely rising to 3;

    • flat 3 allowed over I with the major third sounding, over IV and over V, in soul and blues styles;

    • flat 7 as an ordinary degree in soul, pop and rock, rare in country;

    • both less often in choruses and at cadences, where the major third and the tonic take over.

  4. Relax fix 200 by style. Keep it for hymn mode, carols and country (12 cases in 1,000 notes there). In soul and blues styles, allow the flat 3, flat 7 and flat 5 clash when the note moves on by step or falls to a chord tone, as 77% to 85% of real cases do.

  5. Narrow tri(). Stop it blocking the leading tone over IV and 3 over flat VII, which are diatonic and common; keep it only for the flat 5 outside soul and blues styles.

  6. The leading tone. Cap the leading tone in country and soul near the corpus rates (about 5% and 3%), and prefer it as a passing note. Song 54’s 17.6% shows the current table treats it as an ordinary scale note.

  7. Blue notes in performance only. True between-pitches are rare in the scores and in sung rock (Temperley, Ren and Duan). Write flat 3, flat 5 and flat 7 in the score, and leave the bend to the singer, with a performance note in the songbook for soul and blues styles.

Three more, from the further reading:

  • Two kinds of 6. In soul, let 6 rise to the tonic as often as it falls to 5; in country keep it mostly falling to 5.

  • Harmonize some blue notes. About a third of flat thirds and half of flat sevenths should land on chords that contain them (flat III, flat VII, I7, IV7), the rest left clashing and moving on by step.

  • Leading tone as a moving note. When it appears, it should move on, mostly up to the tonic or down to 6, not be held.

Checks for the port:

  • Each style’s degree shares within the 25th to 75th percentiles of its family’s songs.

  • Flat 3 placement: at least half falling to 1 or 2 or repeated; under 15% rising to 3.

  • Fix-200 cases per 1,000 notes near the family mean, and at least 75% moved on by step.

  • tri() blocks no diatonic note.

  • Song 56 (soul ballad) run under the soul table, songs 54 and 55 under the country table, each compared with its family.

Files and sources

In the repo, studies/genre/ :

  • genre_test.py : the measurement (reads studies/tension/cocopops_bars.json ,

  • made by parse_cocopops.py ; families tagged by artist in the script).

  • genre_results.json : every figure in this report, with the degree tables by family,

  • section and decade.

  • genre_per_song.json (not committed; rebuilt by the script) and README.md .

Data: CoCoPops Billboard, CC BY-NC 4.0; only derived counts are kept.

Sources read:

  • Temperley and de Clercq (2013), “Statistical Analysis of Harmony and Melody in Rock Music”, Journal of New Music Research (PDF).

  • Temperley, Ren and Duan (2017), “Mediant Mixture and ‘Blue Notes’ in Rock: An Exploratory Study”, Music Theory Online 23.1 (MTO).

  • Temperley (2007), “The Melodic-Harmonic ‘Divorce’ in Rock”, Popular Music 26.2 (abstract).

  • Temperley (2011), “Scalar Shift in Popular Music”, Music Theory Online 17.4 (MTO). Heetderks (2023), review of Temperley’s The Musical Language of Rock (MTO).

  • Stoia (2010), “Mode, Harmony, and Dissonance Treatment in American Folk and Popular Music, c. 1920–1945”, Music Theory Online 16.3 (MTO).

  • Stoia (2013), “The Common Stock of Schemes in Early Blues and Country Music”, Music Theory Spectrum 35.2 (OUP blog).

  • Cutting (2019), blue-note pitch clusters in early blues, Empirical Musicology Review (DOAJ).

  • Reed (2022), “An Idiom of Melodic-Harmonic Divorce: Sub-Circle Motion in Popular Music”, Music Theory Online 28.2 (PDF); Nobile, dissertation on divorce types (abstract).

  • Open Music Theory, “Pentatonic Harmony” (chapter).

  • Hein, close readings of Aretha Franklin (“Bridge Over Troubled Water”, “Amazing Grace”): a teacher’s blog, used for illustration only.

Further reading (the section above): Weisethaunet (2001), “Is There Such a Thing as the ‘Blue Note’?”, Popular Music 20.1; Wagner (2003), “‘Domestication’ of Blue Notes in the Beatles’ Songs”, Music Theory Spectrum 25.2; van der Bliek (2007), “The Hendrix Chord”, Popular Music 26.2; Curry (2017), “Two Approaches to Tonal Space in the Music of Muddy Waters”, Music Analysis 36.1; Day-O’Connell (2007), Pentatonicism from the Eighteenth Century to Debussy , through McFarland’s review ( MTO 15.2). Read only at second hand or by abstract: van der Merwe, Origins of the Popular Style (1989); Kubik (2008) and Africa and the Blues (1999); Moore (1995), “The So-Called ‘Flattened Seventh’ in Rock”, Popular Music 14.2; Stoia, Sweet Thing (2021). Found on the way, not read: Titon, Early Downhome Blues (1994); Curry (2015) on Robert Johnson, Popular Music ; Wagner (2004), “Fixing a Hole in the Scale: Suppressed Notes in the Beatles’ Songs”, Popular Music 23.3; Doll (2025) on the Sweet Thing scheme, ZGMTH 22.1.

Part 23. Setting words for Luthier v8: stress, vowels and high notes

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Setting words for Luthier v8: stress, vowels and high notes.

Summary. Luthier v7 already measures stress on the beat, line endings and vowels on held notes, but it set aside a rule for a word’s pitch shape and any vowel table for men, and its songs put weak syllables on the downbeat. In 199 Billboard songs and 80 Rolling Stone 200 songs, weak syllables take beat 1 only 4% to 6% of the time, and a word’s stressed syllable is lower than its other syllables in 18% to 20% of words. Songs 54 and 55 do both about twice as often (10% to 12%, and 34%), mostly through line openings like “And” and “But” on the bar line. On vowels, height alone barely matters; held high notes do, with men’s held top notes open 61% of the time and reduced only 7%. v8 should grade its stress cost, give weak line openings a pickup, add a word-shape rule for pitch, and add a vowel rule for held high notes by voice, all as weights in Part 21’s placement. A second round of reading adds two measured rules: stress and metre should move together between neighbouring syllables (song 54 opposes them 47% of the time across words, against 29% in the corpus), and words ending in a voiced consonant take longer notes (55% against 33%). Across the century (the Pop20c corpus, 1900 to 1999), weak syllables on beat 1 stay near 5% in every period while syncopation more than doubles, so the downbeat band is fixed and the contour targets depend on era and style. After 2000 melodies carry more notes a bar (about 6 against 4.8) and more sixteenths, with fewer anticipations; songs 54 and 55 already have that rhythm, and what they lack is the word placement inside it. In hits from 2000 to 2022 (BiMMuDa) the word rules hold as before: weak syllables on beat 1 are if anything rarer, and the voiced-ending lean remains. Hymns, folk songs and standards with words attached (PDMX and OpenEWLD, 4,535 songs) give v8 its hymn-mode bands: weak syllables on beat 1 up to about 10% in 4/4 and 17% in 3/4, stresses on beat 1 more often, and a looser word pitch shape; song 53, written by sketch, sits inside them.

What Luthier v7 does now

v7 is already strong on words: it measured stress, vowels and line endings on large corpora and built them in. Its gaps are the ones it named itself: no rule for a word’s pitch shape, nothing that keeps weak syllables off the downbeat beyond the stress floor, and no vowel table for men.

What it has (Luthier v7):

  • Stress on the beat (Window 25). On 646,345 karaoke syllables, a syllable on a strong beat is stressed 75% of the time against a base rate of 54%. The engine’s alignment floor reads stressed syllables on beats, with monosyllabic function words counted unstressed.

  • Anticipation credited (Module 10.19, Window 69). A stressed syllable an eighth before an empty strong beat counts as on it (rock does this with about a quarter of its stresses).

  • Length. Stressed syllables are only a tenth longer; the title’s last stress is held about 1.5 times; a line’s last note runs about 1.9 times the rest, and a line that ends short is named. English popular song holds a word’s last syllable rather than its stressed one (Window 98).

  • The high note. The line peaks early (17% of the way in) and its last stress is held low; the peak avoids reduced vowels.

  • Vowels (Window 39). Register does not change the vowel in pop; held notes favour open vowels (56% against 50%), the strongest phonetic hit signal v7 found. A vowel term rewards open vowels on held notes and forbids a reduced vowel on the peak. Lax vowels lean to short notes, tense vowels and diphthongs to long ones (a lean, named per note).

  • Intelligibility (Window 69). Word familiarity is the one large effect; stress mismatch and melisma are small; consonant and mishearing loads are reported. Female vowel bands by pitch (trouble from C5) are carried as information.

  • Entries (fixes 731, 742, 749). The kept line is drawn by its first syllable’s stress; unstressed openings still land on the bar line three or four times as often as in kept songs.

What v7 did not build, in its own words: a pitch-accent rule, male or belt vowel tables, and isochrony. Its reasons were that no English corpus coded accents against melody and the proxies were modest. Two corpora now let both be measured directly (below).

Where songs 54 to 56 struggled with words: two syllables on one onset (749.1, 749.26), placement deaths at long lines (749.3, 749.25, 749.30), and unstressed openings on the bar line (742, 749). Part 21 traced the placement deaths to slots fixed in bars; this study looks at the syllables themselves.

Stress and the beat: what the research says

The text-setting literature treats stress placement as a ranked set of preferences, not a pass-or-fail rule, and it adds two things v7 lacks: stress has levels (inside a word, across words, at phrase ends), and weak syllables on strong beats are worse than strong syllables off them.

  • Halle and Lerdahl, then Hayes. Halle and Lerdahl (1993) gave the first explicit model of how speakers fit new words to a tune; Hayes recasts it as constraint conflict, where a good setting is the best compromise among stressed syllables on strong positions, no long gaps without a syllable, no extreme crowding, and phrase breaks at line ends, and a stress may move to a weak position to avoid a long gap (Hayes, Textsetting as Constraint Conflict). Part 21 already recommends this weighted approach for placement.

  • Stress has levels (Hayes and Kaun 1996, 670 folk-song lines set by ten speakers): Word-internal stress falls are set more strictly than those across words.

    • Phrase ends are set more strictly the bigger the phrase: at the end of an intonational phrase, 1,102 settings matched the metre against 12 that did not. Unfilled positions count as weaker than any unstressed syllable.

    • Inversions (a stress on a weak position) are a last resort and cluster at line ends. Syllables tend to get beats in proportion to their natural length; a long first syllable is not crowded.

  • Natural length in pop. Ryan (2022), on 2,371 English popular songs, found placement on the grid is sensitive to a syllable’s natural duration even after final lengthening is controlled, measured between perceptual centres (English Language & Linguistics).

  • Short stressed syllables and the snap. Temperley and Temperley (2011) tie the Scotch snap (a sixteenth on the beat, then a dotted eighth) to English’s very short stressed syllables; four vowels account for much of both (Music Perception).

  • Composers align better than after-the-fact setters. Palmer and Kelly (1992) found syllables aligned with linguistic or musical accent are sung longer, and compound and phrase stress follow English’s rules (PDF).

  • Stopwords. In 679 popular lead sheets, monosyllabic function words become less likely the stronger the metric position, and unstressed syllables are very unlikely on downbeats (Nichols et al. 2009).

For v8 this means the alignment check should be graded: a word-internal mismatch costs more than one across words; a weak syllable on beat 1 costs more than a stress on an offbeat; a line’s end is strict and its start free.

Stress and pitch: what the research says

In English, pitch is a stronger cue to stress than length, and songs follow speech here: stressed syllables tend to sit higher than their neighbours. The studies are small, which is why v7 left it out; the corpus below measures it directly.

  • Chen and Mok (2014) , 15 English songs, multi-syllable words only (Speech Prosody): Lexical stress matched the metre perfectly in about 68% of cases, a secondary match in 9%, a mismatch in 23%.

    • Judged against the notes either side, primary stresses matched the pitch pattern (higher than the neighbours) 141 times against 92, about 1.5 to 1; for duration the ratio was 1.2.

    • They conclude pitch matches stress better than duration does, as pitch is the stronger cue to English stress in speech.

  • Nichols et al. (2009) , 679 lead sheets: stressed syllables and melodic peaks are associated, and peaks are more often on content words than function words, though the paper reports this only in figures (ISMIR).

  • Across languages. A comparison of Turkish and English children’s songs coded stress against metrical strength and melodic peaks, building on the English findings that stressed syllables align with higher notes (Kabak and Domene Moreno).

  • Speech’s own pattern. In English, pitch accents fall on stressed syllables, which are also longer, louder and have fuller vowels (Zahner, Kember and Braun 2017).

The simplest test of a pitch-accent rule is inside the word, where nothing else changes: is the stressed syllable of “mother” or “believe” higher than the other one? That is what the corpus measure below does.

Vowels and high notes: what the research says

Vowels lose their identity as the sung pitch climbs toward the vowel’s first resonance, and singers answer by adjusting the vowel rather than avoiding it. For men in pop the critical zone is the top of the chest voice, about E4 to A4, where belters tune a resonance to the second harmonic.

Where identification fails. Above about C5 (523 Hz), listeners’ identification of every vowel but /a/ falls toward chance (Friedrichs et al.). Smith and Scott (1980) found isolated soprano vowels above F5 lost half their intelligibility against C♯5, but with a raised larynx, as in popular styles, the drop between C♯5 and F5 was only 10% (Collister and Huron 2008).

  • Men too, at their own pitches. Chan and Kuang (JASA) played words sung by a soprano, mezzo, tenor and baritone from C2 to D6 to 102 listeners: identification declines as the fundamental approaches the first formant, sung vowels decline earlier than synthesized ones, AE and EH are easily confused, and IY is not safe when sung (summary). Its cause is both the singers’ adjustments and the spectrum itself.

  • What male belters do. Six male music-theatre singers, recorded on [e] and [ɔ] at the top of their belt range (about 250 to 440 Hz, roughly B3 to A4), tuned the first resonance to the second harmonic in every quality (Bourne et al. 2016). Titze’s belt examples modify toward /æ/, /a/ and a bright rounded vowel in the G4 to C5 range, and his instructor did not count /i/ as a belt vowel (Titze).

  • Belt against opera. Titze and Worley model belting as vowels shaped like a megaphone, keeping the fundamental and second harmonic below the first formant, where operatic singing lifts the harmonics over it (JASA 2009).

  • Modification is the norm. Pedagogy describes shading vowels so the sung pitch or a harmonic sits near a formant, varying with voice size, note length, loudness and approach (Nix 2004).

Two things follow for the engine. A vowel rule for men belongs at the top of the singer’s chest range and on held notes there, not at a fixed absolute pitch. And close vowels (/i/, /u/) are the risky ones on a held high note, while open and mid vowels are the ones belters can tune.

What the songs do: measured

In real songs a weak syllable almost never takes beat 1 and a word’s stressed syllable is rarely its lowest note; songs 54 and 55 break both about twice as often. On vowels, men’s songs lean to open vowels and away from reduced ones on held high notes, not on high notes as such.

Source: studies/words/words_test.py on CoCoPops Billboard (stress from the CMU dictionary) and Rolling Stone 200 (stress from its own spine), and the lead sheets of songs 54 and 55

The method: studies/words/words_test.py reads every sung syllable of the 4/4 songs in two corpora, with its note, its place in the bar and its word. Billboard (199 songs in 4/4) has lyrics but no stress, so stress comes from the CMU dictionary, with one-syllable function words counted unstressed as v7 does. The Rolling Stone 200 subset (80 songs) carries its own stress marks, from Tan, Lustig and Temperley’s algorithm, and agrees with Billboard on every measure both can make (lines and vowels are read from Billboard only). Songs 54 and 55 are read from their lead sheets the same way; they have only 44 and 41 words of two or more syllables, so their word-pitch figures are rough.

  • Stress and the beat. Stressed syllables take beat 1 19% of the time and beat 3 16%; unstressed syllables take beat 1 4% and beat 3 5% (Billboard; Rolling Stone 21% and 16% against 6% and 5%). Of one-syllable function words, 5% fall on beat 1, against 18% of one-syllable content words. Songs 54 and 55 put 12% and 10% of their weak syllables on beat 1, about two and a half times the corpus, and as many function words there as content words. Most are line openings (“And”, “But”, “I”, “To” on the bar line), the entry problem of fixes 742 and 749, and the rest are articles mid-line.

  • Stress and pitch, inside the word. In 6,380 Billboard words with a primary stress and an unstressed syllable, the stressed syllable is higher 44% of the time, level 36% and lower 20% (Rolling Stone 45%, 37%, 18%). Words that start on their stress are lower only 18% of the time; words stressed later (“believe”) 27%. Songs 54 and 55 sing the stress lower 34% of the time.

  • Local peaks. A stressed syllable is a local peak (above both neighbours) 19% of the time, an unstressed one 9%, about two to one in both corpora. Song 55’s weak syllables are peaks 19% of the time, as often as its stressed ones.

  • Stress and length inside the word. The stressed syllable is longer than the word’s unstressed syllables 30% of the time and shorter 19%; half are the same length. Song 55 sings it shorter 37% of the time.

  • The line’s last stress (3,569 Billboard lines with three stresses or more):

    • It lands on beat 1 or 3 only 21% of the time against 37% for the line’s other stresses, and on an offbeat eighth 47% of the time: it anticipates.

    • It is longer than the line’s mean note 65% of the time (other stresses 42%), and above the line’s mean pitch only 46% (others 57%): held and low, as Window 25 found.

    • It is the rhyme word two times in three.

  • Vowels by register and length, by singer (Billboard, 94 male and 28 female singers by SingerSex.txt; male median note D4, median top note A4):

Notes Men: open Men: close Men: reduced Women: open Women: close Women: reduced
All sung notes 48% 30% 22% 49% 32% 19%
Top tenth of the song’s range 50% 32% 18% 52% 34% 14%
At or above E4 (men) / C5 (women) 49% 32% 19% 51% 39% 10%
Held a beat or more 59% 30% 11% 56% 36% 9%
Held and in the top tenth 61% 32% 7% 55% 38% 8%

Height alone barely moves the vowel, as v7’s Window 39 found; length does, and length at the top does most. Men’s held high notes carry an open vowel 61% of the time and a reduced one 7%, a third of the base rate. Close vowels do not thin out at the top for either sex: singers modify them rather than avoid them, as the acoustics studies describe.

What the further reading adds

The second round of reading confirms the shape of the rules (strict inside words and at line ends, free at line starts, length follows the vowel) and adds two measurable ones: stress and metre should move the same way between neighbouring syllables, and a word ending in a voiced consonant takes a longer note. Both were tested ( studies/words/words_more.py).

  • Halle and Lerdahl’s model starts by assigning accented syllables to the available strong beats from left to right, aiming for settings speakers of the tradition accept (de Castro Arrazola 2018, ch. 6); the original article was not reachable.

  • Hayes’s weighted model gives each candidate setting a probability from weighted rule violations, about 117 candidates a line; its predictions correlate with nine speakers’ vote shares at r = 0.883, and two speakers’ learned weights differed markedly, which Hayes reads as different idioms (Hayes, maxent slides). Weights can be fitted per style.

  • English against French. English matches stress and beat anywhere in a line; French enforces the match rigidly only at line ends (Dell and Halle 2009).

  • Dutch folk songs (3,724 songs, 176,708 syllables): no alignment is avoided at the start of a phrase; inside words both kinds of opposed movement are avoided, the strongest constraints anywhere (de Castro Arrazola 2018, ch. 6). In a listening test with 135 Dutch speakers, parallel stress and metre won over opposed ones; s–p– beat s–p+ in 73% of trials (ch. 7).

  • Anticipation, in full. Tan, Lustig and Temperley’s 80 rock songs: 22.8% of stressed syllables sit on weak eighths, 77% of those just before a strong beat, in 66 of 76 songs above half; the pull is strongest into beat 3 (from the eighth before it) and beat 1 of the next bar (Music Perception 2019). Their stress algorithm is the one in the Rolling Stone files used here.

  • Pop after 2015. White (2022) found postmillennial melodies deliver words faster, spread onsets more evenly, repeat rhythm cells more, and use the last eighth of the bar much less than the rock corpus did (Journal of Mathematics and Music; abstract). The anticipation rules are era-dependent.

  • Vowel length in the laboratory. 87 listeners placed the longer of two words on a half note 63% of the time; tense-lax pairs about 2 : 1, voiced-voiceless pairs about 1.5 : 1, the tense effect the stronger (Gilroy, Blumenfeld and Toivonen 2024).

Measured:

  • Stress and metre as contours. Between neighbouring syllables where both stress and metrical strength change, they move in opposite directions 21% of the time inside a word and 29% across words (Billboard; Rolling Stone 24% and 30%). Inside a word the falling case (“MO-ther”) is opposed only 15%; the rising case (“be-LIEVE”) 39%, and two-thirds of those put the stress on an offbeat eighth, the anticipation. At a line’s first pair, falling stress is opposed only 12%. Song 54 is opposed 47% across words (64% when the stress falls) and 37% inside words, against 29% and 15%; song 55 sits near the corpus (23% and 18%).

  • Voiced endings get longer notes. One-syllable content words ending in a voiced consonant (“bed”, “love”, “eyes”) take a note longer than the song’s median 55% of the time; those ending voiceless (“bet”, “life”, “ice”) 33%, with line-final words left out. Crossed with the vowel: tense and voiced 58%, tense and voiceless 35%, lax and voiced 52%, lax and voiceless 29%. In real songs the voicing effect (about 22 points) is larger than the vowel’s (about 6), the reverse of the laboratory. Songs 54 and 55 show the voicing lean weakly and sing tense vowels on long notes less often than lax ones (26% against 29%, and 40% against 44%).

Across the century

A third round of reading, and a third corpus, show which word rules are fixed and which move with the era. Weak syllables on beat 1 stay at about 5% in every period from 1900 to 1999; syncopation, and with it the share of stresses set against the metre, more than doubles.

  • Where English allows a mismatch. Dell and Halle (2009), as summarised by Proto: in English folk songs a stress-to-beat mismatch is not allowed inside a word, nor across a word boundary when the unstressed syllable comes first (Proto 2013). So “MOther” set backwards is out, and so is “the MAN” with “the” on the beat and “man” off it; “MAN the” the other way round is tolerated.

  • Mismatches have grown rarer over the centuries. In nearly 90 English songs from the 13th century to Shakespeare’s time, about half had at least one mismatch inside a word; present-day English folk song is stricter, and the old leftover is the inversion at the right edge of a phrase (Proto 2013).

  • Listeners hear it. In a sung-word recognition study, words were recognised more often when their stress matched metrical prominence, and wrong answers followed the metre (“disease” sung with the accent on its first syllable heard as “dizzy”) (Taniguchi, AMLaP abstract).

  • Two kinds of syncopation, two roots. Second-position syncopation (an accent on the second quarter of a half-note or quarter-note unit) is common in 19th-century English, Scottish and American song and rare in German, Italian and French; its strongest forms are almost only British, and Temperley ties the snap to short stressed English syllables (Temperley 2019). Fourth-position syncopation, the anticipatory kind, appears in no published 19th-century vocal music and first shows in ragtime around 1900 (Temperley 2021).

  • Syncopation rose all century. In the most popular American song of each year from 1900 to 1999, syncopation increases throughout, and its strong forms rise faster and later than its weak ones (VanderStel and Temperley 2022).

  • Line ends mark the stanza. In Appalachian folk quatrains, truncated lines (a silent last beat) mark line, couplet or quatrain ends; 4444 (203) and 4343 (188) are the commonest forms, and 4333 is essentially absent while 3343 is tolerated, a long-last tendency (Hayes and MacEachern 1998, class notes). Part 21’s phrase rules already cover this at the level of bars.

Measured on Pop20c (the most popular song of each year, transcribed from recordings, with stress; 77 songs in simple quadruple time, studies/words/pop20c_test.py):

Period (songs) Weak syllables on beat 1 One-syllable function words on beat 1 Stresses on an offbeat eighth Of those, anticipations Stress lower than its word Opposed across words Opposed inside words
1900–1929 (29) 5% 7% 14% 55% 31% 15% 5%
1930–1954 (12) 5% 7% 26% 80% 28% 19% 8%
1955–1979 (19) 7% 8% 24% 56% 21% 18% 10%
1980–1999 (17) 5% 5% 34% 65% 23% 38% 26%

The weak-syllable floor on beat 1 holds in every period, so v8’s band for it needs no era setting. The stressed syllable’s place inside its word settles at about a fifth from the 1950s on. Stresses on offbeat eighths more than double, and the share of stress and metre moving against each other rises with them (it counts anticipations as opposed); that target has to be set by era and style. Songs 54 and 55’s weak syllables on beat 1 (10% to 12%) exceed every period.

After 2000

Since 2000 sung melody has got faster and more even: more notes to the bar, more sixteenths, fewer notes on the downbeat, and fewer of the anticipations that marked latecentury rock. Songs 54 and 55 already have a modern rhythm; what they lack is the word placement inside it.

  • Faster, more even, more repetitive. White (2022) compared 192 melodies from 1957–1997 with 24 hits from 2015–2019 (manuscript):

    • Notes per second rose from 1.87 to 2.71, and notes per bar from about 4.3 to 6.8.

    • Onsets are spread more evenly across the bar (entropy 0.81 to 0.89), with fewer on the downbeat and on the bar’s last eighth.

    • Four-note rhythm cells repeat much more (fit slope −4.2 to −6.9).

    • The rap, hip-hop and trap songs deliver faster than the pop ones (3.6 against 2.5 notes per second); the author warns the genre split is statistically fragile.

  • The late century, more syncopated than any songbook. In 124 Billboard songs from 1958–1991, about 28% of all notes are onset syncopations under a broadened definition, and syncopations on the fourth position (anticipations) outnumber those on the second; ones followed by a rest are rare (Condit-Schultz 2019).

  • The century’s trend. Syncopation rises throughout the century, the strong forms faster and later than the weak (VanderStel and Temperley 2022); the full paper was not reachable.

Measured on Pop20c, rhythm only so the 20 post-2000 transcriptions (no lyrics) can join, turned into note lists by the corpus’s own script; songs on a sixteenth grid; medians of songs ( studies/words/pop20c_rhythm.py):

Period (songs) Notes on beat 1 Notes on offbeat eighths Notes on sixteenths Offbeat eighths that anticipate an empty beat Notes per sung bar
1900–1929 (29) 21% 27% 1% 31% 3.3
1930–1954 (12) 20% 35% 2% 44% 3.4
1955–1979 (19) 17% 42% 2% 36% 3.6
1980–1999 (17) 10% 41% 4% 53% 4.8
2000–2019 (11) 11% 42% 13% 26% 6.1
Song 54 13% 41% 13% 21% 4.2
Song 55 12% 40% 15% 38% 4.4

The anticipation peaks in 1980–1999 and falls back after 2000 as sixteenths fill the gaps, as White found. Songs 54 and 55 sit between the late century and today on every rhythm measure; their problem is not the rhythm but which syllables it puts where (the sections above). Only 11 of the 20 post-2000 songs sit on a sixteenth grid, so that row is rough.

Words after 2000

The word rules hold in today’s hits. In one corpus that runs from 1950 to 2022, weak syllables on beat 1 are, if anything, a little rarer after 2000, the stressed syllable’s place inside its word is unchanged, and voiced endings still take longer notes.

The corpus is BiMMuDa (Hamilton and Pearce): the melodies of the top five Billboard year-end singles for every year from 1950 to 2022, transcribed by hand, one MIDI per section, with the lyrics as text but not attached to the notes (repository). Words were attached only where a section’s note count equals a lyric stanza’s syllable count exactly, and a section was kept only if its lyric line ends fall on long notes or before gaps (line-final notes at least 1.5 times the rest), a check that does not use stress. 145 of 165 matched sections passed, from 106 songs in 4/4 ( studies/words/bimmuda_words.py).

Period (songs, sections) Weak syllables on beat 1 Function words on beat 1 Stress lower than its word Opposed across words Voiced ending on a long note Voiceless ending on a long note
1950–1979 (37, 54) 8.8% 9.2% 22% 34% 47% 30%
1980–1999 (29, 35) 9.0% 9.4% 27% 45% 33% 31%
2000–2022 (40, 56) 7.2% 7.7% 24% 39% 40% 29%

Compare these within the corpus only. BiMMuDa writes songs at a slower beat than the other corpora (15% to 22% of its notes are sixteenths in every era, against 1% to 4% in Pop20c before 2000), so its “beat 1” takes in more of what other transcribers would write as beat 3; its levels run higher for that reason. Within it, the after-2000 songs keep weak syllables off beat 1 at least as well as earlier hits, sing the stressed syllable below the rest of its word about a quarter of the time as before, and keep the voiced-ending lean (40% against 29%). Stress and metre pull apart across words most in 1980–1999 and a little less after 2000, matching the fall in anticipations above.

For v8 the word rules carry into a modern style unchanged; only the rhythm targets (notes per bar, sixteenths, anticipations) need the era setting.

Hymns, folk songs and standards

Two open corpora with the words attached to the notes give v8 bands for its hymn mode and its folk and older-style songs. These styles allow more weak syllables on beat 1 than pop (about 10% in 4/4, about 16% in 3/4), put stresses on beat 1 more often, and let a word’s stress sit below the rest of the word more often; the voiced-ending lean holds in all of them.

  • PDMX (Long et al.; public-domain MuseScore scores, Zenodo record 15571083, CC BY 4.0): of 254,077 scores, 15,522 have at least 30 lyric syllables, no duplicates and no licence conflict; 4,176 of them are in English (85% of words in the CMU dictionary) and in 4/4 or 3/4. Categories come from PDMX’s genre and tag fields.

  • OpenEWLD (Simonetta; the public-domain part of the Wikifonia lead sheets, GitHub): 359 English standards and popular songs, dated by first performance.

The words come from the scores themselves, so no alignment is guessed. The scores are transcriptions and arrangements by MuseScore users, of uneven quality; the large numbers are what make them usable ( studies/words/mxl_words.py, score_words.py, pdmx_words.py, openewld_words.py).

Corpus, style and metre (songs) Weak syllables on beat 1 Function words on beat 1 Stresses on beat 1 Stress lower than its word Opposed across words Voiced / voiceless ending long Held top notes: open / reduced
PDMX popular, 4/4 (483) 6.2% 7.3% 22% 25% 27% 55% / 38% 57% / 12%
PDMX hymns and sacred, 4/4 (223) 9.7% 12.5% 36% 28% 17% 47% / 37% 51% / 19%
PDMX hymns and sacred, 3/4 (60) 15.6% 19.5% 57% 33% 18% 59% / 52% 57% / 19%
PDMX folk, 4/4 (185) 9.1% 11.1% 31% 22% 20% 52% / 37% 55% / 16%
PDMX folk, 3/4 (42) 16.9% 18.3% 53% 36% 22% 49% / 42% 55% / 14%
PDMX other classical, 4/4 (2,590) 9.3% 10.5% 36% 28% 18% 50% / 41% 54% / 18%
PDMX other classical, 3/4 (553) 11.0% 13.3% 61% 30% 8% 57% / 50% 53% / 19%
OpenEWLD standards before 1930, 4/4 (98) 9.7% 12.1% 43% 33% 17% 49% / 44% 48% / 17%
OpenEWLD standards 1930 on, 4/4 (66) 7.2% 9.3% 42% 36% 12% 59% / 44% 47% / 20%

What it shows:

  • The method checks out. PDMX’s popular songs land close to Billboard: weak syllables on beat 1 6% against 4%, stresses on beat 1 22% against 19%.

  • Hymn and folk bands. In 4/4, weak syllables on beat 1 run about 9% to 10% and stresses take beat 1 a third of the time; in 3/4, where beat 1 is the bar’s only strong beat, weak syllables on it run about 16% to 17% and stresses take it over half the time. Song 53, written by sketch in 3/4, has no weak syllable on beat 1 and puts 47% to 50% of its stresses there: inside the hymn band, and stricter.

  • The word’s pitch shape is looser in older styles. The stress sits below the rest of its word in 22% to 36% of words in hymns, folk songs and standards, against 18% to 25% in pop. The target should be set by style.

  • Stress and metre pull apart less in hymns and classical song (8% to 18% across words) than in pop (27%), as expected of styles with little syncopation.

  • Voiced endings take longer notes in every category , by 5 to 17 points; the gap is smallest in early standards and 3/4 hymns.

  • Held top notes carry an open vowel 47% to 57% of the time everywhere; reduced vowels there run 12% in pop and 17% to 20% in hymns, classical song and standards, where a held “the” or “-ing” on a long final note is common.

What v8 should do

Keep v7’s word rules and add three: a graded cost for weak syllables on strong beats, a word-shape rule for pitch, and a vowel rule for held high notes by voice. Each fits Part 21’s weighted placement, where a setting is the best compromise rather than a pass or a death.

  1. Grade the stress cost (Hayes and Kaun; Hayes’s constraints):

    • a weak syllable on beat 1 costs most, on beat 3 next; a stress on an offbeat costs little, and nothing when it anticipates an empty beat (10.19 stands);

    • a mismatch inside a word costs more than one across words; a line’s end is strict and its start free.

  2. Weak line openings take a pickup. An unstressed first syllable (“And”, “But”, “I”, “To”, “a”) goes before the bar line, or the line starts on its first stress. This is 742 and 749’s fix, now with a band: weak syllables on beat 1 at most about 6% of weak syllables (corpus 4% to 6%; songs 54 and 55, 10% to 12%), and one-syllable function words on beat 1 at most about 6% of them.

  3. A word-shape rule for pitch (the pitch-accent rule v7 left out): in a word of two or more syllables, the stressed syllable is at or above the word’s other syllables. Target: lower at most about 20% of such words (corpus 18% to 20%; songs 54 and 55, 34%), and a weak syllable a local peak at most about 10% of the time, about half the rate of stressed syllables.

  4. Inside the word, the stress is not the shortest. Stressed syllables shorter than the word’s weak syllables at most about 20% of the time (corpus 19%; song 55, 37%). v7’s finding that stressed syllables are only slightly longer overall stands; this is a floor inside the word, not a lengthening rule.

  5. The line’s last stress. Let it anticipate (about half land on an offbeat eighth), hold it (about two lines in three it is longer than the line’s mean note), keep it at or below the line’s middle pitch, and prefer it on the rhyme word. Most of this is v7’s already; the anticipation of the last stress is new.

  6. A vowel rule by voice and length. On notes held a beat or more in the top tenth of the singer’s range: open vowels at least about 55% and reduced vowels at most about 10% (men 61% and 7%, women 55% and 8%). No rule for height alone. Close vowels (IY, UW) on such notes are allowed, as singers sing them, but the songbook flags each one for the singer to open slightly. For a baritone that zone starts around D4 to E4; for a tenor, around G4 to A4.

  7. Natural length. A long syllable (a tense vowel or diphthong, or a heavy closed syllable) is not crowded onto a sixteenth; v7’s vowel-duration lean becomes part of the placement score (Ryan; Hayes and Kaun).

Two more, from the further reading:

  • Stress and metre move together. Score each pair of neighbouring syllables: opposed movement inside a word costs most when the stress falls (target at most about 15%), across words at most about 30% (about 15% to 20% for a pre-1980 style, up to about 38% for a 1980s one), with an anticipation counted as parallel; at a line’s start only a falling opposition costs.

  • Length follows the ending as well as the vowel. In the placement score, a word ending in a voiced consonant leans to a longer note (about 55% against 33%), alongside v7’s tense-vowel lean, which songs 54 and 55 currently invert. Fit the weights per style, as Hayes’s speakers differ (Part 21’s weighted placement).

  • Set the rhythm targets by era. Notes per bar, sixteenths and the anticipation rate change by era (about 4.8 notes a bar, 4% sixteenths and half of offbeat eighths anticipating in 1980–1999; about 6 notes a bar, 13% sixteenths and a quarter anticipating after 2000). The style’s era should choose them; weak syllables stay off beat 1 in every era, and the word’s pitch shape holds from the 1950s on.

  • Bands by style for hymn mode and folk. Weak syllables on beat 1 at most about 10% in 4/4 and 17% in 3/4 (pop about 6%); stresses on beat 1 about a third of stresses in 4/4 and a half in 3/4; the stress below the rest of its word at most about 30% (pop about 22%); held top notes open at least about half the time. From PDMX and OpenEWLD (“Hymns, folk songs and standards”).

Checks for the port:

  • Rerun songs 54 and 55 and compare with the corpus bands above: weak syllables and function words on beat 1, word-internal pitch and length, weak-syllable peaks, vowels on held high notes.

  • The corpus checks reproduce from studies/words/words_results.json.

No placement death from the new costs: they weigh, they do not forbid (Part 21).

Files and sources

In the repo, studies/words/:

  • parse_words.py: every sung syllable of CoCoPops Billboard and the Rolling Stone 200 files with stress, with its note, place in the bar, length, section and line start.

  • words_test.py: the measures in this report, for the corpora and for songs 54 and 55.

  • words_more.py: the follow-ups from the further reading (stress and metre as contours, voiced endings and length).

  • pop20c_test.py: the same measures by period on the Pop20c corpus, 1900 to 1999.

  • pop20c_rhythm.py: melodic rhythm by period, with the post-2000 songs.

  • bimmuda_words.py: the word measures on BiMMuDa, 1950 to 2022, words attached by exact count.

  • mxl_words.py, score_words.py, pdmx_words.py and openewld_words.py: the measures on scores with words attached (PDMX, OpenEWLD).

  • words_results.json, words_more_results.json, pop20c_results.json, pop20c_rhythm_results.json, bimmuda_words_results.json, pdmx_words_results.json and openewld_words_results.json: every figure in this report. sung_syllables.json is not committed; the parser rebuilds it.

Data: CoCoPops, CC BY-NC 4.0, derived counts only; stress from the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (via the pronouncing package) for Billboard. Luthier v7 Windows 25, 39, 69 and 98 and Module 10.19 for what the engine already does.
