Part 24. Harmony voices for Luthier v8: duets, backing vocals and choirs

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Harmony voices for Luthier v8: duets, backing vocals and choirs.

Summary

  • v7 has more than an on/off switch (my earlier claim was wrong): second-singer rows, ensemble kinds, a duet harmony rule (a third or sixth below, chord tones, no crossing, no parallel fifths or octaves), the never-together duet, the backing echo and a unison anchor. But only the duet harmony has a writer, and every second voice in songs 53 to 56 was written outside the engine.

  • Three of those four songs broke v7’s default: a harmony above the lead (54, 55), a two-note answer (56), a descant and choir (53).

  • Traditions agree the harmony is a chord tone, not a fixed interval, and put it above the lead as often as below: the bluegrass and country tenor, the barbershop tenor, the brother-duet third above.

  • 10,529 PDMX scores measured. v7’s allowed set (3, 4, 8 or 9 semitones below) covers only about a fifth of real harmony pairs. The second voice is above the lead 28% of the time, in unison or octaves about a quarter of the time, and holds still (static or oblique) in about half of all motions. Parallel fifths are rare (about 1 per 100 motions; 3 in pop). Second voices sound under more of the lead as the song goes on, in every group.

  • What v8 should build (section 5): six kinds of second voice with their own writers (double, harmony line, pad, answer, descant, parts); a harmony line by chord tone on the side the style calls for, with motion bands; parallel octaves only in a marked doubling passage; entries that grow with the song’s intensity curve; and the measurement run on every output.

  • DALI: the GitHub repo has no annotations; they are in restricted Zenodo record 3576083 and need an access request.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

A correction first. When I proposed this topic I said v7 has only an on/off backing-vocal row. That was wrong. A reread of v7 finds seven rules that touch a second voice:

Rule in v7 What it does What it leaves out
11.2 amended (v58): second-singer rows Each singer gets a voice row and a register, so a duet can be written for two real voices Nothing about how the two lines relate
v59: ensemble kinds Names solo, duet, band with backing vocals, choir The kinds are labels; only the duet has a writer
v70 fix 2 (Window 88, song 22): the duet harmony A harmony derived from the melody: a third below by default, else a sixth (3, 4, 8 or 9 semitones); every note a chord tone; never crossing; inside the singer’s row; one top note under the lead’s peak in the final chorus; no parallel fifths or octaves Harmony above the lead; motion other than parallel; where harmonies enter and leave; more than two voices
Fix 61: the never-together duet A duet can be marked so the voices only alternate Overlap, echoes, a call answered
Fix 84: the backing echo Backing voices repeat the lead’s last words, a third under or in unison Chords of two or three voices; pads on a vowel
The unison anchor Two voices meet in unison or the octave at an anchor When, and how often
Production table: backing vocals OPTIONAL/ON Whether backing vocals exist in the mix Their notes

Two more places bear on it. Window 57 measured the Open Hymnal’s four-part hymns, and Module 9.14 sets voice-leading and low-interval limits that apply to any added voice. A complaint about descants is on file (line 3181 of the spec) with no rule behind it.

The fix list (Part 1) already holds two findings here. 749.9 found song 52’s harmony parts shadowing the lead (the high part moving with it 74% of the time, never against it) and rewrote them as lines chosen by least cost, contrary and oblique motion cheaper than similar; its check asks that each harmony part move with the lead under half the time. 749.12 proposes a descant module, from song 53’s descant. This report extends both: 749.9’s check is the motion band below, and the descant is one of the six kinds in V1.

What the recent songs needed

  • Song 53, Sung to Sleep (carol, organ and choir). Four-part choir in hymn mode and a soprano descant over the last verse and refrain. All of it was written on the sketch path, outside the engine: the choir in hymn mode, the descant with fix-list finding 749.9’s harmony-as-lines search. v7 has no descant writer; finding 749.12 proposes one.

  • Songs 54 and 55 (country: The Man Mama Prayed I’d Be and Your Yard Man). A harmony voice a third above the lead on the hook, “the crowd singing back”, and on chorus 3’s middle lines. v7’s rule says a third below. The above-harmony was written by my hand, as were song 54’s duet tag lines (him a third below in his octave, her above him).

  • Song 56, Terpsichore. Backing voices answer the lead with a two-note chord over his held note in chorus 3 and the outro. That is call and response, which v7 can’t write; fix 84’s echo repeats the lead’s words in his rhythm.

So every second voice in the last four songs was made outside the engine, and three of the four broke v7’s default (above, not below; a chord, not a line). Jason’s ruling on song 56 stands behind this report: the engine should be writing everything.

2. The academic record

The record on backing vocals is thin. A 2023 Trondheim master’s thesis on backing vocals in pop says the topic has had little research attention, and Susan Fast and Jacqueline Warwick (cited in a 2024 Goldsmiths thesis) note there is no definitive history of the backing singer. Rock theory has mostly studied chords, not lines: Everett’s survey of rock’s tonal systems finds harmony matters more than counterpoint in most rock. Lacasse’s work on vocal staging covers how recorded voices are placed (doubling, panning, reverb), not their notes. So the best guidance comes from the traditions that teach harmony singing by name, and from perception research.

What each tradition does

Tradition Where the melody sits The harmony voice Source
Plain backing vocal (pop, rock) Lead on top or in the middle One line above or below, mostly thirds or sixths that fit the chords; some bands hold long, slow notes under the chorus Encyclopedic summaries of vocal harmony
Brother duet (Delmore, Louvin, Everly) Lower voice A tenor in parallel thirds above, the two moving as one Scaruffi; Country Music Hall of Fame summaries
Bluegrass trio Middle (the “standard stack”) Tenor: the next chord tone above, following the melody’s shape. Baritone: the next chord tone below. Variants: the high lead (both parts under the melody) and the high baritone (both above) No Depression on the Osborne Brothers; bluegrass references
Barbershop Second from the top, the lead Tenor above, bass lowest, baritone fills the chord, often below the lead; four parts on every melody note Barbershop Harmony Society definition
Gospel choir Usually soprano; the tenor often takes it in some arrangers’ work Starts in unison or call and response and builds to full parts as the song goes on Fiveable summary; ACDA on Hogan
Hymn (SATB) Soprano Alto, tenor, bass in chordal rhythm with the tune Window 57 of the spec already

Three points follow. First, the harmony above the lead is as normal as the one below: country and bluegrass put the tenor above by default, which is what songs 54 and 55 needed. Second, the harmony is defined by the chord, not by a fixed interval: the next chord tone above or below. A third is what that usually gives, but on some melody notes it gives a fourth or a sixth. Third, harmonies are placed: gospel builds from unison to parts, and pop holds them for the chorus.

What perception research says about lines

Huron’s derivation of voice-leading rules from perception (Music Perception, 2001; the MIT Press book, 2016) gives the reasons behind v7’s rule. Unisons, octaves and fifths fuse most readily, so parallel motion in them makes two voices sound like one. That is why classical rules ban parallel fifths and octaves, and it is also why close-harmony styles use parallel motion on purpose: Huron treats close harmony as a texture that seeks fusion, where counterpoint seeks independence. He also documents that the highest voice dominates attention, and that listeners can track only a few lines at once. For a backing vocal, then, the question is not “is it independent?” but “is it meant to blend into the lead or to answer it?” v7 has one rule for both.

3. Perception and practice: tuning, blend, balance

These bear on how the demo renders voices and what the songbook tells singers. They don’t change the notes.

Finding Numbers Source
Unison voices should match pitch closely Listeners preferred 0 to 5 cents of scatter; 14 cents was tolerable Ternström 1993, J Voice
Real choirs scatter more than that Typically 20 to 30 cents between singers in unison Ternström 2003 review; Jers and Ternström
Choirs bend thirds Major thirds sung wide (about 416 cents), minor thirds narrow (about 276) Ternström 2003 review
Small ensembles stay near equal temperament A student quintet tuned close to equal temperament, major thirds slightly toward just D’Amario, Daffern, Howard and Pennill
Barbershop tunes chords just The dominant seventh’s seventh sung about 31 cents flat of the piano; dominant sevenths are 35 to 60% of traditional barbershop chords Hagerman and Sundberg 1980; harmonic-seventh references; Choralnet
Singers need to hear themselves Preferred self-to-other ratio about +6 dB (0 to +15) Ternström 1999, JASA
The top voice takes the ear The highest voice is perceptually dominant Huron 2016

What this means for Luthier

  • A harmony above the lead competes with it. Because the top voice takes attention, an above-harmony must sit lower in the mix and be sung lighter. Songs 54 and 55’s songbooks already say “never louder”; v8 should make that a production rule tied to the harmony’s side, not a note in prose.

  • Unison doubling needs a tight match. A doubled lead (the most common backing part in modern pop) should be described as a double, tuned within a few cents, not as a harmony.

  • The demo renders equal temperament. That is right for band songs. For a cappella or choir passages the songbook can tell singers to tune thirds and sevenths by ear; the score stays as written.

  • Practice warns against nonstop parallel thirds. Worship-band teaching material says singers who find the third and never leave it make a part that wears out; it recommends oblique motion, holding a note while the lead moves. Section 4 measures how often real scores do that.

4. Measured: lead against harmony in 10,529 scores

Data. PDMX (Zenodo 15571083, CC BY 4.0): scores with words, deduplicated, no licence conflict, two or more parts. 12,852 qualified; 10,529 had two or more vocal parts and parsed. The lead is the part with the most syllables. At each lead note, the other part’s sounding note gives the interval; consecutive pairs give the motion. The clean duet group is “2 voices, both with words” (799 scores, 100,865 note pairs).

Caveats. PDMX is user-made MuseScore scores, so popular songs are arrangements, not studio parts. The popular duet sample is small (48 scores, 9,170 pairs). Chords aren’t in the files, so chord-tone membership isn’t tested here.

The tables

Intervals (share of sounding pairs, %)

Group Scores Below 3rds 6ths 5ths Unison, 8ve Dissonant v7’s set Crossed
Popular duets 48 67 25 9 14 26 16 18 6
Folk duets 22 65 28 13 9 28 17 18 4
Sacred duets 28 53 23 19 11 30 10 13 6
Classical duets 701 73 31 14 12 25 11 21 5
All duets 799 72 30 13 12 26 11 21 6
All, 3 voices 1,335 66 33 14 14 20 10 20 5
All, 4+ voices 8,059 61 29 15 15 20 10 18 4
Popular, 4+ voices 273 60 22 13 14 23 17 13 6

“Below” is the share of pairs where the second voice is the lower part. “Dissonant” is seconds, sevenths and tritones.

Motion and placement (%, except the per-100 columns)

Group Same onset Static or oblique Contrary Parallel Parallel 5ths per 100 Parallel 8ves, unisons per 100 Present, first → last fifth
Popular duets 77 52 10 28 3.3 10.8 63 → 78
Folk duets 81 53 12 26 0.5 10.6 66 → 76
Sacred duets 78 47 14 31 0.6 16.4 72 → 90
Classical duets 77 45 18 28 0.9 10.2 69 → 81
All duets 77 46 17 28 1.1 10.5 68 → 81
All, 3 voices 75 48 21 20 0.7 4.7 74 → 85
All, 4+ voices 72 54 21 14 0.5 2.9 68 → 78
Popular, 4+ voices 61 67 9 16 1.4 6.9 70 → 79

Intervals are by class, so a tenth counts as a third. “In v7’s set” means exactly 3, 4, 8 or 9 semitones below the lead, which is v7’s whole allowed vocabulary.

What the numbers say

  1. v7’s set covers about a fifth of real harmony. Thirds and sixths together are 34% to 45% of sounding pairs. Restricted to below the lead and inside the octave, as v7 requires, they are 13% to 21%.

  2. The harmony is above the lead a third of the time (28% in duets, 33% in popular duets). v7 forbids it.

  3. About a quarter of all pairs are unison or octave. These are doubling stretches, where the two voices sing the same tune. Parallel unisons and octaves run 10 to 16 per 100 motions in duets. v7’s ban on parallel octaves rules out the commonest duet texture.

  4. Parallel fifths really are rare: under 1 per 100 motions except in popular duets (3.3). v7’s ban fits everything but pop.

  5. Real harmony holds still. About half of all motions are static or oblique; parallel motion is 28% in duets and 14% in four parts; contrary motion 10% to 21%. A rule that adds a fixed interval to the melody is parallel by construction, so v7’s writer would invert this profile.

  6. Dissonance is normal on the way through: 10% to 17% of pairs are seconds, sevenths or tritones, nearly all short passing notes.

  7. The voices mostly move together: 77% of lead notes start with the harmony note (61% in popular four-part, where pads and held notes are common).

  8. Harmony grows through the song. In every group the second voice sounds under more of the lead in the last fifth than in the first: popular duets go from 63% to 78%, sacred duets from 72% to 90%.

Song 53’s choir could not be measured here: its scores live in the song’s output folder, which is not in the repo. The measurement can be rerun on it when the folder is rebuilt (the parser reads the engine’s own MusicXML).

5. What v8 should do

Keep what v7’s rule gets right: chord tones on strong notes, inside the singer’s row, no crossing, the harmony’s peak under the lead’s. Replace the rest with a writer for each kind of second voice, and bands from section 4.

V1. Six kinds of second voice, each with its own writer

v59’s ensemble kinds become writers. Each passage of a second voice is one of:

Kind What it is Used in
Double The lead’s tune in unison or an octave away Pop choruses, duets’ shared lines, hymns
Harmony line A line above or below that follows the lead’s rhythm Songs 54 and 55’s hook, duets
Pad Held vowels (“ooh”, “ah”) on chord tones under the lead Pop and gospel backing
Answer Its own words between or over the lead’s phrases Song 56; gospel call and response
Descant An independent line above a choir or congregation Song 53’s last verse
Parts Three or four voices on every melody note (trio stack, barbershop, SATB) Song 53; bluegrass; hymns

The intake asks which kinds the song uses and where. Fix 84’s echo becomes a case of Answer, fix 61’s never-together duet a constraint on Double and Answer.

V2. The harmony line by chord tone, on either side

  • Side by style. Above (the tenor) for country, bluegrass, brother duets and anthems; below for pop, folk and singer-songwriter by default; the intake can override. v7’s “a third below” becomes the pop default, not the rule.

  • The note. The next chord tone above (or below) the lead’s note, as bluegrass and barbershop teach. That gives a third most of the time and a fourth or sixth where the chord requires. On short weak notes a passing note may stand (10% to 17% of pairs are dissonant in real scores).

  • Bands for a harmony line, from the duet scores: thirds and sixths at least 35% of pairs; static or oblique about half (45% to 55% in duets, up to about two thirds where held notes are common, as in popular four-part writing and song 52’s revised high part, 66%); parallel 25% to 35%; contrary at least 10%; crossing at most 6%.

  • Parallel fifths at most 1 per 100 motions, 3.5 in pop. Parallel unisons and octaves only inside a passage marked Double.

V3. Where second voices go

  • Presence grows: the share of the lead covered by a second voice in the song’s last fifth exceeds the first fifth’s by at least 10 points (every group measured did so).

  • The first entry is on a hook or chorus; the last chorus adds lines (songs 54 and 55 already did this by hand). Gospel and worship songs may build from unison through Answer to Parts.

  • Tie the entries to the song-wide intensity curve (749.17), so a new voice is one of the steps that lift each return.

V4. Production and the songbook

  • A second voice above the lead is mixed and sung lighter than one below (the top voice takes the ear). The production table states the side, not only ON.

  • Doubles are described as doubles, tuned tight; a cappella passages tell singers to tune thirds and sevenths by ear.

V5. Tests

  • voices_pdmx.py ’s measures, run on every engine output through parse_parts.py

  • (it reads the engine’s MusicXML), reported against the V2 and V3 bands in the test report.

  • A control run with v7’s rule: the profile should show the near-total parallel motion section 4 predicts, so the change is visible.

  • Rerun on song 53’s choir once its output folder is rebuilt, and on songs 54 to 56’s hand-written parts as the first targets the engine must match.

6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/voices)

  • parse_parts.py : every part of a MusicXML score, aligned in time (reads PDMX and

  • the engine’s own scores).

  • voices_pdmx.py : the section 4 measurement; voices_pdmx_results.json : its

  • results; README.md .

Part 25. Song edges for Luthier v8: intros, endings, the way in and out

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Song edges for Luthier v8: intros, endings, the way in and out.

Summary

  • v7 checks the edges but doesn’t write them. It has an intro-bar median (4), a chorusarrival limit, the peak-end design spec and four ending kinds (resolved, open, abrupt, return). Every intro and ending in songs 52 to 56 was chosen by hand, and four of the five intros are 4 bars (song 53’s organ introduction grew to 8).

  • Intro length is an era setting. In 739 Billboard songs the intro doubled from about 9 seconds (1958–64) to 17 (1985–91), 4 bars to 8; Léveillé Gauvin found the time to the voice then fell to about 5 seconds by 2015. Neither length nor time to the voice separates hits from misses, so v7’s single median of 4 bars is right only for a 1960s sound.

  • The first five seconds matter: a quarter of Spotify plays end there. Whatever the era, something identifiable (hook tune, riff or voice) should sound in them.

  • Endings: 61% of Billboard songs to 1991 fade (71% in the late 1970s); fades then nearly vanished. Cold endings land on the tonic 81% of the time, by V–I (a third), IV–I (nearly a third; Temperley’s grand plagal cadence, which songs 54 and 55 used) or ♭VII–I (growing after 1980). A fade keeps listeners’ pulse running past the end; a final slowing adds no pleasure.

  • What v8 should build (section 5): six intro kinds (own figure, hook preview, verse vamp, buildup, voice first, none) with era bands; ending kinds that name the cadence and add the fade, the bookend and the coda; a fade only where the song shouldn’t end; the demo rendering fades and held last chords; and bands for the commercial profile.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 has more at the edges than its form tables suggest, but almost all of it is a check, not a writer.

Rule in v7 What it says What it leaves out
Window 29 (form) Intro bars: median 4 (middle half 3 to 8) in Billboard and POP909; first chorus at bar 20, 45 seconds in, 21% of the way through How long an intro is by era or genre; outro length
Design spec, chorus arrival If the chorus doesn’t arrive by bar 16 to 20, the intro or verse is too long Nothing on what the intro holds
Window 29: form features Intro length, time to the chorus and song length don’t separate top-ten records from the rest (AUC 0.50 to 0.56) Whether that holds after 1991
Peak-end design spec; the role table “The bridge is the peak. The tag is the end.” The tag carries the simplest material, voices forward, call and response How the last bars are built
11.9, fixes 77 and 93: the ending’s kind Resolved, open, abrupt, or return (a hook phrase over an open last chord), checked against the last chord and the outro’s length A fade-out; a slowing; a held last chord; a cold stop on the beat
Fix 71: the commercial profile Prints length, intro seconds, the bar the title arrives, chorus repetitions, the ending Bands to check them against
Fixes 21 and 23: the quote and the one-phrase peak An intro can quote a sung section’s tune; a one-phrase intro peaks in its second half Riff intros, vocal-first starts, chord-only intros
Arrangement rule (Window on the band) The intro has half the fullest band or fewer; bars before the voice 4.25 to 9 in the band files (Part 19 found real intros carry about 70% of the fullest band)
The M/N Nocturne type Its tag fades: tempo down, last sound fades rather than concludes Fades for any other type

What the recent songs did

  • Song 52 (6/8 ballad): a 4-bar guitar intro on the verse’s chords; a 4-bar outro on new chords, guitar and cello, slowing to the last chord.

  • Song 53 (carol): a 4-bar organ introduction in the first edition, rewritten to 8 bars in the third; the last refrain’s final word held by the choir, then an organ coda.

  • Songs 54 and 55 (country): a 4-bar intro with the fiddle playing the hook; a tag, then a 2-bar ending, IV to I, the fiddle bringing the hook home, the last chord ringing. No fade.

  • Song 56: a 4-bar intro planned; the ending waits for v8.

Every intro began at 4 bars (song 53’s grew to 8 in its third edition), and every ending was chosen by hand. None of the songs asked whether 4 bars suits a song of its era and style, whether to start with the voice, or whether to fade.

2. The academic record

Pop theory has studied song middles far more than edges. Nick Braae’s 2026 Music Theory Online article on closure in 1970s rock opens by noting that intros have had some attention and endings much less. What exists:

Intros

  • Summach’s module theory (dissertation, Yale 2012, top-20 rock 1955 to 1989) treats the intro as its own module. An intro often shares material with the outro, giving a “bookend”; several intro modules in a row are possible, and having none is less common than having more than one.

  • The buildup introduction (Robin Attas, dissertation 2011 and later work; Nicole Biamonte in the Routledge Companion): layers of the groove enter one at a time, so the intro teaches the listener the beat and the band before the voice. Attas calls intros “a site for first impressions”. Spicer’s accumulative form (2004) is the largerscale version.

  • The attention economy. Hubert Léveillé Gauvin (Musicae Scientiae, 2018) measured 303 US top-10 singles from 1986 to 2015: the time before the voice fell from about 20 seconds to about 5, tempo rose (Part 28 places this after the 1990s low), and the title arrived sooner. A second test, 60 hits paired with less popular songs by the same artists, found none of these features separated the hit from the miss. Both halves agree with v7’s Window 29: intro length tracks the era, not success.

Endings

  • Kinds. Teaching texts and Braae’s model list the usual closing devices: a final tonic chord (often held), completion of the melody on the tonic, a ritardando, the fade-out, a coda of new material, and a modulation in the last section. Braae sorts them into structural closing markers (that make the music complete) and rhetorical ones (that signal “this is the end”), following David Heetderks’s term “closing markers”. Codas present new material; outros repeat old material with closing rhetoric (Open Music Theory, after Summach).

  • The grand plagal cadence. Temperley (Music Theory Online, 2011) names a rock ending: a strongly emphasised IV to I, often with a held last chord, that comes once, near the end. Songs 54 and 55 ended this way by instinct; v7 has no name for it.

  • Terminally climactic form. Osborn (2013) describes songs, mostly post-1990s alternative rock, whose last section is new material and the climax. Spicer’s cumulative form ends at its fullest texture.

  • The fade-out’s rise and fall. William Weir’s survey of Billboard’s year-end top 10 since 1946 (reported by NPR, 2014) found fade-outs peaked in 1985, when all ten year-end songs faded, then declined through the 1990s until they almost vanished.

v7 already has resolved, open, abrupt and return endings. Missing from it: the fade, the held final chord, the slowing, the grand plagal cadence, the bookend, the buildup intro, and the coda of new material.

3. Listeners: the first seconds and the last

Finding Numbers Source
Listeners decide fast 24% of Spotify plays skipped within 5 seconds, 29% within 10, 35% within 30; 48.6% before the song ends; skipping highest in teenagers Paul Lamere, “The Skip” (Spotify data, billions of plays, 2014)
Hits got to the voice sooner Time before the voice in US top-10 singles fell from about 20 s (mid-1980s) to about 5 s (2015); tempo rose; the title came sooner Léveillé Gauvin, Musicae Scientiae 2018 (303 songs, 1986–2015)
But it doesn’t pick the hit Hits and less popular songs by the same artists did not differ on any of these features Léveillé Gauvin 2018, study 2 (60 pairs, 2015)
A fade keeps the song going in the head With a fade-out, listeners went on tapping the pulse after the sound stopped; with an arranged (“cold”) end they stopped tapping before the end Kopiez and colleagues (Hannover), “When the pulse of the song goes on”, Psychology of Music (80 listeners, three versions of one song)
A final slowing doesn’t add pleasure Ordinary final ritardandi did not make endings more pleasant; exaggerated ones made them less pleasant; the closing harmony mattered more Kleinsmith, Friedman and Neill 2016 and follow-up
Closure is expectation met A cadence’s last event is highly predictable, and predictability drops right after it, which is felt as an ending Huron 2006; Sears, Caplin and McAdams
Phrase ends are lengthened Performers, and even non-musicians pacing chords themselves, lengthen phrase ends Palmer 1989; dwell-time studies

What this means for Luthier

  • The first five seconds matter on streaming. A quarter of plays end there, before most intros finish. That argues for an intro that carries something identifiable (the hook’s tune, a riff, the voice) rather than for a short intro as such, since length alone didn’t separate hits from misses.

  • Era sets the length. A song written to sound like 1975 can take 15 seconds before the voice; a song meant for streaming now wants the voice or the hook within about 5.

  • A fade is a meaning, not a default. It leaves the pulse running: right for a song that shouldn’t end (a vamp, an endless love, a nocturne), wrong for a song that resolves. v7 offers it only to the nocturne.

  • The ending is in the harmony. The cadence carries closure more than a slowing does. A held last chord after a strong cadence is the reliable close; a ritardando is optional and should be slight.

4. Measured: 739 Billboard songs and 909 POP909 songs

Data. The McGill Billboard annotations (Burgoyne, Wild and Fujinaga; 739 distinct songs charted 1958 to 1991) mark sections with times, the lead voice’s entry, the lead instrument, fade-outs and every chord. POP909 (909 Chinese pop songs, 2000s and 2010s) has human structure labels with intro and outro lengths in bars. After 1991 I rely on Léveillé Gauvin’s measurements (section 3); BiMMuDa’s melody files proved unreliable for the voice’s entry (a rap verse before the sung tune counts as silence).

Intros

Period Songs Song length (s) Has an intro Intro (s), median and middle half Intro (bars) Voice enters (s)
1958–64 121 151 89% 9 (7–13) 4 8
1965–69 116 171 90% 10 (7–15) 4 10
1970–74 131 199 91% 13 (9–19) 5 12
1975–79 129 216 95% 15 (10–19) 8 15
1980–84 125 230 98% 15 (9–21) 8 16
1985–91 117 252 93% 17 (12–24) 8 19
All 739 206 93% 13 (9–19) 6 (4–8) 13
POP909 909 96% 8 (4–8)

  • What the intro plays. 55% of intros have material of their own, used nowhere else; 27% share it with an instrumental section later (interlude, solo, outro: the riff or instrumental refrain); 11% play the verse’s music and 7% the chorus’s.

  • Who leads it. Where the annotators marked a lead instrument, guitar led most often before 1980, synthesizer after 1985. The voice starts inside the intro in 8% of songs (spoken words, vocal ad-libs, an a cappella line).

  • Bookends. 13% of songs end on the intro’s material.

v7’s “median 4 bars” holds for 1958 to 1969 only. From 1975 the Billboard median is 8 bars, and POP909’s is 8. The 45 seconds to the first chorus v7 quotes is an average over eras whose intros doubled in length.

Endings

Period Fade-out Cold endings: last section outro or coda chorus verse Last chord the tonic V–I IV–I ♭VII–I Outro, fades (s) Outro, cold (s)
1958–64 49% 29% 32% 27% 94% 50% 29% 2% 9 13
1965–69 58% 49% 24% 18% 86% 24% 43% 8% 11 14
1970–74 56% 57% 26% 9% 79% 30% 28% 7% 15 28
1975–79 71% 55% 32% 8% 76% 26% 32% 8% 16 19
1980–84 66% 70% 19% 9% 79% 33% 28% 14% 17 18
1985–91 69% 42% 36% 6% 67% 25% 14% 11% 19 27
All 61% 49% 28% 14% 81% 33% 29% 8% 15 20

The chord columns are for songs that don’t fade. POP909: 70% of songs have an outro (median 4 bars, middle half 2 to 6), and 71% end on instrumental bars after the last sung section.

  1. Fades were the majority ending from 1965 to 1991, rising to 71% in the late 1970s. That agrees with Weir’s year-end count peaking in 1985. The later collapse (section 2) is after this corpus.

  2. A cold ending lands on the tonic 81% of the time, but the approach varies: V–I in a third, IV–I (the plagal close) in nearly a third, ♭VII–I in about one in ten, growing after 1980. The plagal close peaked in the late 1960s (43%).

  3. Before 1965, a third of songs ended on the last verse or chorus itself; later, most cold endings have an outro or coda (70% in 1980–84). Outros grew from about 13 seconds to over 20.

  4. Fades run 9 to 19 seconds from the start of the fading section, lengthening by era, typically 8 bars of a repeated chorus or vamp.

5. What v8 should do

Keep v7’s ending kinds, chorus-arrival check and commercial profile. Add a writer for each edge, with bands by era and style.

E1. Six kinds of intro

Kind What it is Evidence
Own figure A riff or figure used nowhere else, or only in instrumental sections 55% own material, 27% shared with an instrumental section (Billboard)
Hook preview The chorus’s or hook’s tune on an instrument Songs 54 and 55’s fiddle; 7% play the chorus’s music
Verse vamp The verse’s chords and groove, the band settling in 11% play the verse’s music
Buildup Layers enter one at a time until the band is full Attas; Spicer’s accumulative form
Voice first The voice alone or nearly alone: a pickup line, an a cappella phrase, a spoken word 8% of Billboard intros carry the voice
None The voice on bar 1 7% of Billboard songs; common after 2000 (Léveillé Gauvin)

The intake (or the style default) chooses one; the arrangement writer’s layer counts (Part 19) fill it.

E2. Intro length by era, and the first five seconds

  • Bands from the tables: a 1958–69 sound, 4 bars and about 9 to 10 seconds before the voice; a 1975–91 sound, 8 bars and about 15 to 19 seconds; a streaming-era sound, the voice or the hook’s tune within about 5 seconds.

  • The first five seconds carry something identifiable : the hook’s tune, the riff, or the voice. This is a check for every era, since a quarter of streaming plays end there and length alone doesn’t make hits.

  • Window 29’s chorus-arrival bar should be read with the era’s intro, not the cross-era median.

E3. The ending’s kinds

v7’s resolved, open, abrupt and return stay. Make “resolved” say how, and add three:

Kind Built as Use
Resolved: authentic V–I, last chord held The default before 1965 (half of cold endings)
Resolved: plagal IV–I, once, emphasised, last chord held (Temperley’s grand plagal cadence) Rock, country, gospel, hymns; songs 54 and 55
Resolved: ♭VII–I The Mixolydian close Rock after 1980 (about one in ten)
Fade The chorus or a vamp repeated, about 8 bars and 10 to 20 seconds, the level falling to nothing Only where the song shouldn’t end: a vamp, an ongoing state, the nocturne. The last words heard are the hook’s. On streaming, long fades and trailing silence attract skips (Montecchio and colleagues, Part 6), so keep fades short there
Bookend The intro’s material returns to close 13% of songs
Coda New material at the end, possibly the climax (Osborn’s terminally climactic form) Alternative rock, worship builds
Open, abrupt, return As in v7 As in v7

  • Slowing: optional and slight. Listeners find ordinary final ritardandi no more pleasant and exaggerated ones less pleasant; the cadence does the work.

  • Outro length: cold outros of 4 to 15 bars (median 7, Billboard); POP909 median 4. A song ending straight on the last chorus is a pre-1965 sound.

E4. The demo and the documents

  • The demo renders a fade (a volume ramp over the fading bars) and a held last chord (a fermata, written in the score and rendered in the MIDI).

  • The songbook says which ending it is and how to play it live: a fade needs a live ending, usually the hook once more and a held chord.

E5. Tests

  • The commercial profile (fix 71) gets bands: intro bars and seconds against the chosen era, the voice’s entry, what sounds in the first five seconds, the ending’s kind and last two chords, the outro’s length.

  • Songs 52 to 56 as the first test: four have 4-bar intros, right for a 1960s sound and short for a 1975–91 sound, and song 53’s 8-bar organ introduction suits a carol; songs 54 and 55’s IV–I endings match the grand plagal kind; none fades.

6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/edges)

  • edges_billboard.py : per-song intro, voice entry, intro material and lead, ending kind,

  • outro, last two chords, bookend; edges_billboard.json .

  • edges_tables.py : the section 4 tables by period; edges_tables.json .

  • edges_pop909.py : POP909 intro and outro bars; edges_pop909.json .

Data

  • McGill Billboard annotations (Burgoyne, Wild and Fujinaga 2011), salami_chords.txt via ChoCo (Zenodo 7706751), with billboard-2.0-index.csv for chart dates.

  • POP909 (Wang et al. 2020) with Dai, Zhang and Dannenberg’s structure labels.

Sources

  • Lamere, P. (2014). The Skip. Music Machinery blog (Spotify data), as reported by Spin, RAIN News and Hypebot.

Part 26. Vocal ornament and expression for Luthier v8: melisma, slides, vibrato, breath

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Vocal ornament and expression for Luthier v8: melisma, slides, vibrato, breath.

Summary

  • v7 counts melisma and renders vibrato, and nothing else of delivery. It adds twonote turns at corpus rates, bans melisma on cadence notes, and sets a delayed MIDI vibrato. No score or songbook for songs 52 to 56 named a scoop, fall, cry, run or vibrato style.

  • 6,716 songs measured. Chart pop sets 8% to 11% of syllables on more than one note (rising from the 1960s), arrangements of pop half that, hymns and folk about 5% to 8%, standards almost none. Melismas gather at phrase ends (2.5 to 3 times their share), are two notes three times in four, and increase through the song in every corpus. v7’s cadence-note ban runs against this.

  • Delivery research: scoops are the commonest pop inflection (short, under half a second); many pop singers barely use vibrato while gospel voices use it wide and fast; the country breaking voice falls on grief words; runs are mostly pentatonic, 4 to 7 notes, at the ends of long notes near the song’s peak.

  • What v8 should build (section 5): a written tier (melisma by style bands and placement, runs as designed moments) and a performed tier (inflections and vibrato by style, named in the songbook and rendered in the demo), with an ornament card in the test report.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 measures melisma carefully and treats the rest of vocal delivery as MIDI rendering.

Rule in v7 What it says What it leaves out
Window 30, finding 3 (karaoke corpus) A second note on one syllable on 11.5% of sung syllables, 15.4% at line ends; two notes in 44% of melismas; the commonest shapes a step down or a step up. The hook designer adds a two-note turn on held syllables at these rates (75% a step down) Longer runs; how rates differ by genre and era
Window 95, step 4 (theory corpus) Syllables with a melisma: 16% in the median charting song, 9% in the Lied, 0% in the standard. A third of pop’s melismas fall on the phrase’s last syllable; pop’s summit is a melisma in 39% of songs Hymns, gospel, R&B, country
Module 27 A melisma never lands on a cadence note Why; whether singers agree
10.19, intelligibility Melisma lowers word understanding a little (84% to 77%, and only on one-syllable words; Johnson, Huron and Collister 2014)
Module 9.5 (MIDI performance) Vibrato by CC1, delayed and ramped in over the first quarter of a held note; phrase “breathing” by CC11 Vibrato rate and depth by style; straight tone; scoops, falls, bends in the voice
Window 30 and the role table (2.8) Commas are breaths: an eighth’s rest after a comma; a phrase over 13 syllables dies in the search Where breaths go in long lines; breath as expression
The blues window Blue notes come from just intonation (Kubik); the blues voice uses a cry and crosses the passaggio A notation for the bent third or seventh in the voice
11.11 (genre sounds) The pedal steel’s slide-in bends and swells in General MIDI The same for the voice

What the recent songs did

  • Songs 52 to 56: every melisma in the sung lines came from the engine’s two-note turn or the sketch tables. No score carried a grace note, a slide, a fall, an ad-lib or a vibrato marking for the voice.

  • Song 54: the fiddle answered the voice with a bend from the note above into a chord tone, the only written inflection, and it was for an instrument.

  • The songbooks describe the singer’s range, blend and where to stay below the lead, but say nothing about runs, scoops or tone.

So v7 can tell how often a syllable carries more than one note, but not what a singer does with a note: the inflections a gospel, country, R&B or soul singer adds, or the plain delivery a hymn or folk tune wants.

2. The academic record

Melisma and runs

  • Where it came from. Writers on gospel and soul trace pop’s runs to Black church singing: Anthony Heilbut (The Gospel Sound; his NPR guide, 2007) names Sam Cooke, Ray Charles and Aretha Franklin as the singers who carried melisma into the mainstream, and voice-science and music-press histories name Whitney Houston’s “I Will Always Love You” (1992) and Mariah Carey’s “Vision of Love” (1990) as the records that made heavy runs a pop norm. Country has its own older line of melisma from Appalachian and Celtic singing.

  • What a run is made of. Teaching material and analysis agree that runs are mostly pentatonic or blues-scale, in small steps and even fast notes. Tilo Hähnel’s portrait of Mahalia Jackson (Weimar and Jena DFG project “Voices and Singing in Popular Music in the USA”, 2012) finds nearly every tone she sings in the pentatonic scale, melismas of 4 to 7 notes at the ends of long tones, single grace notes or glides at their starts, and ornaments growing toward the song’s emotional centre, where she also sings her highest note.

  • Ornament grows with the song. Hähnel’s Jackson portrait describes ornament concentrated where the song peaks, much as gospel choirs build from unison to full parts (Part 24).

  • Riff and run. Pedagogy distinguishes a run (a fast scalar passage) from a riff (a short repeated figure, any intervals). The CCM pedagogy literature (Bartlett and Naismith 2020, via Voice Science) describes R&B as light delivery with heavy embellishment and fast vibrato.

Inflections beyond melisma

  • A vocabulary by style. Edrie Means’s NATS teaching list of vocal stylisms gives, for country: add-on notes, bent notes, cry, fall-offs and fall-ups, slides, tails, waves, yodel; for pop and rock: flip onsets (the “pop appoggiatura”), cry, fall-offs, fry, growl, slides, tails; for R&B and gospel the same plus riffs, shouts and shadow vowels.

  • The breaking voice carries grief. Paul and Huron (Empirical Musicology Review, 2010) found 31 breaking-voice moments in country recordings and showed the word under the break was more grief-related than the matched word in control songs, at the level of the single word, not the line or the stanza.

  • Yodel types. Timothy Wise (Radical Musicology, 2007) classifies falsetto effects in popular singing, from the hillbilly yodel onward, by the moment the voice breaks register.

  • Portamento. Schubert and Wolfe argue the voice is built for pitch glides and that their near absence from emotion research reflects how hard they are to measure, not their rarity.

Folk and hymn

v7’s own theory corpus already shows the plain end: the median standard has no melismas, folk song about 4.5% (Dutch folk songs), the Lied 9%. Hymn tunes are set syllabically, with occasional two-note slurs. Section 4 measures them.

3. The singing voice measured

Finding Numbers Source
Classical vibrato is narrow in rate 5.5 Hz (Pavarotti) to 6.7 Hz (Marian Anderson) on long notes, extent about ±60 cents; the rate rises in the last cycles of a long note Prame, JASA 1994 (ten singers, Schubert’s Ave Maria)
Ranges by style Classical voices about 4.5 to 6.3 Hz in one review; faster in other styles; women’s tend toward 7 Hz Larrouy-Maestri et al., J Voice 2014 (review); Titze and others
A gospel voice Vibrato about 6 to 7 Hz, extent over 200 cents Hähnel on Mahalia Jackson (2012)
Many pop singers barely use vibrato In 168 J-pop hits by 42 singers, several singers rarely used it “Analysis and detection of singing techniques in repertoires of J-POP solo singers” (arXiv 2210.17367, 2022)
The scoop is the commonest pop inflection Scooping was the most frequent technique, then vibrato, bend and drop; every singer scooped more than 29 times in four songs’ openings; techniques last 0.1 to 1 s (mean 0.4 s) and cover 23% of singing time The same J-pop study
Listeners hear through a scoop, and hear it Pitch is judged as an average across the note and the scoop is also heard against its context Larrouy-Maestri and Pfordresher, “Pitch perception in music: do scoops matter?” (2018)
Melisma costs a little intelligibility Word understanding 84% to 77% on melismas, only on one-syllable words Johnson, Huron and Collister 2014 (already in v7)
Phrases fit a breath A phrase is held in memory up to about 8 seconds; v7’s Window 3 sets phrases of 5 to 8 seconds Part 11 (psychoacoustics) and fix-list finding 749.21; v7 Window 3

What this means for Luthier

  • Vibrato is a style choice, not a constant. v7’s delayed-onset CC1 is a classical habit. Pop and folk singers often sing straight tone with vibrato only on long held notes; gospel and R&B use wide, fast vibrato. The demo should set rate and depth by style and leave short notes plain.

  • Scoops and falls are the everyday ornaments of popular singing, short (under half a second) and nearly constant. They are performance, not notes: the score shouldn’t write them, but the songbook can name where the style wants them (a scoop into a stressed long note, a fall off a line’s last note), and the demo can render them with pitch bend.

  • Runs are notes and belong in the score when they’re part of the song (a written turn or run), and in the songbook as optional when they’re the singer’s to add.

4. Measured: melisma in 6,716 songs

Data. CoCoPops transcriptions of 214 Billboard songs (1958–1991) and 80 Rolling Stone 200 songs, sung syllables with their notes; 5,981 English songs with words in PDMX (Zenodo 15571083), by PDMX’s genre and tag categories (the word-setting study, Part 23, used 4,176 of the same scores: those in 4/4 or 3/4 that its stress measures read); 441 OpenEWLD standards. A melisma is a syllable sung on two or more different notes (ties merged). Phrase end: the syllable before a rest, the end, or line-ending punctuation (MusicXML), or the last syllable of a transcribed line (Billboard).

Rates, lengths and placement

Corpus Songs Melismatic syllables Song median (middle half) Songs with none 2 notes / 3 / 4 / 5+ At phrase ends (base) First, middle, last third of song
Billboard, 1958–69 71 8.0% 6.7% (2.2–12.9) 1% 72 / 18 / 4 / 6 24% (8%) 7.4, 7.8, 8.9
Billboard, 1970–79 68 11.0% 8.3% (3.8–16.4) 6% 70 / 20 / 5 / 5 18% (7%) 10.0, 10.6, 12.6
Billboard, 1980–91 75 10.4% 9.1% (4.2–18.2) 5% 75 / 16 / 5 / 4 19% (8%) 9.3, 10.2, 11.8
Rolling Stone 200 80 8.8% 8.2% (4.8–12.0) 1% 70 / 19 / 6 / 5 7.8, 8.9, 9.7
PDMX popular 590 4.7% 3.5% (1.1–7.7) 12% 63 / 16 / 6 / 14 48% (15%) 3.9, 4.4, 5.8
PDMX hymns and sacred 407 7.3% 5.6% (1.5–13.2) 19% 73 / 13 / 5 / 9 25% (16%) 6.1, 7.6, 8.3
PDMX folk 330 7.9% 4.8% (0–12.5) 26% 77 / 11 / 4 / 8 23% (14%) 7.1, 7.8, 8.8
PDMX other classical 4,654 7.5% 5.4% (1.9–12.6) 15% 74 / 12 / 4 / 9 21% (17%) 6.9, 7.2, 8.3
OpenEWLD standards 441 1.9% 0% (0–2.2) 55% 81 / 6 / 3 / 9 38% (12%) 1.5, 1.7, 2.3

Shape (MusicXML corpora): 45% to 64% of moves inside a melisma are steps of one or two semitones; the first move goes down in 52% to 59%; a melisma ends lower than it began in 52% to 60%. Grace notes are almost never written: 0 to 0.18 per 100 sung notes.

What the numbers say

  1. Chart pop is melismatic at about 8% to 11% of syllables, rising from the 1960s to the 1970s and holding after. Arrangements of pop songs in PDMX carry half that (4.7%): the same flattening v7 found in its karaoke corpus. Standards are almost syllabic (median 0%).

  2. Melismas gather at phrase ends: 2.5 times their share of syllables in Billboard lines, about 3 times in PDMX popular and standards. v7’s rule that a melisma never lands on a cadence note works against this: the line’s last syllable is where singers ornament most.

  3. Two notes is the norm (63% to 81% of melismas); three notes in 6% to 20%; runs of five or more in 4% to 14%, the most in popular arrangements.

  4. Melisma grows through the song in every corpus: the last third carries more than the first (Billboard 9.0% to 11.3%; PDMX popular 3.9% to 5.8%; standards 1.5% to 2.3%). This matches Hähnel’s observation that ornament concentrates toward a song’s peak.

  5. v7’s figures differ by method. Window 95’s “16% in the median charting song” is about twice the CoCoPops median here (8.6%); the karaoke corpus’s 11.5% sits between. The likeliest cause is counting tied or repeated notes as melisma. v8 should fix one definition (different pitches, ties merged) and recompute its bands.

No open corpus of gospel, R&B or soul with notes and words was found, so their higher rates and longer runs rest on the literature (section 2), not on counts.

5. What v8 should do

Split ornament into two tiers: what is written (notes in the tune) and what is performed (described in the songbook, rendered in the demo, never engraved as notes).

O1. The written tier: melisma by style, placed where singers put it

  • One definition: a syllable on two or more different pitches, ties merged. Recompute v7’s bands with it.

  • Bands by style (share of syllables): standards and art-song-like ballads 0% to 2%; hymns and folk about 2% to 13%, median about 5%; chart pop 4% to 18%, median about 8% to 9% (post-1970 sound), 7% (1960s sound).

  • Placement: melismas at phrase ends at 2.5 to 3 times their syllable share; on wordfinal syllables; more in the last third than the first.

  • Length: two notes in about three quarters, three notes in about a sixth; five or more only as a designed run.

  • Shape: mostly steps, first move down a little more often than up.

  • Retire the cadence-note ban. Replace “a melisma never lands on a cadence note” with: the cadence note may carry a short melisma (two or three notes) that ends on the cadence pitch.

O2. Runs (gospel, R&B, soul, worship)

  • A run is 4 to 7 notes, pentatonic or blues-scale, on a long note at a phrase end, concentrated near the song’s peak and in its last sections, rarely in verse 1.

Because no counted corpus exists, a run is a designed moment (11.9’s vocabulary), chosen at intake for the styles that use them, and written in the score as an optional small-note line or described in the songbook as the singer’s to add.

O3. The performed tier: a vocabulary by style

Style Inflections to name in the songbook Vibrato
Country Scoops into stressed long notes, falls at line ends, the cry or break on a grief word (Paul and Huron), slides, the yodel flip Light, on long notes
Pop and rock Scoops, flip onsets, falls, fry at phrase starts, growl for intensity Straight on short notes, late on long ones
R&B, soul, gospel Runs, scoops, falls, cry, shouts, wide vibrato on held peaks Fast and wide (about 6 to 7 Hz)
Hymn, folk, choir Plain; tune by ear; no scoops on the beat Little or none in unison; light in solo
Art song, classical Legato, written ornaments only About 5.5 to 6.5 Hz, about ±60 cents

The intake’s style picks the column; the songbook’s “for the singer” paragraph names the two or three inflections that matter, and where (computed from the record: the stressed long notes, the line ends, the peak, the grief words).

O4. The demo

  • Render scoops (a short bend up into the note, under half a second) on stressed long notes and falls on line-final notes, by style.

  • Set vibrato rate and depth by style; none on notes under about half a second.

  • Breath: keep v7’s comma rule, Window 3’s 5 to 8 seconds and 749.21’s 8-second ceiling; render a short gap before each new line.

O5. Tests

  • The test report gets an ornament card: melisma share, length distribution, phrase-end ratio, third-by-third trend, against the style’s band.

  • The songbook check: the singer’s paragraph names the style’s inflections and every bar it cites comes from the record.

  • First targets: songs 54 and 55 (country inflections and the cry), song 56 (soul runs at its peak), song 53 (plain, choir).

6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/ornament)

  • ornament_corpora.py : melisma rates, lengths, placement, shape, thirds of the song,

  • and grace notes, from PDMX, OpenEWLD and CoCoPops; ornament_results.json .

Data

  • CoCoPops Billboard and Rolling Stone 200 (Computational Cognitive Musicology Lab, GitHub), via ../words/sung_syllables.json.

  • OpenEWLD (public-domain lead sheets, GitHub).

Sources

  • Hähnel, T. (2012). A brief portrait of Mahalia Jackson; and Analysis of vocal recordings: twang. DFG project “Voices and Singing in Popular Music in the USA”, HfM Weimar.

  • Paul, B. and Huron, D. (2010). An association between breaking voice and grief-related lyrics in country music. Empirical Musicology Review 5(2), 27–35.

Part 27. Key choice for Luthier v8: by genre, instrument and singer

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Key choice for Luthier v8: by genre, instrument and singer.

Summary

  • v7 picks a key from the hook and the voice only (27.14 ranks keys by where the hook’s degrees land). Songs 52 to 56 got instrument-friendly keys (D, E♭, G, A, E minor) because they were chosen by hand.

  • Instruments shape keys. In 739 Billboard songs, guitar-led songs sit in open-string keys 65% of the time and in E, A or B major twice as often as piano-led songs; piano, strings and synthesizer songs use flat keys about twice as often as guitar songs. Spotify’s 30 million tracks lean the same way (G, C, D, A major first).

  • Minor rose and open-string keys fell: BiMMuDa’s hits go from 11% minor before 1970 to about half after 1990, and from about half in open-string keys to under a third. Country and rock stay in open major keys; R&B, soul and hip-hop live in flat keys and minor.

  • The singer: a hit’s sung range is about an octave, with its floor on the tonic or the dominant below and its top near the fifth above the octave, so the key follows from the voice’s floor and the frame. Key colour is a myth on equal-tempered instruments (Powell and Dibben).

  • What v8 should do: choose the frame from the voice, filter by the lead instrument (with a capo when needed), set the mode default by genre and era, and only then rank by the hook as 27.14 does now.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 chooses a key from the voice and the hook alone.

Rule in v7 What it says What it leaves out
27.14, the key from the contract When the writer names no key, list for each key the pitches where the hook’s required degrees land inside the voice’s approach window; rank keys by how many; offer two to hear The instruments, the genre, the era, the key the band will want to play in
Module 11.2, the voice rows One table of ranges, breaks and finals per voice (male 52–66, break 64; female 57–71, break 69; gospel, worship, congregational and bass rows) serves the search, 27.14 and the range check How a real singer’s key relates to their range
Fix 20, the capo An intake field; capo shapes printed beside concert chords When a capo is the right answer
Fix 92, editions A second edition by transposition or octave, with an ossia Choosing which editions a song needs
Fix 34, spelling Pitches spelled from the key (sharps in sharp keys, flats in flat keys)
Module 9-M.4, metal The tonic is the lowest open string of the tuning The same logic for every guitar song

What the recent songs used

  • Song 52 (6/8 guitar ballad): D major. Song 53 (carol, organ and choir): E♭ major, the last verse up to F. Song 54 (country): G major. Song 55 (country): A major. Song 56 (soul ballad): E minor.

  • Four of the five sit in the keys a guitar plays openly (D, G, A, E minor) and the organ carol in a flat key, which is what players of those instruments would expect. Each was chosen at intake by hand; nothing in v7 asked for an open-string key, or said that a carol for organ and choir usually sits in a flat key.

2. The academic record

  • Instruments shape the key. Spotify’s Kenny Ning analysed the keys of some 30 million tracks (2015): G major 10.7% and C major 10.2%, then D and A; more than a third of all songs sit in G, C, D or A major, and the commonest minors (A, E, B minor) are their relatives. His explanation: E suits guitar but not piano, C suits piano but not guitar, and G suits both. Guitar teaching sources say the same about open strings (E, A, D, G and their minors).

  • Minor has risen. Schellenberg and von Scheve (Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 2012; over 1,000 Billboard year-end top-40 songs, 1965–2009) found the share of minor-mode hits doubled over five decades, while tempo fell and songs got longer (Part 28 shows tempo rising again after the 1990s). Press summaries of the paper give 85% major in the 1960s against 42.5% in 2005–09.

  • Key colour is a myth on equal-tempered instruments. Powell and Dibben (Musicae Scientiae, 2005): about three quarters of participants claimed key-mood associations, which matched 18th-century beliefs (sharps bright, flats mellow), but no one could identify mood from key or key from mood, and moving a piece to another key didn’t change its perceived mood. What does change is pitch height relative to the voice, and the instrument’s open strings and tone.

  • Hymnals choose keys for the congregation. Joey Stanley’s count of the Latter-day Saint hymnal (341 hymns) finds G major 22%, D 16%, C, E♭ and F about 14% each, B♭ 11%, A♭ 6%, and almost no A or D♭. Half the hymns top out at D5, and only about 2% go above E5.

  • Untrained voices are narrow. Kuhn, Wachhaus, Moore and Pantle (Journal of Research in Music Education, 1979; 597 non-music undergraduates) found 98% could sing comfortably from B♭3 to G4, 84% from G3 to B4, 75% from G♭3 to C5. Worshipleading advice built on it: lower the key when the tune goes above C5 unless people sing parts.

3. Measured: keys by instrument, era and genre

Data. McGill Billboard (739 songs, 1958–1991): the annotated tonic, mode from the tonic chord, and the lead instrument the annotators marked most often. BiMMuDa (381 top-five singles, 1950–2022): tonic, mode and genre from its metadata. “Open-string keys” means E, A, D, G and C major and E, A and D minor; “flat keys” means F, B♭, E♭, A♭ and D♭ major.

By lead instrument (McGill Billboard)

Lead instrument Songs Minor Open-string keys Flat keys (of major) E, A or B major (of major) Commonest keys
Guitar 335 17% 65% 23% 31% D, G, E, A, C
Piano 48 2% 56% 43% 15% C, G, B♭, D♭
Synthesizer 61 34% 49% 42% 20% G, A♭, D, E
Strings 30 13% 50% 50% 15% C, E♭, F
Horns or sax 59 15% 64% 30% 16% C, D, F, E♭
All 739 17% 62% 29% 27% C, D, G, E, A

By era and genre (BiMMuDa, with McGill for comparison)

Group Songs Minor Open-string keys Flat keys (of major)
1950–69 102 11% 52% 42%
1970–89 102 32% 46% 29%
1990–2009 102 49% 36% 44%
2010–22 75 45% 31% 46%
McGill, 1958–69 / 1970–79 / 1980–91 237 / 260 / 242 10% / 16% / 26% 61% / 62% / 62% 34% / 27% / 25%
Rock 81 30% 53% 23%
Country 16 0% 62% 31%
Pop 139 27% 43% 42%
Funk and soul 44 36% 36% 50%
R&B 42 48% 31% 50%
Hip-hop 31 68% 26% 60%

I also read the notated key signatures of 16,000 PDMX and OpenEWLD scores, but usermade scores default heavily to C and lead sheets are often transposed for convenience, so those counts describe the notation, not the records, and are left out.

What the numbers say

  1. Guitar songs sit in guitar keys. Guitar-led Billboard songs use open-string keys 65% of the time and the sharp guitar keys (E, A, B major) twice as often as piano-led songs (31% against 15%). Piano, strings and synthesizer songs use flat keys about twice as often as guitar songs (42% to 50% against 23%).

  2. Minor rose steadily: 10% to 26% in Billboard between the 1960s and the 1980s, 11% to about half in BiMMuDa by 1990–2009, which agrees with Schellenberg and von Scheve. CoCoPops’s 214 transcribed Billboard songs (Part 22) give 23% minor by the melody’s key against McGill’s 17% by the tonic chord: the same era, two definitions.

  3. Open-string keys fell as guitars gave way to keyboards and production: from about half of BiMMuDa’s hits before 1970 to under a third after 2010.

  4. Genre separates sharply: country and rock live in open-string major keys; R&B, funk, soul and hip-hop in flat keys and minor. Hip-hop is two-thirds minor.

  5. Songs 52 to 56 match their instruments: four guitar-led songs in D, G, A and E minor, and an organ carol in E♭.

4. The singer: where the tonic sits in the range

A key is a choice of where the song’s frame lands in a voice. I measured where the tonic falls inside the sung range of real hits (the range taken as the 5th to 95th percentile of the melody’s notes, so a stray note doesn’t decide it).

Corpus Songs Range (semitones), median and middle half Lowest note above the tonic below it Highest note above that tonic Commonest lowest notes Commonest highest notes
BiMMuDa, 1950–2022 374 12 (10–14) median 5 median 17 the tonic (26%), the dominant (22%) the 5th above the octave (20%), the 3rd above it (11%)
CoCoPops Billboard 214 12 (9–14) median 5 median 16.5 the tonic (32%), the dominant (14%), the 6th (14%) the 5th above the octave (17%), the 3rd above it (13%)

Two frames cover most songs. The melody’s floor is the tonic (an “authentic” range, 1 up to 8 and a little over) or the dominant below it (a “plagal” range, 5 to 5 an octave up). The ceiling is most often the fifth above the upper tonic.

  • The sung range of a hit is about an octave, with the middle half 9 to 14 semitones. v7’s voice rows are 14 to 17 semitones wide, so a song uses most of a row, not all of it.

  • So the key follows from the voice and the frame. For a singer whose comfortable floor is L, the tonic is L (authentic frame) or L plus 5 (plagal frame); the top lands near the tonic plus 16 to 19. Choosing between the two frames, and among nearby keys the instruments like, is the real decision.

  • For a congregation, a floor around B♭3 to D4 and a top at D5 (Kuhn and colleagues; the hymnal’s commonest top note) give the familiar hymn keys of G, D, E♭ and F when the melody spans tonic to tonic or 5 to 5.

5. What v8 should do

Keep 27.14’s hook check. Put it third, after the voice and the instruments.

K1. The voice and the frame first

  • From the voice row and the melody’s frame, list the candidate tonics: the row’s floor as the tonic (authentic frame) or the floor plus 5 (plagal frame), with the song’s span (median 12, middle half 9 to 14) under the row’s top. This turns 27.14’s search over all twelve keys into two or three candidates.

  • For congregational songs, keep the top at D5 (E♭5 at most) and the floor at about B♭3, as hymnals do.

K2. The instruments next

Lead instrument Prefer Avoid unless asked
Acoustic or electric guitar E, A, D, G, C major; E, A, D, B minor; a capo for anything else, printed as shapes E♭, A♭, D♭without a capo
Piano C, G, F, B♭, D, E♭ Many-sharp keys (B, F♯)
Organ and choir; hymns G, D, E♭, F, C, B♭ A and D♭(rare in hymnals)
Horns, strings F, B♭, E♭, C E, A, B major
Synthesizer, production-led pop, R&B, hip-hop No instrumental constraint: choose by voice; flat keys and minor common
Fiddle, mandolin, banjo (country, bluegrass) G, D, A, E, C Flat keys

When the voice’s candidates and the instrument’s preferences don’t meet, offer the capo (guitar) or say which is being given up.

K3. Mode by genre and era

  • Default minor share by genre and era for the mode question at intake: country and 1960s pop about one song in ten; rock about three in ten; pop after 1990 about half; R&B about half; hip-hop about two thirds.

  • Don’t attach moods to particular keys (Powell and Dibben); the mood comes from mode, tempo and where the melody sits in the voice.

K4. Then the hook

27.14 ranks the remaining candidates by where the hook’s required degrees land in the voice’s approach window, and offers two to hear, as now.

K5. Tests

  • The key report prints the frame (authentic or plagal), the span against the row, the instrument’s preference, the capo if used, and the hook’s landing.

  • Songs 52 to 56 as targets: the chooser should arrive at D, E♭, G, A and E minor or name the near alternative and why.

6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/keys)

  • keys_corpora.py : keys and modes by lead instrument and era (McGill Billboard), by

  • era and genre (BiMMuDa), and the notated keys of PDMX and OpenEWLD (not used in the report); keys_results.json .

  • tonic_in_range.py : where the tonic sits in the sung range (BiMMuDa, CoCoPops

  • Billboard); tonic_in_range.json .

Data

  • McGill Billboard annotations via ChoCo (Zenodo 7706751); BiMMuDa (Hamilton and Pearce); CoCoPops Billboard; PDMX (Zenodo 15571083); OpenEWLD.

Sources

  • Ning, K. (2015). The most popular keys of all music on Spotify (Spotify Insights; reported by Hypebot, Gizmodo and Digital Trends).

  • Schellenberg, E. G. and von Scheve, C. (2012). Emotional cues in American popular music: five decades of the Top 40. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts.

  • Powell, J. and Dibben, N. (2005). Key-mood association: a self perpetuating myth. Musicae Scientiae 9(2).

  • Stanley, J. LDS Hymn Stats: key signatures; highest soprano notes.

  • Kuhn, T. L., Wachhaus, G., Moore, R. S. and Pantle, J. E. (1979). Undergraduate nonmusic major vocal ranges. Journal of Research in Music Education; as summarised by Reformed Worship, “Highs and lows of singing”.

  • Guitar Command, guitar keys and open strings.

Not measured: the fiddle, mandolin and banjo row of K2 comes from practice, not counts; no corpus marks those instruments with keys.

Part 28. Tempo, feel and song length for Luthier v8: by era and genre

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Tempo, feel and song length for Luthier v8: by era and genre.

Summary

  • v7 has one tempo figure (104 bpm, all eras), channel design specs, a fixed 2:1 shuffle and no length band. Songs 52 to 56 chose tempo and length by hand.

  • Tempo is an era setting. Top-five hits ran 116 bpm in the 1960s, 91 in the 1990s (a third under 80) and 108 since 2010; both published trends sit on this curve. R&B is the slow genre; minor-key hits aren’t slower. A fifth of hits sit in the 80–95 zone v7 says to avoid.

  • Feel changed: 12/8 was a third of 1950s hits and has vanished; hits are now almost all straight 4/4, and tempo has grown steadier since click tracks (1979 on). Swing ratio depends on tempo: about 3.5:1 slow, 2:1 medium, near straight fast.

  • Length: median 2:31 in the early 1960s, 4:12 by 1985–91, a 1992 peak, and about 3:15 now.

  • What v8 should do: tempo, feel and length bands read from the chosen era and style; swing rendered by tempo; tempo steady unless designed otherwise; the form’s length checked against the era.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

Rule in v7 What it says What it leaves out
Window on tempo (top-five singles) 104 bpm at the median (middle half 88–120, 10th–90th 72–138); in Billboard-matched Lakh songs hits sit at 114 against 120 for other charting songs Tempo by era and by genre
The two channels (design spec) 65–80 bpm for contemplative songs (the cardiac channel), 95–120 for energetic and dance (the motor channel), 80–95 a transition zone where the song must commit Whether real songs cluster this way
Earworms Earworm tunes run about 9 bpm faster than matched non-earworms
Chorus arrival The chorus within 60 seconds; at 65–80 bpm a 16-bar path takes 55–60 s, at 95–120 about 32–40 s Era (Part 25)
Shuffle and groove The blues shuffle divides the beat long-short (about 2:1); groove peaks at moderate syncopation (Witek and others); microtiming in Module 9.2 How much swing by style and tempo; half-time feels
Fix 71 and Protocol 0b The commercial profile prints the song’s length; form options print their length at intake A length band to check it against

What the recent songs used

  • Tempos: song 52 at ♩. = 54 in 6/8 (♩ = 81); song 53 at about ♩ = 88 to 92 in 3/4; songs 54 and 55 at ♩ = 120, straight; song 56 planned at ♩ = 72.

  • Lengths: form options at intake printed lengths from about 3 to almost 5 minutes, and the writer chose among them with nothing to say which lengths suit the era or the genre.

  • Feel: straight eighths in 54 and 55 by choice; no song so far asked whether the style wants swing, a shuffle, or a half-time feel.

2. The academic record

Tempo

  • A preferred tempo near 120. Moelants (2002) combined DJ bpm lists with tapping experiments and found tempi concentrated between about 115 and 127 bpm, peaking at 125; later work places preferred tempo in popular music nearer 120 than the 100 once claimed (de Clercq 2023 reviews this). Groove experiments find an optimum for drum breaks around 100 to 120 bpm.

  • Hit tempo moved, both ways. Schellenberg and von Scheve (2012; over 1,000 Billboard top-40 hits, 1965–2009) found average tempo fell from about 116 bpm in the 1960s to about 100 in the 2000s. Léveillé Gauvin (2018; top-10 hits 1986–2015) found tempo rising over his later window. The two overlap only from 1986, and the rise came after the 1990s low.

  • Tempo got steadier. Carter and von Appen (Integral, 2025; Billboard hits 1966–1995) found a steep fall in tempo variability from 1979, which they attribute to click tracks and sequencing; Condit-Schultz and Clark (2024; 45,000 Spotify tracks) found tempo stability rising in rock, country and blues across the 20th century.

Feel

  • Swing depends on tempo. Friberg and Sundström (Music Perception, 2002) measured jazz drummers’ ride cymbal: the long-short swing ratio reached 3.5:1 at slow tempos and fell to 1:1 at fast ones; the textbook 2:1 holds only at medium tempos. v7’s “about 2:1” shuffle is right only there.

  • Groove peaks at moderate syncopation (Witek and colleagues; already in v7).

Song length

  • Up, then down. A 2025 count of all 6,618 Billboard year-end hits (1959–2025, Spotify durations) gives median lengths of 2:44 (1960s), 3:35 (1970s), 4:06 (1980s), 4:21 (1990s), 3:58 (2000s), 3:40 (2010s) and 3:15 (2020s). The mean peaked at 4:39 in 1992 and bottomed at 3:13 in 2019. Two thirds of 2019’s hits ran 2:30 to 3:30. Weighting by Spotify plays lengthens the average slightly: the biggest hits aren’t the shortest.

  • Earlier counts agree. Schellenberg and von Scheve found hits lengthening from under three minutes in the 1960s to about four in the 2000s; MIDiA Research found top-10 hits shortening by 16% from 2000 to 2020, to 3:42, with intros falling from 13.1 to 7.4 seconds.

3. Measured: tempo, metre and length

Data. BiMMuDa’s metadata (381 top-five singles, 1950–2022): tempo, time signature, mode and genre per song. McGill Billboard (739 songs, 1958–1991): metre and length from the annotations.

Tempo by era (BiMMuDa)

Era Songs Tempo (bpm), median and middle half Under 80 80–95 95–130 Over 130
1950–59 52 102 (87–126) 12% 27% 40% 21%
1960–69 50 116 (95–128) 8% 16% 50% 26%
1970–79 52 104 (84–115) 17% 17% 56% 10%
1980–89 50 104 (91–117) 14% 18% 56% 12%
1990–99 52 91 (70–102) 33% 28% 31% 8%
2000–09 50 104 (87–119) 14% 22% 58% 6%
2010–22 75 108 (91–128) 9% 18% 53% 20%

Tempo by genre and mode (BiMMuDa)

Group Songs Median (middle half) Under 80 Over 130
R&B 42 93 (80–110) 24% 12%
Pop 139 103 (87–120) 16% 11%
Country 16 105 (89–119) 6% 12%
Hip-hop 31 105 (90–126) 6% 16%
Rock 81 107 (86–132) 16% 28%
Funk and soul 44 109 (93–120) 16% 5%

Minor 128 108 (94–120) 8% 14%

Metre and feel

Period 4/4 12/8 6/8 3/4
BiMMuDa 1950–59 54% 35% 4% 6%
BiMMuDa 1960–69 88% 8% 2% 0%
BiMMuDa 1970–79 87% 12% 0% 2%
BiMMuDa 1980–2009 92–94% 2–6% 0–2% 0–2%
BiMMuDa 2010–22 97% 0% 3% 0%

McGill 1985–91 100% 0% 0% 0%

Length (McGill Billboard)

Period Songs Length, median (middle half) Under 3:00 Over 4:00
1958–64 121 2:31 (2:20–2:42) 91% 2%
1965–69 116 2:51 (2:28–3:16) 66% 10%
1970–74 131 3:19 (2:54–3:55) 33% 23%
1975–79 129 3:36 (3:11–4:09) 19% 29%
1980–84 125 3:50 (3:26–4:10) 11% 36%

After 1991 the year-end count in section 2 continues the curve: medians of 4:21 (1990s), 3:58, 3:40 and 3:15 (2020s).

What the numbers say

  1. Tempo is an era setting, with a 1990s dip. Hits ran fastest in the 1960s (median 116), slowest in the 1990s (91, a third of them under 80), and have climbed back to 108 since 2010. Both published trends are in this curve: Schellenberg and von Scheve’s fall to the 1990s, Léveillé Gauvin’s rise after it.

  2. v7’s 104 bpm is the all-era median. It fits the 1970s, 1980s and 2000s and misses the 1960s and 1990s by more than 10 bpm. De Clercq’s figure of about 120 for songs in four (Part 21) differs by corpus (rock and chart corpora against top-five singles), by average (a mean against a median) and by whether slow songs are counted at their felt or doubled pulse; read together, a median near 104 and a felt pulse usually between 100 and 120.

  3. v7’s two channels are real but leaky. Half of hits sit in its motor band (95–130) and 15% under 80, but a fifth sit in the 80–95 zone it calls a place to avoid.

  4. R&B is the slow genre (median 93, a quarter under 80); rock the fastest and widest (28% over 130). Minor-key hits are not slower than major ones (108 against 101), the opposite of the sad-is-slow expectation.

  5. The swung ballad metre vanished. 12/8 (the doo-wop and soul ballad shuffle) was a third of 1950s hits and is absent after 2010; hits now are almost all straight 4/4. Compound and triple metres are a choice of style or era, not a default.

  6. Length follows the format. From 2:31 in the early 1960s to 4:12 by 1985–91 and back to about 3:15 now.

4. What v8 should do

The same principle as Part 25’s intros: tempo, feel and length are era and style settings. Give the intake an era (or “now”) and a style, and read the defaults and bands from the tables.

T1. Tempo bands by era and style

  • Default tempo: the era’s median, adjusted by genre (R&B about 10 bpm slower, rock and funk a little faster); the band is the era’s middle half. Now: 108 (91–128). A 1990s sound: 91 (70–102). A 1960s sound: 116 (95–128).

  • Keep v7’s channels as a description (contemplative under 80, motor 95–130), but drop the instruction to avoid 80–95: a fifth of hits live there.

  • Don’t slow a song because it’s minor; mode doesn’t set tempo in hits.

  • Tempo is steady by default (click-track era); a free or drifting tempo (a rubato intro, a slowing outro) is a designed moment.

T2. Feel

  • Feel is an intake choice: straight, shuffle (swung eighths), 12/8 or 6/8, triple, half-time. Straight 4/4 is the default for anything after 1980; 12/8 is a 1950s and early-1960s ballad or soul sound, and blues and country shuffles are style choices.

  • Swing ratio by tempo , from Friberg and Sundström: about 3:1 at slow tempos, 2:1 around medium, approaching straight at fast tempos. The demo renders the ratio for the tempo rather than a fixed 2:1.

T3. Length

  • Bands by era, checked by the commercial profile (fix 71): 1960s about 2:20 to 3:15; 1970s 2:55 to 4:10; 1980s 3:25 to 4:35; 1990s around 4:20; now about 2:30 to 3:30 (two thirds of 2019’s hits), median about 3:15.

  • The form options at intake print their length against the band, so the writer sees when a form runs long for the era.

T4. Tests

  • The test report prints tempo, feel and length against the chosen era’s bands, and the swing ratio the demo used.

  • Songs 52 to 56 as targets: 54 and 55 at 120 sit in the modern band; 56 at 72 is in the slow tail, right for a soul ballad; the 4- to 5-minute forms offered at intake are long for now and right for the 1980s and 1990s.

5. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/tempo)

  • tempo_corpora.py : tempo by era, genre and mode, and time signatures (BiMMuDa);

  • metre and length by period (McGill Billboard, lengths from ../edges/edges_billboard.json); tempo_results.json .

Sources

  • Moelants, D. (2002). Preferred tempo reconsidered. ICMPC 7; via Dancetempo (JNMR) and de Clercq (2023), Harmonic rhythm in popular music.

  • Schellenberg, E. G. and von Scheve, C. (2012). Emotional cues in American popular music: five decades of the Top 40. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts. Léveillé Gauvin, H. (2018). Drawing listener attention in popular music. Musicae Scientiae 22(3).

  • Carter, D. S. and von Appen, R. (2025). Tempo variability in Billboard Hot 100 songs, 1966–1995. Integral 38.

  • Condit-Schultz, N. and Clark, B. (2024). Have we sold our souls to the drum machine? A historical analysis of tempo stability in Western music recordings.

  • Friberg, A. and Sundström, A. (2002). Swing ratios and ensemble timing in jazz performance. Music Perception 19(3).

  • “Are songs really getting shorter? 6,618 Hot 100 hits, 1959–2025” (DEV Community, 2025), Billboard year-end hits with Spotify durations.

  • MIDiA Research, How the DNA of a hit has changed over 20 years.

  • Etani and colleagues (2018), optimal tempo for groove, Frontiers in Psychology.
