Part 29. Instrumental solos and breaks for Luthier v8

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Instrumental solos and breaks for Luthier v8.

Summary

  • v7 writes the instrument around the voice (figures, riffs, fills, answers) but has no solo, and only metal places one. Songs 52 to 55 had 2- to 4-bar links quoting the hook; none had a solo.

  • Solos rose, then fell. In 739 Billboard songs the share with a solo grew from 22% (1958–64) to 46% (1985–91); three quarters of 1980s hits had a mid-song instrumental section. Later sources describe the decline: instrumental content in number ones fell with hip-hop’s rise in the 1990s, and about half of Japan’s 2021 year-end hits had no solo at all.

  • A solo is about 8 bars and 20 seconds, starts just past the middle (0.45 to 0.65 of the song), most often follows the second chorus and leads into the last verse or chorus, and plays its own chords half the time (the verse’s 30%, the chorus’s 20%). Guitar leads about half; saxophone led early-1960s solos; synthesizer appeared in the 1980s.

  • Short links are nearly universal: 4 bars in nine of ten POP909 songs, 8-bar interludes in Billboard.

  • What v8 should do: two kinds of instrumental section (link and solo) with bands for length, place and material; a solo default by era and style; the solo’s line from the style’s lead instrument, restating or elaborating the tune or building on its scale, and handing back to the voice for a fresh re-entry.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 writes the instrument around the voice in detail, and has no solo.

Rule in v7 What it says What it leaves out
27.21 and fixes 10, 21, 35, 90, 91 The instrumental line’s kinds: a figure, a riff repeated in every instrumental section, a quote of a sung section, a texture, a restatement, an answer A solo: an instrumental section of its own, with its own line
The band window (fills) The voice sounds through 72% of a song, the lead instrument 55%; of the lead’s time, 18% in intros, interludes and outros; fills of 2 to 3 beats and 4 to 6 notes in the voice’s gaps How long instrumental sections are, and where
Form options (fixes 13, 31, 56) Interludes priced into the form’s length Whether a song of this era and style should have one
Module 9-M (metal) The solo or breakdown goes in the bridge Every other style
The blues window Bars 11–12 of a twelve-bar are the instrument’s answer
Stop-time breaks (karaoke corpus) A break before a line occurs about 2,900 times in 1,014 songs

What the recent songs did

  • Song 52: a 4-bar interlude where the cello sings the hook.

  • Song 53: a 2-bar organ link between verses.

  • Song 54: a 4-bar turnaround with the fiddle playing the hook and the steel answering.

  • Song 55: a 4-bar break of fiddle call and answer with a steel reply, the last bar the acoustic alone.

  • Song 56: no instrumental section planned beyond intro and outro.

All four instrumental sections were 2 to 4 bars and quoted the hook. None of the songs had a solo, and nothing in v7 says whether a song of its style and era would.

2. The academic record

Where a solo goes in the form

  • In verse-chorus form, Open Music Theory (Hughes and Lavengood, after Covach 2005) describes the solo as able to stand in for a section: in their model analysis the last cycle begins with a guitar solo that functions as a bridge and replaces the verse.

Covach’s compound AABA reading of rock puts the contrasting middle (bridge or solo) after the second verse-chorus cycle.

  • In blues-based forms, Carter (Music Theory Online 31.1, 2025), studying blues-based songs, names a “solo-bridge model”, AABA interrupted by an instrumental solo before the bridge, and an AABA-solo-BA “two-bridge” model.

  • In metal, a 2022 Oregon dissertation on verse-chorus-bridge form shows bridges given to instrumental passages and dance sections, diverting the usual chorus goal; v7’s metal module already puts the solo or breakdown there.

  • At the end, Osborn’s terminally climactic forms and Spicer’s cumulative form let the last section, often instrumental, be the climax (Part 25).

How common solos are

  • Guitar solos in number ones (Michael Rays, Number One with an Axe, rating every Billboard number one from 1955): the high-water mark was 1957, 40% of number ones; the early 1960s were a “drought” with under 10%; in 1965 only 20% had a guitar solo though 68% had a riff.

  • Instrumental content in number ones (Chris Dalla Riva, 1940–2021): the average share of a hit without voice declined in two steps, the sharpest beginning in the 1950s and in the 1990s with hip-hop’s rise.

  • Now: a 2021 count of Japan’s year-end Kohaku hits found nearly 70% had no guitar solo and almost half had no solo of any kind. Hit Songs Deconstructed reports electric guitar on 61% of US top-10 hits in the first half of 2025, up from 38% in 2024, so instrument use swings with fashion.

What a solo plays

Analysts describe three common materials: the verse’s chords (the “solo over the verse”), the chorus’s chords, and new chords of the solo’s own; and three common contents: a melodic restatement of the tune, an improvised line on the section’s scale, and a riffbased break. None of the sources gives counts; section 3 counts the chords.

3. Measured: 739 Billboard songs and 909 POP909 songs

Data. The McGill Billboard annotations label each section (solo, interlude, instrumental, theme), give its time, chords and section letter (shared letters mean shared music), and mark the lead instrument and the lead voice. A mid-song instrumental section here is one that is neither the first nor the last section. POP909’s structure labels mark instrumental

sections in lower case. The lead-voice share here (median 81%) is higher than the 72% in v7’s band window, which read Lakh MIDI files rather than annotations; the trend over time is the point here, not the level.

How often (McGill Billboard)

Period Songs With a solo With any mid-song instrumental section Share of the song with a lead voice, median
1958–64 121 22% 41% 87%
1965–69 116 30% 58% 83%
1970–74 131 34% 53% 77%
1975–79 129 34% 60% 82%
1980–84 125 41% 75% 79%
1985–91 117 46% 77% 76%
All 739 35% 61% 81%

POP909 (Chinese pop, 2000s–2010s): 92% of songs have a mid-song instrumental section, median 4 bars (middle half 3–4), at 47% of the song.

What a solo is (342 solos)

Period Solos Length (s) Length (bars) Starts at (share of song) Plays the chords of: own / verse / chorus Lead: guitar / horns or sax / synthesizer
1958–64 32 16 (12–21) 8 (8–12) 0.53 34 / 34 / 28% 28 / 31 / 0%
1965–69 49 19 (13–28) 9 (8–16) 0.57 63 / 24 / 10% 49 / 10 / 0%
1970–74 64 20 (15–33) 8 (8–16) 0.51 50 / 28 / 22% 59 / 8 / 0%
1975–79 59 27 (17–32) 12 (8–16) 0.54 41 / 36 / 22% 51 / 10 / 2%
1980–84 65 20 (16–28) 9 (8–16) 0.57 45 / 34 / 17% 45 / 17 / 14%
1985–91 73 19 (16–28) 8 (8–16) 0.52 51 / 27 / 21% 41 / 10 / 8%
All 342 20 (15–30) 9 (8–16) 0.54 (0.45–0.65) 48 / 30 / 20% 47 / 13 / 5%

The other mid-song instrumental sections (interludes, instrumental themes): median 8 bars (4–12), 15 seconds.

Where it sits: a solo follows a chorus 40% of the time, a verse 18%, the bridge 11%, and leads into a verse 33%, a chorus 24%, a second solo 10%, the fade 7%.

What the numbers say

  1. Solos rose through the corpus: from about a fifth of early-1960s hits to nearly half by 1985–91, and three quarters of 1980s hits had some mid-song instrumental section. The literature’s later decline (Dalla Riva; the Kohaku count) falls after 1991, so v8 needs an era setting here too.

  2. A solo is 8 bars, sometimes 16, about 20 seconds, and sits just past the middle of the song (median 0.54, middle half 0.45 to 0.65), the same place as v7’s breath-and-reentry window (749.19, 0.55 to 0.60).

  3. Half of solos have chords of their own; the rest play over the verse (30%) or the chorus (20%). Almost none use the bridge’s chords: the solo is the bridge, or sits next to it.

  4. The usual path is chorus, solo, verse or chorus: the solo is the contrast after the second chorus, before the last cycle.

  5. The lead instrument follows the era: saxophone and horns led early-1960s solos as often as guitar; guitar led about half from 1965 on; synthesizer took 14% in the early 1980s.

  6. Short instrumental links are everywhere: a 4-bar link in nine of ten POP909 songs, and 8-bar interludes in Billboard. Songs 52, 54 and 55’s 4-bar breaks fit this, not the solo.

4. What v8 should do

S1. Two kinds of instrumental section

Kind What it is Length Where Material
Link (interlude, turnaround, break) A short instrumental passage between sections, usually playing the hook or the riff 2 to 8 bars (POP909 median 4; Billboard interludes 8) Between a chorus and the next verse; may recur The intro’s figure, the hook, or a call and answer (songs 52, 54, 55)
Solo An instrumental section that takes the song’s middle 8 bars, sometimes 16; about 20 seconds After the second chorus, starting at 0.45 to 0.65 of the song, leading into the last verse or chorus; may replace the bridge or follow it Its own chords (half), the verse’s (30%) or the chorus’s (20%)

The intake asks whether the song has a solo, defaulting by era and style: rare in an early1960s sound (about one in five); common in a 1970s or 1980s rock or pop-rock sound (a third to a half); uncommon now outside rock, country and worship. Songs without a solo still get links.

S2. The solo’s line

  • Instrument: the style’s lead (guitar in rock and country; saxophone in early-1960s pop, soul and R&B; synthesizer in 1980s pop; fiddle or steel in country; organ or piano in gospel).

  • Content, in three kinds: a restatement of the hook or verse tune on the instrument (the safest, and what songs 52 to 55’s links did), an elaboration (the tune with fills and runs), or a new line built on the section’s scale, using 27.21’s figure and riff tools.

  • Shape: it rises to its peak in its second half and hands back to the voice with a fill (the band window’s fill rules), so the voice’s re-entry is the fresh moment of 749.19.

  • Intensity: at or above the chorus before it (749.17’s rising returns); the arrangement thins only if the song’s plan puts a breakdown there instead.

S3. The documents

The lead sheet prints the solo’s chords and a written line (or slashes with “solo, 8 bars” when it’s to be improvised); the parts give the soloist the line or the changes; the songbook says what the solo should do in a sentence.

S4. Tests

  • The form report prints each instrumental section’s kind, length, place and material against these bands and the era’s solo share.

  • The solo’s line passes the instrumental-line floors (27.21) and the perception checks (no masking of the voice, which is silent there).

  • First targets: song 54 or 55 rerun with an 8-bar fiddle solo over the verse’s chords after chorus 2, and song 56 with a saxophone or guitar solo over its own chords before the bridge.

5. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/solos)

  • solos_billboard.py : solos and other mid-song instrumental sections in McGill

  • Billboard (length, place, neighbours, material, lead instrument), per song (solo, instrumental, share with lead voice); solos_results.json .

  • solos_pop909.py : mid-song instrumental sections in POP909; solos_pop909.json .

Sources

  • Covach, J. (2005). Form in rock music: a primer. In Engaging Music; via Open Music Theory (Hughes and Lavengood), Verse-chorus form.

  • Carter (2025), on form in blues-based songs (the solo-bridge and two-bridge models), Music Theory Online 31(1), mto.25.31.1.carter.

  • Formal dialectic in heavy metal music (PhD dissertation, University of Oregon, 2022). Osborn, B. (2013), terminally climactic forms; Spicer, M. (2004), (ac)cumulative form.

  • Rays, M. Number One with an Axe; Culture Sonar series on guitar in number-one hits (1955–1984).

  • Dalla Riva, C. The decline and fall of the hit instrumental song. The Honest Broker. Soundhouse (Japan), guitar solos in the 2021 Kohaku Uta Gassen songs.

  • Hit Songs Deconstructed, The State of the Hot 100 Top 10, 2025 mid-year report (preview).

  • McGill Billboard annotations (Burgoyne, Wild and Fujinaga) via ChoCo; POP909 (Wang et al.) with Dai, Zhang and Dannenberg’s structure labels.

Not reached: the counts behind Dalla Riva’s chart, and any study of what solos play note by note in popular song.

Part 30. The hook for Luthier v8: what makes a chorus stick

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc The hook for Luthier v8: what makes a chorus stick.

Summary

The songs people recognise fastest have choruses built from common cells and plain intervals. Our choruses do the opposite: they repeat themselves less than at least 94% of real choruses their length.

  • v7 has more hook theory than any other area: Module 23, Window 17, the money note, the quotable line. It never tested a hook against recognition, and its strength indicators reward an unusual interval.

  • The research that measured memory (Hooked, 1,715 sections of 321 songs) found the voice, typical sound and melody, and repetition made sections recognisable. Distinctiveness did not. Listeners name a familiar song by about the 6th note, helped by long notes, downbeats and phrase boundaries more than by pitch.

  • Measured on 22,407 Hooktheory sections: a chorus is mainly higher than its verse (67% of songs, +1.5 semitones). It is only a little more repetitive and no more typical. The 14 fastest-recognised songs’ choruses sit at the 81st percentile for typical cells, the 33rd for interval variety and the 27th for surprise.

  • Titles (156 Billboard hits): sung in the chorus in 87% of songs with one, about twice per chorus and 8 times per song, in the chorus’s first line more often than its last (40% against 28%), first heard at about 39 seconds.

  • Songs 52 to 56: every chorus at the 1st to 6th percentile for self-repetition; in songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus. Song 56 never sings its title.

  • For v8: six rules (section 5). Score typicality instead of an unusual interval, make the chorus repeat its own cell, place the title as hits do, carry identity in rhythm, keep each section’s job, and test both recognition and singing back.

Eleven new lines of work came from the bibliographies and arXiv (section 3). The strongest next one is YouTube’s replay curve, a moment-by-moment listener outcome.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 has more hook theory than any other area, but it has never measured a hook against what a hook is for: being recognised and recalled. Every test so far used the chart, weeks on the chart or views, and found almost nothing. The recognition data that could measure the hook itself (Hooked on Music) was named in Window 63 as not reachable from the build.

Rule in v7 What it does What it leaves out
Module 23 (v30): hook architecture A hook specification in four terms (place, melodic feature, words, compound channels), five hook types, the approach (a withheld resolution of two bars or more, a held approach note, a build), a four-step prosody audit, six strength indicators (four needed) The indicators come from the literature and were never tested in the engine
Window 17 (v30): memory and hook science Earworms, the unfinished phrase, the anticipation and arrival reward, phrase endings as memory anchors A review, with no measurement
Module 4 (v44): the motif detector Four-note motifs (contour and rhythm) that return exactly or varied; real verse and chorus pairs score a median of 0.79 Weak against hits (AUC 0.52); says nothing about recall
Window 42 (v56): the money note Under the title’s last content word the chord is I 37%, IV 22%, V 17%; the chorus peak is on an unstable degree 40% of the time; listeners’ arousal rises at peak notes Arousal, not memory
Window 45 (v57): convergence In 97 rated hits arousal climbs with the number of convergence elements at a bar Arousal, not memory
Window 48 (v61): the earworm profile Jakubowski’s three earworm features measured on 12,163 choruses; demoted after AUC 0.48 to 0.51 against the chart Tested against sales, not against being stuck in the head
Windows 62 and 63 (v79): survival and description length Survival among hits close to unpredictable (concordance 0.531); compressibility null The hook’s own outcome, said to be out of reach
Module 10.20 (v89): the quotable line Ranks a song’s lines against each other; the writer’s blind picks are the label Words only, not the tune
Module 27.4 and v63: title-first design, the refrain kernel The title’s cell copied where it ends chorus lines; hooks aimed at a stressed full vowel Where the title goes and how often is not drawn from data

What the recent songs needed

Songs 52 to 56 had their hooks set by design questions or by sketch, and v7 checked them. Nothing could tell the engine whether one candidate hook is stickier than another. Finding 749.8 keeps each hook exact while inner chorus lines vary, so the hook is also the one part of a song that must not drift.

2. The academic record

The studies that measured memory itself point away from Module 23’s “unusual interval”. The sections people recognise fastest have the voice up front, sound typical of pop, and repeat within the song. Distinctiveness helps in one narrow way: a rare cell makes a passage feel familiar, even when it is new.

Catchiness measured as recognition

Burgoyne and colleagues defined a hook as the most salient, easiest-to-recall fragment of a song, and catchiness as long-term musical salience. Their game Hooked drops the needle at the start of a section and times how fast players recognise the song (Burgoyne et al. 2013). The Dutch game logged 167,704 responses from 1,986 players. The UK version, Hooked on Music, drew over 160,000 players and over 3 million responses on 1,000 excerpts from 200 chart-toppers (Van Balen 2016, ch. 7).

Study Data What made a section recognisable
Van Balen et al. 2015; thesis ch. 8 1,715 sections of 321 songs, 973 players; 99 songs transcribed Vocal prominence, the strongest (+0.14 per SD); a typical sound, melody, harmony and range (+0.05 to +0.09); melodic repetitiveness (+0.12); typical motifs (+0.07). No support for distinctiveness. Between-song differences were 37% to 40% of the variance
Korsmit et al. 2017 Hooked on Music, 4,082 players, 184 fragments Listener differences: female vocals from 2006 to 2013, songs of the listener’s teens (1990s), a rap and beat factor; one factor for fragments easy to sing along with
Schulkind et al. 2003 34 familiar songs, played note by note Named by about the 6th note (mean 6.35). Helped by phrase boundaries, long notes (over a beat), the first beat of the bar, the first note of a repeated pair, a completed up-down alternation. Pitch height and interval size did not matter
Dalla Bella et al. 2003, via Filipic et al. 2010 Familiar songs on piano Familiar after about 4 notes (2.3 s), sure after about 6 (3.1 s). From the real recording, half a second can be enough
Jakubowski et al. 2017 100 earworm tunes against 100 matched A more common overall contour; less common gradients between turning points; tempo 124 against 116 bpm (a trend). How popular and how recent the song was mattered more
Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014 80 pop phrases, unfamiliar to the listeners Rare motifs (against the other test phrases) gave more correct recognitions; rare motifs against the pop corpus gave more false “I’ve heard it”
Sonic logos (Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts) 90 brand logos, 1,860 listeners Complexity helped recognition and hurt singing it back

What listeners carry away

  • The chorus. It is the section most often reported stuck in the head, and pieces with vocals are about twice as likely to be (Liptak et al. 2022, citing Beaman and Williams, Liikkanen, and Floridou).

  • Exposure first. Tempo and lyrics shape earworms only through what the listener habitually hears (Liptak et al. 2022). Popularity and recency outweighed the melody in Jakubowski’s data.

  • Singing along. In 1,054 song events in English pubs, context explained about 40% of sing-along and the music about another 25%, vocal performance above all (Pawley and Müllensiefen 2012).

  • Repetition sells. In 2,480 Hot 100 songs, each extra chorus repetition raised the odds of a number one by 14.5% (Nunes, Ordanini and Valsesia 2015, as reported).

Recognisable is catchy. In ratings of 54 excerpts, recognisability raised catchiness strongly (B = 0.29), and catchiness went with the urge to move (ρ ≈ 0.49) (Bechtold, Curry and Witek 2025).

What this means

Recognition and recall pull apart. A hook has to be recognised in a few notes and also sung back. The research says: put the voice on it, keep its frame typical, repeat it, land it on long notes and strong beats at a phrase boundary, and give it one rare cell. Module 23’s six indicators reward an unusual interval and an arch, which is half of that.

3. New vectors found in appendices, bibliographies and arXiv

Following the reference lists and appendices opened eleven lines of work that v7 does not have. Three are used in this study; the rest are listed for v8 and later studies.

Vector Where it came from What it adds Here
Song-based and corpus-based typicality Van Balen et al. 2015, built on FANTASTIC (Müllensiefen 2009) Two different measures: how much a section repeats its own song, and how common its cells are across all songs Used (self-repetition, typical cells)
The cohort model of melody recognition Schulkind et al. 2003, citing Marslen- Wilson’s spoken-word model; Dalla Bella et al. 2003; Thiesen, Kopiez and Müllensiefen 2020 A melody is identified when its opening stops matching other songs, around notes 5 to 7; section, duration, voice and orderliness change speed Used (notes until unique)
The fastest-recognised list Hooked on Music’s published top 20 with recognition times ( as reported) An outcome for hooks, not sales Used (14 songs)
Recognition against sung recall Sonic logos study; Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014; Silas and Müllensiefen 2023 Complexity helps recognition and hurts singing back; length is the main limit on learning a tune A two-sided test for v8
A rare cell feels familiar Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014, citing Rhodes and Castel 2009 One distinctive motif makes a new song feel already known A rule for v8
Listener differences Korsmit et al. 2017, citing Krumhansl and Zupnick 2013 on reminiscence bumps What is recognised depends on the listener’s age and the singer’s sex An audience row at intake
Catchiness and groove Bechtold, Curry and Witek 2025 and their 2023 and 2024 studies Catchiness in 1 second and in 10 seconds are different; both go with the urge to move Ties the hook to Part 10’s rhythm layer
YouTube’s “most replayed” graph arXiv: Rhapsody (2505.19429), YTMR500 (2309.06102), Mr. HiSum A replay curve in 100 steps for most videos with 50,000 views or more: a moment-by-moment listener outcome for millions of songs Not reachable from this workspace; the strongest next study
Memorability of unfamiliar music arXiv 2405.12847 (ISMIR 2023, YTMM) Recall of instrumental intros after a delay; higher valence, arousal and tempo helped Background
Repetition structure and hook detection arXiv 2209.00182 (over half of POP909 phrases repeat at once); 2410.19540 (expert hook labels); 2205.14700 (verse and chorus from audio) Tools to mark hooks in real recordings and in our demos For the demo check
Hookpad Aria arXiv 2502.08122 Hooktheory’s own melody assistant: 318,000 suggestions, 74,000 accepted by users A preference signal, if its logs were ever shared

One more vector is a request, not a search. The full Hooked on Music data (over 3 million responses on 1,000 excerpts) was never released. It would test every claim in this study on real recognition times. The team is at the University of Amsterdam (Burgoyne, Music Cognition Group); asking them for it is worth one email.

4. Measured: hooks in our corpora

Three measurements, and one result stands above the rest. The choruses players recognised fastest are built from common cells and plain intervals. Our songs 54 to 56 have choruses that repeat their own cells less than about 90% of real choruses.

Chorus against verse in the same song

Hooktheory gives 22,407 transcribed sections of 16 notes or more, with their section names. In 2,839 songs with both a chorus and a verse, each chorus was compared with its own verse (studies/hooks, hooks_analyse.py).

Measure Chorus higher in Median difference
Mean pitch 67% of songs +1.5 semitones
Self-repetition (share of the section’s 3- to 5-note cells heard again in it) 56% +0.03
Surprise (bits per note, model trained on other songs) 54% +0.06
Typical cells (how many other songs share each cell) 46% slightly less typical
Notes per beat 47% −0.02
Notes until the opening is unique to the song no difference

The chorus is mainly higher. It is only a little more repetitive than its verse, and no more typical. So what makes a chorus the part people carry away is mostly not in its intervals: it is the voice, the register, the words and how often it comes round.

The other sections each have a job. Intros, where instrumental hooks live, are the most repetitive part of the song: against the verse (1,026 songs) they repeat more in 64% and their main cell covers more of the notes in 71%. Pre-choruses (871 songs) sit higher than the verse in 64% but repeat less (37%) and surprise more (57%). Bridges (665 songs) repeat less than the chorus (41%) and surprise more (57%).

Inside a chorus, the most frequent 4-note cell returns a median of 3 times (middle half 2 to 4). It is first heard in the opening quarter of the chorus in 88% of choruses and covers a quarter of its notes.

Openings become unique to their song quickly when rhythm counts: by the 6th note in about half of choruses and by the 8th in 86%. By intervals alone, only 8% are unique by the 6th note and 39% by the 8th. That matches Schulkind’s finding that rhythm and long notes, not pitch, drive identification.

The songs players recognised fastest

studies/hooks: hooks_catchiest.py (14 of the 20 songs Hooked on Music players recognised fastest, published November 2014) and hooks_our_songs.py

Fifteen of the 20 published fastest-recognised songs are in Hooktheory, 14 with chorus transcriptions. Their choruses sit at the 81st percentile for typical cells (11 of 14 above the median, p = 0.057), the 27th for surprise and the 33rd for interval variety (12 of 14 below, p = 0.013). Their openings also take longer than most to become unique (12 of 14, p = 0.013). Self-repetition and the main cell’s share are ordinary. Fourteen songs is a small sample, but the direction is Van Balen’s: recognisable means typical.

Where the title goes

CoCoPops transcribes 214 Billboard hits (1958 to 1991) with their sung syllables (hooks_titles.py; lines read from punctuation, rests of 3/4 beat or more and section changes). The title is sung in 156 of them.

Measure Result
Times the title is sung median 8 (middle half 4 to 12)
Songs with a chorus that sing the title in it 87% of 134
Where the title is sung chorus 57%, verse 22%, outro and fade 11%
Choruses carrying the title 82% of 375; median 2 times each (75th percentile 3), in a third of the lines
Place in the chorus first line 40% (chance 33%), last line 28%, the very first word 27%
Rhythm starts on a beat 73%, on beat 1 33%; its notes held 1.33 times the song’s median note, the longest 2 times
Pitch on the section’s top note 31%
First heard median 39 s (middle half 16 to 60 s), 18% of the way in

The title opens the chorus more often than it closes it. The songwriting habit of saving the title for the last line is the minority case in these hits.

Songs 52 to 56

Each section was measured as a Hooktheory clip is and placed against clips of the same kind and similar length (hooks_our_songs.py, hooks_our_titles.py). Percentiles:

Song Self-repetition Interval variety Typical cells Surprise Title
52, chorus 1 48 40 60 sung 3 times, first at 38 s
53, refrain 6 50 83 93 not read
54, chorus 6 68 35 53 full title 3 times, first at 116 s (47% in); its key words in every chorus
55, chorus 2 74 49 49 7 times, first at 41 s, opening every chorus
56, chorus 5 90 27 74 never sung; the chorus’s own phrase twice in each

Every chorus repeats its own cells less than at least 94% of real choruses its length. In songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus (percentiles 16 against 6, 42 against 2, 75 against 5), the reverse of the norm. Song 56’s chorus is the furthest from the fastest-recognised profile: high variety, less typical cells, above-median surprise.

5. What v8 should do

v8 should score hooks for recognition, not novelty: a typical frame, a chorus that repeats itself, the title placed where hits place it, and one fresh note where the voice comes back. Each rule below has a check that runs on every song. If they go on the fix list, they would be findings 749.24 onward.

H1. Rewrite Module 23’s strength indicators

Now (23.6) Replace with Why
An unusual interval at the turning point (high weight) The chorus’s cells at or above the 60th percentile of chorus typicality (aim for the 75th), its interval variety and surprise per note at or below the median Van Balen 2015; the 14 fastest-recognised choruses sit at the 81st, 33rd and 27th percentiles
(none) One fresh note per hook phrase, placed at the re-entry after a breath Part 9 and finding 749.19; Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014 (a rare cell feels familiar)
A common arch or descent (medium) Kept, as a report only Jakubowski 2017; Window 48
Compound hook, approach, prosody, cadence Kept Byron et al. 2025; the pre-chorus corpus result below

H2. The chorus repeats itself

Rule: the chorus’s self-repetition sits at or above the median of real choruses its length, and above its own verse. Its main 4-note cell returns at least 3 times (real choruses: median 3, middle half 2 to 4), first inside the opening quarter, covering about a quarter of the notes.

  • How: the chorus’s lines share a rhythm cell (lines 1 and 3, or 1 and 2, sung to the same cell), the way v63’s cell grammar already copies the refrain kernel.

  • Why it matters now: songs 52 to 56 sit at the 1st to 6th percentile, and in songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus.

  • Check: hooks_our_songs.py on every pick.

H3. The title

  • In the chorus (87% of hits with a chorus), about twice in each chorus (75th percentile 3), about 8 times in the song (flag under 4).

  • In the chorus’s first line more often than its last (40% against 28%); first heard by about 40 seconds (middle half 16 to 60 s).

  • On a beat (73%), its notes held longer than the song’s median note (1.3 times; the longest twice). The top note is optional (31%).

  • A song whose hook phrase is not its title (song 56) applies these to the hook phrase and prints where the title falls.

H4. Identity through rhythm

The hook’s opening should become unique to the song by its 8th note when rhythm is counted (86% of real choruses), while its intervals stay common (only 39% are unique by intervals alone). Long notes and downbeats at the phrase boundary carry identification (Schulkind et al. 2003). Check: the uniqueness point against the Hooktheory index, at or under 8 notes.

H5. Each section keeps its job

Section Corpus result (against the verse unless noted) v8 target
Intro The most repetitive part: main cell covers more in 71% of songs An instrumental hook built from one repeated cell (with Part 25 and v7’s instrumental hook)
Pre-chorus Higher in 64%, repeats less in 63%, surprises more in 57% The approach: rising, less settled (Module 23.4 confirmed)
Chorus Higher in 67%, repeats a little more in 56% H1 to H4
Bridge Repeats less than the chorus in 59%, surprises more in 57% Contrast, as Part 18 says

H6. Recognise it and sing it back

A hook must pass two tests that pull against each other: recognition (helped by one distinctive cell) and singing back (hurt by complexity and length). The hook phrase stays inside one breath and one phrase (the memory ceiling of about 8 seconds, Part 11), repeats, and keeps its one fresh note. The voice carries it: vocal prominence was the strongest predictor of recognition, so the mix keeps the lead on top at every hook (Module 9.12’s stems rule).

Tests for v8

  1. Songs 52 to 56 rerun: every chorus at or above the 50th length-matched percentile for self-repetition and the 60th for typical cells, interval variety at or below the 50th.

  2. Title rules H3 pass, or the exception is printed.

  3. Uniqueness point at or under 8 notes with rhythm counted.

  4. Finding 749.8’s varied repeats still leave the hook and first line exact.

  5. A blind A/B with Jason: the v7 pick against the H1 to H4 pick for one song, his choice logged.

6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/hooks)

  • hooks_hooktheory.py: features of 22,407 Hooktheory sections (self-repetition, typical cells, surprise, the main cell, uniqueness points); writes hooks_clips.json (derived numbers only)

  • hooks_analyse.py: chorus against verse, intro, pre-chorus and bridge in the same song; hooks_hooktheory_results.json

  • hooks_catchiest.py: the 14 fastest-recognised songs against all choruses; hooks_catchiest_results.json

  • hooks_titles.py: where titles fall in 214 CoCoPops hits; hooks_titles_results.json (no lyrics kept)

  • hooks_our_songs.py and hooks_our_titles.py: songs 52 to 56; hooks_our_songs.json, hooks_our_titles.json

Data

Part 31. What arXiv adds for Luthier v8: a pass across the research topics

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc What arXiv adds for Luthier v8: a pass across the research topics.

Summary

arXiv adds tools and data, not corrections. Across the 13 topics no paper reverses a rule in Parts 18 to 30, so a full redo of every research round is not warranted.

  • One real miss: Chordonomicon, 666,000+ songs’ chords with sections, genres and dates. It was skipped earlier as unavailable; it is public, but its file host is blocked from this workspace. It could retest harmony, chromatic chords and keys at about 900 times McGill’s size.

  • Two small additions: a long-note band for word setting (songs 54 and 56 fall short of it), and a floor on predictability (elevator music).

  • Outcome signals: Spotify’s skip curves (skips cluster at the start and at transitions) and YouTube’s replay curves, both measuring listeners moment by moment.

  • Tools: Python versions of the standard melodic features and of IDyOM, to check the studies’ own measures.

Most music-psychology and music-theory work, which the earlier parts rest on, is published outside arXiv, so its absence there is expected.

1. How the pass was done

Each of the 13 research topics behind Parts 18 to 30 was searched on arXiv, with PsyArXiv and the ISMIR archive where arXiv was thin, for papers mostly from 2022 to 2026. A paper counts only if it changes a rule in Parts 18 to 30, adds data the engine could use, or gives a better way to measure an outcome. Papers on audio generation, voice cloning or model training alone are noted once and skipped.

The workspace cannot query arXiv’s own search, so the pass uses web search restricted to arXiv and reads the papers it returns. That means a paper with unusual wording can be missed; each topic got at least two different searches to reduce that.

2. Topic by topic

No arXiv paper reverses a rule in Parts 18 to 30. Most of what arXiv holds on these topics is generation methods; the useful part is data, tools and outcome measures.

Topic (Part) What arXiv adds Changes a rule?
Harmony (18) Chordonomicon:over 666,000 songs’ chord progressions with section labels, genre, release date and Spotify IDs. BeatlesFC:harmonic-function labels for the Beatles (predominant 16.5%, dominant 13.2% of chords) Not yet. Chordonomicon could retest Part 18 at about 900 times McGill’s size (section 3)
The band (19) Accompaniment and texture generators ( AccoMontage, METEOR, whole-song hierarchical generation); no new corpus statistics No
Tension (20) A tension model on tonal interval vectors steered generation and passed a listening test ( 2511.19342); learned chord embeddings compared with human tension ratings ( 2609.36460) No; a second tension reader to check Part 20’s against
Metre above the bar (21) Models that find 2-, 4-, 8- and 16-bar hypermeter in MIDI ( 2209.10259, 2210.17183); over half of POP909’s phrases repeat at once( 2209.00182) No; confirms, and gives a check for our songs
Melody by genre (22) Melodic diversity shaped by information and motor limits across cultures ( 2408.12635); melody and rhythm compared in 27,628 songs from 59 countries ( 2605.05982); a Python package of the standard melodic features ( 2608.19061) No; the package could replace our own feature code
Setting words (23) In human-written lyrics, syllable stress tracks metric strength, melodic peaks and note length; one version of the paper puts long notes on stressed syllables 73% of the time, another 82% ( LOAF-M2L) Adds a band (below)
Harmony voices (24) Voice separation and an automatic four-part vocal harmonizer ( 2506.18143) No
Song edges (25) Spotify skips follow one shape: most skips come in the first seconds, with spikes at transitions such as a chorus starting or a voice entering, and a rise near the end that is not universal ( Donier 2020) No; supports Part 25’s short intros and early voice
Ornament (26) Singing-technique labels in 168 J-pop songs ( 2210.17367)and a nine-language technique corpus ( GTSinger) No
Key (27) Little: keys skew major in high-valence clips ( 2407.20176) No
Tempo and length (28) Number-one songs have tripled their chart lifetime since the 1960s ( 2405.07574); Hot 100 songs’ complexity sits closer to the mean than random songs’ ( 1907.04292) No
Solos (29) Large guitar tablature sets ( DadaGP, GOAT) No; DadaGP could give solo note statistics Part 29 lacked
The hook (30) Covered in Part 30 (replay curves, memorability, hook labels) Already in Part 30
Surprise (Part 8, for completeness) A Python reimplementation of IDyOM ( GraphIDyOM); surprisal from a diffusion model shows the inverted U with liking ( 2310.03500) No; a check on our own surprise model

One PsyArXiv study is worth a line: elevator-music covers of popular songs were rated less pleasurable, surprising and arousing than the originals (PsyArXiv xqs8b). Predictable wins (Parts 8 and 30), but there is a floor; Part 30’s target of the 75th percentile for typical cells, not the 100th, keeps clear of it.

Part 32. Lyric craft for Luthier v8: what makes words great

17 November 2026. Words and music: Jason Bryant. The live copy is the Doc Lyric craft for Luthier v8: what makes words great.

Summary

The songs artists and critics call greatest repeat fewer of their lines than ordinary hits (0.42 against 0.57 of lines), use plainer words and range wider in feeling. The chart rewards repetition; peers reward lines that keep moving.

  • v7 already holds the deepest lyric research in the spec, but almost all of it asks whether a lyric charted. After v7’s own language correction, what stands is chorus repetition, predictability, constraints per line, “you” as object and familiar words.

  • New research: story can now be measured (agents, events, a world), and Grammynominated country songs tell more of it than their album-mates. Songs with sad endings and fall-then-rise or rise-then-fall shapes did better in a national contest. Lyrics draw an interest of their own, apart from plays.

  • Measured on 64 greatest-list songs against 209 Hot 100 songs (1958 to 1991): fewer repeated lines (the one result that survives a strict correction), fewer rare words, a wider range of feeling, more absolutes. A crude story proxy did not separate them.

  • Songs 52 to 56: unusually concrete and varied words, a strength. Songs 54 and 55 repeat too few lines even by the peers’ standard, and songs 53, 55 and 56 hold a narrow range of feeling.

  • For v8: seven rules (section 5): repetition between the two channels’ medians, carried by the chorus; a range of feeling with the arc printed; low endings offered; a story dial for story styles; plain words; absolutes allowed; concreteness kept as style.

1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7’s lyric research is the deepest in the spec: more than a dozen windows on 15,941 lyrics, tested against the chart, against songs that lasted and against the hymnal. Two gaps remain. Almost every test asked whether a lyric charted, never whether people who judge songs think it is good, and nothing measures story.

Area in v7 What it found Standing after v7’s own correction (Windows 64 and 65)
Repetition (Window 27) Chorus type-token ratio 0.23 against the verse’s 0.575; hits repeat more even in verses Stands
Predictability (Window 58) Hits are more predictable word by word; inside the chart, bigger hits more so Stands, weaker
Constraints per line (Window 59) A line held by rhyme, metre, repetition and a concrete act lasts; about 1.5 constraints a line in every lasting form Stands on persistence and the hymnal
Address (Windows 31, 34) “You” as the object of a line, from Packard and Berger Rests on their experiments
Common words (Window 34) Familiar words are sung more intelligibly Rests on Johnson, Huron and Collister; the chart signal fell to chance
Concreteness and the senses (Windows 32, 91) Plain concreteness null; hits lean on body words, songs that last on visual words Stands, as a dial
Meaning (Window 60) Hits range in meaning; the title’s company changes by the last chorus Chart support gone; kept as craft rules
Blending (Window 61) Remote word pairs and two-world titles Chart support gone or reversed
The quotable line (Module 10.20) Lines ranked against each other; the writer’s blind picks as the label Stands
The writing room (Modules 10.10 to 10.16, 28) Story questions, twelve candidates by named moves, coaching, never-say lists, the mouth test Process, not tested against an outcome

What the recent songs needed

Songs 52 to 56 were written from Jason’s own poems and stories, so the writing room’s coaching and the mouth test did most of the work. What no rule told them is how much story a song should tell, where its feeling should end, and how its words compare with songs that musicians and critics call great.

2. The academic record

Since v7’s lyric windows, the research has moved to three things v7 never measured: story, the emotional arc, and judgements by peers rather than sales. All three point the same way: what peers reward in words is not simply what charts reward.

Story

Narrativity, measured. Bamman and colleagues scored lyrics on three axes (particular agents, events in sequence, an inhabitable world) and trained a model that matches human ratings closely (Spearman 0.84; frontier language models managed 0.53 to 0.59). In 5,745 Billboard year-end hits, mean narrativity rose from 2.58 to 3.72 between 1960 and 2024, led by hip hop (4.01) and country (3.43); disco and soul were lowest (Bamman et al. 2025).

  • Peers reward it in country. Grammy-nominated Best Country songs scored 3.61 against 3.40 for non-nominated songs from the same album (n = 259, p = 0.002). Song of the Year nominees scored 4.2% higher, at the edge of significance; rock, R&B and rap showed no gap.

  • What carries it. Past-tense verbs, time words, places and concrete objects; firstperson pronouns alone predicted nothing.

  • The arc. In 12,280 lyrics and 2,823 greatest hits, songs set the stage early, move the plot steadily and peak in internal tension in the middle. Country and rap set the scene in more detail; pop moves faster and holds more conflict (Alberhasky and Durkee 2024).

The emotional arc

In a German national song contest (176 songs, 2005 to 2015), songs with sad endings drew more points than happy endings (4.06 against 3.35 on a 0 to 12 scale), and higher emotional peaks drew fewer. Of the classic story shapes, “man in a hole” (fall, then rise) and “Icarus” (rise, then fall) did best (Rösch and Rauch 2025). Correlational, one contest, but the only outcome study of lyric arcs.

What changed in the words

Across 353,320 English lyrics from 1970 to 2020, lyrics became simpler, more repetitive, more negative and more personal. People’s views of the lyrics on Genius behave differently from their listening counts, so lyrics hold an interest of their own (Parada- Cabaleiro et al. 2024).

Already in v7 and still standing

Chorus repetition and the chart (Nunes, Ordanini and Valsesia 2015), “you” as the object of the line (Packard and Berger 2020), moderate topic atypicality (Berger and Packard 2018), constraints per line (Rubin), familiar words for sung intelligibility (Johnson, Huron and Collister 2014), and concrete object words as the mark of professional poems (Kao and Jurafsky). This study does not repeat them.

4. Measured: greatest-list songs against ordinary hits

The songs artists and critics call greatest repeat fewer of their lines than ordinary hits, use fewer rare words, and swing wider in feeling from line to line. Story features did not separate them.

CoCoPops transcribes, as sung, 64 songs from Rolling Stone’s 500 Greatest Songs and 209 songs from a random sample of the Hot 100, both from 1958 to 1991 and by the same project (studies/lyrics). Lines were cut by one rule for both: a gap of half a beat, a word held two beats, or a new section. Each comparison is shuffled within decades to control for era.

Measure Greatest (median) Hot 100 (median) AUC (greatest higher above 0.5) p within decade
Repeated lines (share of lines sung more than once) 0.42 0.57 0.37 0.001
Rare content words (Zipf under 3) 3.2% 4.8% 0.41 0.03
Feeling’s range across lines (spread of line valence) 0.26 0.22 0.60 0.02
Absolutes per line (always, never, forever) 0.054 0.034 0.60 0.01
Words per line 4.4 3.8 0.62 0.003
Proper nouns per 100 words 0.6 1.2 0.42 0.06
“You” per word 0.031 0.047 0.43 0.10
Concreteness of content words 2.90 3.01 0.44 0.11
Narrativity index (past tense, time, place, names, he/she/they) −0.15 −0.08 0.45 0.25
Lexical variety, rhyme density, ending, mean valence 0.47 to 0.51 over 0.5

Twenty-four measures were compared, so only the repeated-lines result clearly survives a strict correction. The words-per-line gap may partly reflect how the two sets were encoded. The story proxy is cruder than Bamman’s model, so its null says little about story itself.

This is the music’s two-channel pattern again (Parts 7 and 12). The chart rewards repetition; the people who judge songs reward lines that keep moving. Part 30’s hook rules and this result fit together: the chorus repeats its cell and its hook phrase, and the rest of the song keeps changing.

Songs 52 to 56

Percentiles against the greatest-list songs (song 53 is read from its lyric as written, so its repetition is not comparable):

Song Repeated lines Rare words Feeling’s range Concreteness Lexical variety “You”
52 53 (0.43) 6 69 91 73 53
53 not comparable 52 6 83 67 6
54 19 (0.28) 48 41 100 97 20

Jason’s lyrics are unusually concrete and varied: four of five songs sit in the top fifth for concreteness. Songs 54 and 55 repeat fewer lines than four in five greatest-list songs, so their choruses carry too little return even by the peers’ standard. Songs 53, 55 and 56 hold a narrow range of feeling across their lines.

5. What v8 should do

v8’s writing room should aim for both channels: a chorus that returns, a song whose lines move, a wide range of feeling, and story where the style calls for it. Each rule has a check that runs on every lyric. If added to the fix list, they would follow Part 30’s numbers.

Rule What v8 does Check
L1. Repetition by channel The share of lines sung more than once sits between 0.42 (the greatest-list median) and 0.57 (the Hot 100 median). The chorus and hook phrase carry the repeats (Part 30, H2 and H3); verses do not repeat lines lyrics_our_songs.py; songs 54 and 55 (0.28, 0.27) would be raised
L2. A range of feeling Line-by-line feeling spreads at least as wide as the Hot 100 median (valence spread 0.22, aim 0.26). The arc is printed with the lyric: where it falls, where it turns, where it ends Songs 53, 55 and 56 (6th to 14th percentile) flagged
L3. Endings may land low A sad or bittersweet ending, and a fall-then-rise or rise-then-fall shape, are offered as options at the story questions; the arc is reported, not scored Report only (one contest study)
L4. A story dial For story styles (country, folk, narrative, hymn testimony), the writing room asks for agents, events in order and a place, and reports past-tense verbs, time words, places and concrete objects per 100 words Report; a narrativity model can replace the proxy later
L5. Plain words Rare content words at most about 4% (greatest-list median 3.2%), which also serves sung intelligibility (v7’s familiarity rule) Already near for all five songs
L6. Absolutes allowed Remove the verse penalty v7 keeps on always, never and forever (Window 34); greatest-list songs use more of them Module 28’s imagery term
L7. Keep the concreteness Jason’s concreteness is a strength, not a lever; leave it as a style dial (v7, Window 91) None

Tests for v8

  1. Songs 52 to 56 rerun on lyrics_our_songs.py: repeated lines within L1’s band (song 53 read as sung), feeling’s range at or above 0.22.

  2. Every lyric prints its arc, its story readings and its repetition against both medians.

  3. A blind pick by Jason between a v7 lyric revision and an L1 to L4 revision of one song, his choice logged.
